Eyes and their adnexae function normally
Is not suffering from any safety-relevant pathological condition (either acute or chronic), nor any sequelae of surgery or trauma
Has a distant visual acuity of 6/9 or better in each eye separately and 6/6 or better binocular (with or without correcting lenses)

Can read (with or without correcting lenses) an N5 chart (or its equivalent) binocularly at a distance that he or she selects (in the range of 30 to 50 centimetres), and can read an N14 chart binocularly (with or without correcting lenses) at a distance of 1 metre Note: A person who needs correcting lenses to meet this criterion must have the appropriate lenses available while carrying out duties under a relevant licence—see regulation 67.200.
Has a near point of accommodation no further away than 30 centimetres (with or without correcting lenses)

If using contact lenses to meet the visual standards set out in items 3.29 to 3.35: (a) is able to wear those lenses for twice the projected length of duty time for the person without deterioration in visual acuity or discomfort; and (b) if the lenses are of the hard or gas-permeable variety, demonstrates the ability, immediately after removing the lenses, to read at least 6/9 with spectacles binocularly

Can readily distinguish the colours that need to be distinguished for the safe exercise of privileges, or performance of duties, under the relevant licence Note: For how to demonstrate this, see subregulation 67.160(6).

section.heading: Directions about examinations for issue of medical certificates

content.p: If CASA has reason to believe that an applicant for the issue of a medical certificate has a condition (including a condition other than a medical condition) that may, if he or she is issued the medical certificate, endanger the safety of air navigation, CASA may direct the applicant to do either or both of the following:

submit to an examination carried out by a medical practitioner, specialist psychiatrist, clinical psychologist, audiologist, optometrist, orthoptist, orthotist, occupational therapist, specialist prosthetist or a practitioner of another kind specified in the direction;
submit to an examination or test by a person (not necessarily a medical practitioner) expert in the safe performance of the particular activity in respect of which the medical certificate is sought.
For paragraph (1)(a), CASA may nominate a particular practitioner, of a kind mentioned or referred to in that paragraph, who is to carry out the examination.
For paragraph (1)(b), CASA may nominate a particular person who is expert in the safe performance of the activity concerned to carry out the examination.
If a person submits to a relevant examination by a DAME or DAO, the DAME or DAO must ask the person to produce evidence of his or her identity before finishing the examination.
The evidence must include a photograph of the person.
Example: The identification might take the form of a passport or any of the following that includes a photograph: a driver’s licence, a workplace identification document, a student’s identity card.
However, subregulation (1) does not require the DAME or DAO to ask the person to produce the evidence if the DAME or DAO knows or reasonably believes the person is who the person claims to be.

If the DAME or DAO has asked the person to produce evidence of his or her identity under subregulation (1), the DAME or DAO may refuse to carry out, or finish, the examination until the person produces the evidence.
A person may apply to CASA for the issue of a medical certificate.

Note 1: An application must be in the approved form, include all the information required by these Regulations and be accompanied by every document required by these Regulations—see regulation 11.030.
Note 2: Part 11 deals with applications and decision making.

Subject to subregulation (7) and regulation 11.055, on receiving an application under regulation 67.175, CASA must issue a medical certificate to the applicant if the applicant meets the requirements of subregulation (2).
For subregulation (1), the requirements are:
the applicant has undergone any relevant examinations that, in the opinion of CASA, are necessary in the particular case; and
each relevant examination has been carried out by an examiner to whom subregulation (4) applies; and

for each relevant examination, the applicant answers every question asked by the examiner that the examiner considers necessary to help CASA to decide whether the applicant meets the relevant medical standard; and
subject to subregulation (5), the applicant authorises the disclosure to CASA and the examiner of any information or documents about the applicant:
that are held by a person, organisation, body or authority mentioned in subregulation (6); and
that may help CASA to decide whether the applicant meets the relevant medical standard; and
either:
the applicant meets the relevant medical standard; or
if the applicant does not meet that medical standard—the extent to which he or she does not meet the standard is not likely to endanger the safety of air navigation; and
if, in addition to any relevant examinations that the applicant has undergone under paragraph (a), CASA has directed the applicant to undergo an examination under subregulation 67.165(1):
the applicant has undergone that examination; and
having taken into account the result of the examination, CASA is satisfied that issuing a medical certificate to the applicant would not endanger the safety of air navigation.

Note 1: The routine examinations that an applicant for the issue of a medical certificate must undergo to establish whether he or she meets the relevant medical standard for the certificate are those set out in the Designated Aviation Medical Examiner’s Handbook.
Note 2: Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 operates to prevent any requirement to disclose a spent conviction. For details, see that Part.
Note 3: A false statement in relation to the issue of a certificate is an offence punishable by imprisonment for 12 months—see the Criminal Code, section 137.1.

Note 4: A person may not meet any of the medical standards if the person has a history of ‘problematic use of substances’—see items 1.5 and 1.6 of table 67.150, items 2.5 and 2.6 of table 67.155 and items 3.5 and 3.6 of table 67.160.
Note 5: For the period for which a medical certificate remains in force, see regulation 67.205.
This subregulation applies to an applicant:
(a) whose medical certificate (the old certificate) has expired; and
who:
applies to CASA for the issue of a new medical certificate within 3 months after the old certificate expired; and
in the opinion of CASA, is not required to undergo any relevant examinations for the issue of the new certificate.

Note: If a medical certificate is issued to an applicant referred to in subregulation (3), the medical certificate remains in force for the period (which must not be longer than 2 months) set out in the certificate—see subregulation 67.205(4).
This subregulation applies to the following persons:
a DAME;
a DAO;
a specialist medical practitioner, or any other medical practitioner, who CASA has directed may carry out medical examinations for the purposes of subregulation (2);
if CASA has directed that the applicant be assessed by a specialist psychiatrist or clinical psychologist—the psychiatrist or psychologist who carried out the assessment;

if CASA has directed that the applicant be assessed by an audiologist, optometrist, orthoptist, orthotist, occupational therapist, specialist prosthetist, or similar practitioner—the practitioner who carried out the assessment;

if CASA has directed that the applicant be assessed by a person (not necessarily a medical practitioner) expert in the safe performance of the particular activity in respect of which the medical certificate is sought—the person who carried out the assessment.
An authorisation under paragraph (2)(d) does not require a person, organisation, body or authority to disclose:
information or a document that was collected for use as evidence in a legal proceeding, and has not been tendered or admitted as evidence in a court; or
(b) information or a document that could not, because of Part 3.10 of the Evidence Act 1995, be given in evidence in a proceeding to which that Part applies.

Note: Part 3.10 of the Evidence Act 1995 is about: client legal privilege; religious confessions; self-incrimination in other proceedings; and evidence excluded in the public interest. For details, see that Act.
For paragraph (2)(d), the persons, organisations, bodies or authorities are as follows:
a medical practitioner;
any other person or organisation (including a hospital) that has made a physical, psychological or psychiatric examination of the applicant;
any other person or organisation (including a hospital) that has treated the applicant for a medically significant condition;
an employer (including a former employer) of the applicant;

(e) any other person, organisation, body or authority (including a police force or police service and, subject to Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914, a court) that holds information or a document of the kind referred to in paragraph (2)(d).
CASA must not issue a medical certificate to an applicant if it is satisfied that the applicant:
has knowingly or recklessly made a false or misleading statement in relation to the application for the medical certificate; or
does not satisfy the requirements of this regulation; or
has not, in the course of undergoing a relevant examination for the medical certificate, complied with a request made under subregulation 67.170(1).

A medical certificate issued to an applicant who does not meet the relevant medical standard for the issue of the certificate, or to whom subparagraph (2)(f)(ii) applies, must bear a note of that fact.

The fact that an applicant who does not meet the relevant medical standard in all respects has previously been issued with a medical certificate under subparagraph (2)(e)(ii) or (f)(ii) does not automatically entitle him or her to the issue of a further such medical certificate.

section.heading: Notice of decision to refuse medical certificate

content.p: If:
CASA refuses to issue a medical certificate to a person; and
the reasons for the refusal included that the person failed to meet the relevant medical standard;
the notice given to the person under regulation 11.060 must state the respects in which the person did not meet the standard.
Failure to comply with subregulation (1) in relation to a decision does not affect the validity of the decision.

section.heading: Reconsideration of decision to refuse medical certificate

content.p: A person to whom CASA has refused to issue a medical certificate, or to whom CASA has issued a medical certificate subject to a condition not sought by the person, may apply to CASA in writing for reconsideration of the decision.
The application must be made within 21 days after the day when the person is told by CASA, in writing, that it:
has refused to issue a medical certificate to the person; or
has issued a medical certificate subject to a condition not sought by the person.
The reconsideration of an application submitted to CASA must not be carried out solely by the CASA officer who made the decision being reconsidered.
Note: A refusal to issue a medical certificate is reviewable by the Administrative Review Tribunal—see the Act, section 31 and regulation 201.004.
Without limiting regulations 11.056 and 11.067, CASA may issue a medical certificate subject to a condition that the period during which the certificate remains in force may be extended only by CASA.

section.heading: Conditions applicable to certain medical certificates—correcting lenses

content.p: In addition to any other condition imposed by or under this Part or Part 11, a medical certificate issued to a person who needs correcting lenses to satisfy the requirements of item 1.36 of table 67.150, item 2.36 of table 67.155 or item 3.34 of table 67.160 is subject to the conditions set out in subregulations (2) and (4).
The person must have those correcting lenses available for use while exercising the privileges of a licence for which the certificate is required.

If the person is the holder of, or an applicant for, a licence for which he or she is required to meet medical standard 1 or 2, the correcting lenses may be a pair of spectacles or a combination of contact lenses and a pair of spectacles.

A person to whom subregulation (3) applies must have within reach, while he or she is performing duties essential to the operation of an Australian aircraft during flight time, a spare pair of spectacles for each pair of correcting lenses that he or she requires to meet the relevant medical standard.
The holder of a medical certificate that is subject to a condition set out in subregulation (2) or (4) must not contravene the condition.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An offence against subregulation (5) is an offence of strict liability.
In this regulation:
appropriate day means:
for a medical certificate issued to a person who:
has never held a medical certificate, or a person who has previously held a medical certificate that has expired; and
has undergone any relevant examinations required for the purpose of the issue of the certificate;
the day when the last relevant examination is completed; and
for a new medical certificate issued to a person:
(i) who holds a medical certificate that is in force (the current certificate); and
who has undergone any relevant examinations required for the purpose of the issue of the new certificate; and
whose last relevant examination is completed more than 28 days before his or her current certificate is due to expire;
the day when the examination is completed; and
for a new medical certificate issued to a person:
(i) who holds a medical certificate that is in force (the current certificate); and
who has undergone any relevant examinations required for the purpose of the issue of the new certificate; and
whose last relevant examination is completed 28 or fewer days before his or her current certificate is due to expire;
the day when the current certificate is due to expire.
Example 1: A person who has never held a medical certificate has an examination for the issue of a medical certificate on 1 January 2003. The appropriate day for the certificate is 1 January 2003.

Example 2: A person who holds a medical certificate that is due to expire on 1 January 2004 has an examination for a new certificate on 1 November 2003. The appropriate day for the new certificate is 1 November 2003.

Example 3: A person who holds a medical certificate that is due to expire on 1 January 2004 has an examination for a new certificate on 20 December 2003. The appropriate day for the new certificate is 1 January 2004.

Example 4: A person who held a medical certificate that expired on 1 January 2003 has an examination for a new certificate on 1 March 2003. The appropriate day for the new certificate is 1 March 2003.
A medical certificate comes into force:

if the holder has undergone any relevant examinations required for the purpose of the issue of the certificate and complies with the relevant medical standard in all respects—on the certificate’s appropriate day; or
in any other case—on the day when the certificate is issued.

Subject to subregulation (6) and regulations 67.215 and 67.220, a medical certificate issued by CASA to a person who has undergone any relevant examinations required for the purpose of the issue of the certificate remains in force for the period set out in the certificate, being a period of not more than:
in the case of a class 1 medical certificate—1 year after the day when the certificate comes into force; and
in the case of a class 2 medical certificate:
if the person is less than 40 years old when the certificate is issued to him or her—4 years after the day when the certificate comes into force; or
if the person is 40 years old or older when the certificate is issued to him or her—2 years after the day when the certificate comes into force; and
in the case of a class 3 medical certificate—2 years after the day when the certificate comes into force.

Subject to subregulation (6) and regulations 67.215 and 67.220, a medical certificate issued by CASA to a person who has not been required to undergo any relevant examinations for the purpose of the issue of the certificate remains in force for the period (which must not be longer than 2 months) set out in the certificate.
Subject to subregulation (6), a medical certificate issued by a DAME remains in force for the period (which must not be longer than 2 months) set out in the certificate.

If a new medical certificate is issued to a person who holds a current medical certificate, and the new certificate comes into force before the current certificate is due to expire, the current certificate ceases to be in force at the last moment of the day before the day when the new certificate comes into force.

section.heading: Medical certificates—application for extension of period in force

content.p: The holder of a current medical certificate issued by CASA may apply for an extension of the period during which the medical certificate remains in force.
The application may be made to:
CASA; or
if the certificate is not subject to a condition to the effect that the period during which the certificate remains in force may be extended only by CASA—a DAME.

section.heading: Medical certificates—extension of period in force by CASA

content.p: If, on receiving an application under regulation 67.210 for an extension of the period during which a current medical certificate remains in force, CASA is satisfied that extending the period will not adversely affect the safety of air navigation, CASA may extend the period by:
entering the period of the extension on the certificate; or
giving to the holder of the certificate a written notice setting out the period of the extension.

An extension by CASA of the period during which the certificate remains in force must not be for longer than 1 year after the day when the certificate would expire if the period had not been extended.

section.heading: Medical certificates—extension of period in force by DAMEs

content.p: A DAME must, on receiving an application under regulation 67.210 for an extension of the period during which a current medical certificate remains in force:
deal with the application in accordance with the Designated Aviation Medical Examiner’s Handbook; and
extend the period only if the DAME is satisfied that this will not adversely affect the safety of air navigation.
If the DAME extends the period during which a medical certificate remains in force, the DAME must:
enter the period of the extension on the certificate; or
give to the holder of the certificate a written notice setting out the period of the extension.
A medical certificate may be extended by a DAME only once.

An extension by a DAME of the period during which the certificate remains in force must not be for longer than 2 months after the day when the certificate would expire if the period had not been extended.

section.heading: Medical certificates—new medical certificates issued by DAMEs

content.p: A person whose medical certificate has expired may apply to a DAME for the issue of a medical certificate under this regulation if the medical certificate:
was issued by CASA; and
was not subject to a condition that the period during which the certificate remains in force may be extended only by CASA.
An application must be made within 3 months after the medical certificate has expired.
On receiving an application under subregulation (1), a DAME must:
deal with it in accordance with the Designated Aviation Medical Examiner’s Handbook; and
subject to this regulation, issue a new medical certificate to the applicant only if satisfied that:

the applicant has, subject to subregulation (5), authorised the disclosure of his or her medical information and documents to the DAME, being information and documents held by any of the persons, organisations, bodies or authorities mentioned in subregulation (6); and
issuing the medical certificate to the applicant will not adversely affect the safety of air navigation.

Note: If a medical certificate is issued to a person by a DAME, the medical certificate remains in force for the period (which must not be longer than 2 months) set out in the certificate—see subregulation 67.205(5).
The DAME must not issue a medical certificate to the applicant if the DAME is satisfied that the applicant:
has knowingly or recklessly made a false or misleading statement in relation to the application for the medical certificate; or
does not satisfy the requirements of this regulation; or
has not, in the course of undergoing a relevant examination for the medical certificate, complied with a request made under subregulation 67.170(1).
An authorisation under subparagraph (3)(b)(i) does not require a person, organisation, body or authority to disclose:
information or a document that was collected for use as evidence in a legal proceeding, and has not been tendered or admitted as evidence in a court; or
(b) information or a document that could not, because of Part 3.10 of the Evidence Act 1995, be given in evidence in a proceeding to which that Part applies.

Note: Part 3.10 of the Evidence Act 1995 is about: client legal privilege; religious confessions; self-incrimination in other proceedings; and evidence excluded in the public interest. For details, see that Act.
For subparagraph (3)(b)(i), the persons, organisations, bodies or authorities are as follows:
a medical practitioner;
any other person or organisation (including a hospital) that has made a physical, psychological or psychiatric examination of the applicant;
any other person or organisation (including a hospital) that has treated the applicant for a medically significant condition;
an employer (including a former employer) of the applicant;

(e) any other person, organisation, body or authority (including a police force or police service and, subject to Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914, a court) that holds information or a document of the kind referred to in subparagraph (3)(b)(i).

section.heading: CASA may require medical examination of certificate holders

content.p: If it is necessary, in the interests of the safety of air navigation, for the holder of a medical certificate to demonstrate:
that he or she continues to meet the relevant medical standard; or
that holding the certificate does not adversely affect the safety of air navigation;
CASA may direct the holder to do any 1 or more of the following:

submit to an examination carried out by a medical practitioner, specialist psychiatrist, clinical psychologist, audiologist, optometrist, orthoptist, orthotist, occupational therapist, specialist prosthetist or a practitioner of another kind specified in the direction;
submit to an examination or test by a person (not necessarily a medical practitioner) expert in the safe performance of the particular activity to which the medical certificate relates;

authorise the disclosure to CASA of any information or document about the holder, held by a person, organisation, body or authority referred to in subregulation (4), that may help CASA to decide whether:
the holder continues to meet that medical standard; or
the holder’s holding the certificate may adversely affect the safety of air navigation.
For paragraph (1)(c), CASA may nominate a particular practitioner, of a kind mentioned or referred to in that paragraph, who is to carry out the examination.
For paragraph (1)(d), CASA may nominate a particular person who is expert in the performance of the activity concerned to carry out the examination.
For paragraph (1)(e), the persons, organisations, bodies and authorities are as follows:

a medical practitioner, specialist psychiatrist, clinical psychologist, audiologist, optometrist, orthoptist, orthotist, occupational therapist, specialist prosthetist or similar practitioner who has examined or treated the holder;
any other person or organisation (including a hospital) that has made a physical, psychological or psychiatric examination of the holder;
any other person or organisation (including a hospital) that has treated the holder for a medically significant condition;
an employer (including a former employer) of the holder;

(e) any other person, organisation, body or authority (including a police force or police service and, subject to Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914, a court) that holds information or a document relevant to deciding whether the person’s holding the certificate may adversely affect the safety of air navigation.
A medical certificate held by a pregnant woman who holds, or is an applicant for, a licence is taken to be suspended:

during the period beginning immediately after the end of the 30th week of gestation and ending when a DAME certifies that she is fully recovered following delivery or the termination of the pregnancy; or
if in a particular case CASA directs in writing that a different period should apply—during the period so directed by CASA; or

if, before the start of the period mentioned in paragraph (a), the pregnancy ends in miscarriage or premature labour, or is terminated by medical intervention—from the time of the miscarriage, premature labour or intervention until a DAME certifies that the woman is fully recovered.
Note: This regulation does not preclude a pilot who is pregnant from undertaking or receiving instruction in a flight simulator at any stage of the pilot’s pregnancy.
Despite subregulation (1), a pregnant woman who holds an ATC licence may continue to exercise the privileges of the licence until the end of the 38th week of gestation if:
the medical practitioner who is attending the woman certifies her continued medical fitness to do so each week beginning at the 31st week of gestation; and
a DAME certifies the woman’s continuing fitness to do so each week beginning at the 31st week of gestation; and
another person who holds an ATC licence, and is medically fit and able to take over responsibility for the function, is on duty and available at the times when she does so.

If CASA directs the holder of a medical certificate to submit to an examination under regulation 67.230, or to authorise the disclosure of information to CASA under that regulation, CASA may, in writing, suspend the medical certificate.
If CASA suspends a medical certificate, CASA must give the holder of the certificate written notice of the suspension and of the reasons for the suspension.
A suspension of a medical certificate takes effect when the holder of the certificate is told of the suspension, either orally or in writing.
If:
CASA suspends a medical certificate; and
the holder of the certificate submits to an examination or test directed by CASA, or authorises the disclosure of information to CASA; and
the examination, test or information shows that:
the holder meets the relevant medical standard; and
the continued holding of the certificate by the holder will not adversely affect the safety of air navigation;
CASA must:
end the suspension; and
tell the holder in writing that the suspension has ended.
If:
CASA suspends a medical certificate; and
the holder of the certificate submits to an examination or test directed by CASA, or authorises the disclosure of information to CASA; and
the examination, test or information shows either or both of the following:
the holder fails to meet the relevant medical standard;
the continued holding of the certificate by the holder will adversely affect the safety of air navigation;
CASA must tell the holder in writing the respect in which the holder does not meet the medical standard.

section.heading: Suspension of medical certificates—special arrangements for service in urgent cases

content.p: If there is reason to believe in a particular case that:
the holding of a medical certificate by a person may seriously and adversely affect the safety of air navigation; and
it is necessary, in the interests of the safety of air navigation, to suspend the certificate immediately; and
the person is likely to attempt to evade service on him or her of the notice of suspension;
CASA may give the notice to the person in any way by which it is likely to be quickly brought to the person’s attention.

In particular, if no other method of giving the notice is practicable in the circumstances, the notice may be given by fixing it in a prominent position to an aircraft that the person is likely to fly.
A notice that is fixed to an aircraft is taken to have been given to the person at the time it is fixed to the aircraft.
If CASA suspends a medical certificate, its holder is taken not to be the holder of a medical certificate during the period of the suspension.

section.heading: Medical certificates—cancellation if medical standard not met

content.p: If, after undergoing an examination for the purposes of regulation 67.180 or under regulation 67.230, the holder of a medical certificate fails to meet the relevant medical standard for the certificate (or, in the case of a person who did not, at the time the certificate was issued, meet the standard in all respects, fails to meet the standard in an additional respect), CASA must:
by written notice given to the holder, cancel the certificate; and

if CASA is satisfied that the holding of a medical certificate by the holder will not adversely affect the safety of air navigation—issue to the holder a medical certificate that is subject to any conditions that are necessary in the interests of the safety of air navigation.
CASA must include in the notice the reasons for the holder’s failure to meet the relevant medical standard.

section.heading: Medical certificates—cancellation and suspension in other cases

content.p: CASA may, by written notice given to the holder of a medical certificate, cancel the certificate, or suspend it for a specified period, if there are reasonable grounds for believing that the holder:
has contravened a condition to which the certificate is subject; or
has contravened subregulation 67.265(3) or (4); or
has failed to comply with a direction under regulation 67.230.
A notice must set out the grounds for the cancellation or suspension.
Before cancelling or suspending a medical certificate, CASA must:

give a show cause notice to the holder of the certificate of the facts and circumstances that, in the opinion of CASA, justify consideration being given to the cancellation or suspension of the certificate; and

allow the holder to show cause (within the time CASA sets out in that notice, being a period of not less than 14 days after the notice was given), why the certificate should not be cancelled or suspended.
Subpart 67.D—Modified Austroads medical standards

section.heading: Definition of meets the modified Austroads medical standards

content.p: Unconditional licence under the private vehicle driver standards
(1) A person meets the modified Austroads medical standards if the person is fit to hold an unconditional licence under the modified Austroads medical standards.
Conditional licence under the private vehicle driver standards
(2) Also, a person meets the modified Austroads medical standards if all of the following apply to the person:
the person is fit to hold a conditional licence under the modified Austroads medical standards;

under the standards, the only reason that the person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence is because the person’s uncorrected visual acuity does not meet the standard for the issue of an unconditional licence;
the person’s visual acuity is corrected by lenses to at least 6/12 in one eye and at least 6/18 in the other eye.

section.heading: Definition of modified Austroads medical standards for Subpart 67.D

content.p: In this Subpart:

modified Austroads medical standards means the private vehicle driver standards in the Austroads medical standards modified to provide that a person with a medical history or condition mentioned in subregulation (2) does not meet the standards.
For subregulation (1), the medical histories and conditions are the following:
subject to subregulation (3)—a history of cancer within the 5-year period before the day the privileges of the licence are exercised;
a history of ECG changes, with or without symptoms;
subject to subregulation (4)—a history of heart failure;
inability to hear a conversational speaking voice at a distance of 2 metres, whether unaided or with the assistance of a medically prescribed hearing aid;

any musculoskeletal disability, disorder or disease of the bones, joints, muscles or tendons that would limit or restrict the normal manipulation of aircraft controls, or would require physical modifications to the aircraft to enable appropriate manipulation of the controls;
a history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke;
a history of multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy or Parkinson’s disease;
a history of one or more of the following in relation to a head injury:
loss of consciousness;
post-traumatic amnesia;
abnormal findings on head CT or MRI investigation;
a history of renal colic or calculi;
active vertigo or a history of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
For paragraph (2)(a), a history of cancer for a person does not include a history of basal cell skin cancers if:
each basal cell skin cancer has been treated by excision with no metastasised sequelae; and

(b) since at least the last occurrence of a basal cell skin cancer, the person has been under active and continuous case management by a medical practitioner who is a specialist oncology physician or surgeon (the treating practitioner); and

the person is assessed for the issue of a recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificate by the treating practitioner or, if the treating practitioner is not available, by another medical practitioner with knowledge of the person’s basal cell skin cancer history.
For paragraph (2)(c), a history of heart failure for a person does not include a history in which the person meets all of the following requirements:
the person has not had an episode of heart failure for at least the previous 3 years;

(b) since at least the last episode of heart failure, the person has been under active and continuous case management by a medical practitioner who is a specialist cardiovascular physician or surgeon (the treating practitioner);

the person is assessed for the issue of a recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificate by the treating practitioner or, if the treating practitioner is not available, by another medical practitioner with knowledge of the person’s history of heart failure.
In this regulation:

Austroads medical standards means the medical standards set out in the publication Assessing fitness to drive for commercial and private vehicle drivers, published by Austroads in March 2012, or any later version, as in force from time to time.
Subpart 67.E—Responsibilities of holders of medical certificates and recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificates
Note: The text of the standards could in 2013 be viewed on Austroads’ website (www.austroads.com.au/assessing-fitness-to-drive/).

section.heading: Obligation to tell CASA of changes in medical condition—medical certificate holders

content.p: This regulation applies in relation to the following licences:
a flight crew licence;
a balloon flight crew licence within the meaning of subregulation 5.01(1) of CAR;
an ATC licence.
(2) In this regulation, a reference to a DAME includes, in relation to a medically significant condition that affects a person’s vision, a DAO.
If:
the holder of a class 1 medical certificate and a licence:
knows that he or she has a medically significant condition; and
is reckless as to whether the condition has been disclosed to CASA; and
the condition continues for longer than 7 days; and
the condition has the result that his or her ability to do an act authorised by the licence is impaired;
he or she must tell CASA or a DAME about the condition as soon as practicable after the end of the 7 days.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If:
the holder of a class 2 or class 3 medical certificate and a licence:
knows that he or she has a medically significant condition; and
is reckless as to whether the condition has been disclosed to CASA; and
the condition continues for longer than 30 days; and
the condition has the result that his or her ability to do an act authorised by the licence is impaired;
he or she must tell CASA or a DAME about the condition as soon as practicable after the end of the 30 days.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If the holder of a medical certificate and a licence:
knows that he or she has a medically significant condition; and
is reckless as to whether the condition has been disclosed to CASA; and
the condition has the result that his or her ability to do an act authorised by the licence is impaired;
he or she must not do the act until a DAME certifies that the holder can safely do such acts.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

Note: If the holder of a medical certificate tells a DAME about a medically significant condition, and the condition is safety-relevant, the DAME must tell CASA in writing of that fact within 5 working days—see regulation 67.125.

It is a defence to a prosecution under subregulation (5) that, in the circumstances, the relevant act was a reasonable measure to save life (including the holder’s own life) or avoid damage to property.

section.heading: Offence—doing act while efficiency impaired—licence holders

content.p: This regulation applies in relation to the following licences:
a flight crew licence;
a balloon flight crew licence within the meaning of subregulation 5.01(1) of CAR;
an ATC licence.
The holder commits an offence if:
the holder does an act authorised by the licence; and
at the time of doing the act:
the holder knows that he or she has a medically significant condition; and
the condition has the result that the holder’s ability to do the act is impaired.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Class 1 medical certificates
The holder commits an offence if:
the holder does an act authorised by the licence; and
the holder knows that he or she has had a condition mentioned in paragraph (2)(b); and
the holder’s normal ability to do the act is not fully restored within 7 days after the holder first becomes aware that he or she had the condition; and
the holder is authorised to do the act only if the holder also holds a class 1 medical certificate; and
the holder has not been given a certificate by a DAME to the effect that the holder’s normal ability to do the act is no longer impaired.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Class 2 and 3 medical certificates
The holder commits an offence if:
the holder does an act authorised by the licence; and
the holder knows that he or she has had a condition mentioned in paragraph (2)(b); and
the holder’s normal ability to do the act is not fully restored within 30 days after the holder first becomes aware that he or she had the condition; and
the holder is authorised to do the act only if the holder also holds a class 1, 2 or 3 medical certificate; and
the holder has not been given a certificate by a DAME to the effect that the holder’s normal ability to do the act is no longer impaired.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificates
The holder commits an offence if:
the holder does an act authorised by the licence; and
the holder knows that he or she has had a condition mentioned in paragraph (2)(b); and
the holder’s normal ability to do the act is not fully restored within 30 days after the holder first becomes aware that he or she had the condition; and
the holder is authorised to do the act only if the holder also holds a class 1, 2 or 3 medical certificate or a recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificate; and
the holder does not meet the requirement in subregulation (6).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
For paragraph (5)(e), the requirement is that:
the holder has been given a certificate by a DAME to the effect that the holder’s normal ability to do the act is no longer impaired; or
if the holder held a recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificate at the time the holder had the condition—the holder is:
assessed by a medical practitioner as meeting the modified Austroads medical standards after having the condition; and
given a certificate by the medical practitioner to that effect.
Note: For when a person meets the modified Austroads medical standards, see regulation 67.262.

section.heading: Offence—doing act while efficiency impaired—student pilots

content.p: A student pilot commits an offence if:
the student pilot conducts a solo flight or takes a flight test; and
at the time of the solo flight or flight test:
the student pilot knows that he or she has a medically significant condition; and
the condition has the result that the student pilot’s ability to conduct the solo flight or take the flight test is impaired.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A student pilot commits an offence if:
the student pilot conducts a solo flight or undertakes a flight test; and
the student pilot knows that he or she has had a condition mentioned in paragraph (1)(b); and

the student pilot’s normal ability to conduct the solo flight or undertake the flight test is not fully restored within 30 days after the student pilot first becomes aware that he or she had the condition; and
the student pilot does not meet the requirement in subregulation (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
For paragraph (2)(d), the requirement is that:
the student pilot has been given a certificate by a DAME to the effect that the student pilot’s ability to conduct a solo flight or undertake a flight test is no longer impaired; or
if the student pilot held a recreational aviation medical practitioner’s certificate at the time the student had the condition—the student pilot is:
assessed by a medical practitioner as meeting the modified Austroads medical standards after having the condition; and
given a certificate by the medical practitioner to that effect.
Note: For when a person meets the modified Austroads medical standards, see regulation 67.262.
CASA may require, by written notice, the holder of a medical certificate to surrender the certificate to CASA within a reasonable time specified in the notice.
The person must comply with the requirement.
Penalty: 5 penalty units.

A person who contravenes subregulation (2) is guilty of an offence in respect of each day during which the person refuses or fails to comply with the requirement, including the day of any conviction for such an offence.
The person must not destroy, mutilate or deface the certificate with intent to evade the obligation to comply with the requirement.
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
Note: This Part heading is reserved for future use.

Subpart 90.A—General
This Part sets out airworthiness requirements for an aircraft that are in addition to:
the type certification basis for the aircraft; and
any requirements for the issue of a certificate of airworthiness for the aircraft under Part 21.
Note: For the definition of type certification basis, see the Dictionary.

If a provision of this Part imposes a more stringent requirement (however described) in relation to an aircraft than a comparable requirement under any other provision of these Regulations, the more stringent requirement prevails.

Despite subregulation (1), this Part is not intended to limit any other provision of these Regulations that permits an aircraft to be operated with a defect or an inoperative instrument, indicator, item of equipment or system.
In this Part:
Class C cargo or baggage compartment has the same meaning as in FARs section 25.857, as in force from time to time.
Class D cargo or baggage compartment has the same meaning as in FARs section 25.857, as in force on 16 June 1986.
Class E cargo compartment has the same meaning as in FARs section 25.857, as in force from time to time.
emergency exit means an external door, hatch or window on an aircraft intended for use by passengers or crew in an emergency.
large aeroplane means an aeroplane with a maximum take-off weight of more than 5 700 kg.
non-transport category aeroplane means an aeroplane of a type that was originally certificated in a category other than the transport category.
operating has the meaning given by subregulation (2).
originally certificated has the meaning given by subregulation (3).
Part 90 Manual of Standards means the Manual of Standards issued by CASA under regulation 90.020.
side-facing seat, for an aircraft, means a seat that faces more than 18° from the aircraft’s longitudinal axis.
small aeroplane means an aeroplane with a maximum take-off weight of 5 700 kg or less.
transport category aeroplane means an aeroplane of a type that was originally certificated in the transport category.

(2) For this Part, an aircraft is operating from the moment at which the aircraft first moves (whether or not under its own power) for the purpose of taking off for a flight until the moment at which it comes to rest for the purpose of disembarking any persons or cargo on board after:
it lands; or
the flight is aborted.
(3) For this Part, an aircraft of a particular type is originally certificated as follows:
if the aircraft’s State of Design is Australia—when CASA first issues a type certificate in respect of an aircraft of that type;
if the aircraft’s State of Design is a foreign country—when the national aviation authority of the State of Design first issues a foreign type certificate in respect of an aircraft of that type.

section.heading: Exclusions in relation to particular provisions

content.p: The registered operator of an aircraft may apply in writing to CASA for exclusion of the aircraft, or an aeronautical product that is part of, or used in, the aircraft, from the operation of a provision of this Part.
On receiving an application, CASA may, in writing, exclude the aircraft or aeronautical product from the operation of the provision.
In making a decision under subregulation (2), CASA must:
regard as paramount the preservation of a level of aviation safety that is at least acceptable; and
have regard to any reasons given in the application.

However, CASA may exclude an aircraft or aeronautical product under subregulation (2) only if CASA is satisfied that it is not practicable for the aircraft or aeronautical product to meet the requirements of the provision.
CASA may, in an instrument of exclusion under subregulation (2), provide that the exclusion is subject to 1 or more conditions.

An instrument of exclusion under subregulation (2) applies to a particular aircraft or aeronautical product only while the registered operator of the aircraft, or the aircraft that the aeronautical product is part of, or used in, complies with each condition of the exclusion.
Note: See regulation 201.004 for review of an exclusion decision.
(1) This regulation applies if, before 1 December 2010, CASA has, under regulation 39.004, excluded (the exclusion):
a particular aircraft or aeronautical product; or
a particular kind of aircraft or aeronautical product;
from the operation of an airworthiness directive, or a requirement of an airworthiness directive, mentioned in column 2 of an item in table 90.015 (the item).

Subject to subregulation (3), the provision mentioned in column 3 of the item does not apply to an aircraft or aeronautical product that, immediately before 1 December 2010, was subject to the exclusion.

Subregulation (2) applies to a particular aircraft or aeronautical product only while the registered operator of the aircraft, or the aircraft that the aeronautical product is part of, or used in, continues to comply with each condition of the exclusion.
Note: On 1 December 2010, the airworthiness directives mentioned in table 90.015 were cancelled.

p.b: Provisions covered by exclusions relating to each airworthiness directive

content.p: For the purposes of subsection 98(5A) of the Act, CASA may issue a Manual of Standards for this Part prescribing matters:
required or permitted by these Regulations to be prescribed by the Part 90 Manual of Standards; or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Part.
In particular, the Part 90 Manual of Standards may set out matters relating to the airworthiness of, or design standards for, aircraft, including standards for the following:
cabin crew seats and related equipment;
escape devices;
access to emergency exits;
interior and exterior emergency exit marking;
interior and exterior emergency lighting;
floor proximity emergency escape paths;
over-wing escape routes;
materials used in the interior of cabins;
symbols identifying emergency exits;
landing gear aural warning systems and associated devices.
Note: Subpart 11.J sets out procedures for the issue, amendment and revocation of a Manual of Standards.
Subpart 90.B—General provisions
This Subpart applies to aircraft other than the following:
balloons;
airships;
sailplanes;
powered sailplanes;
an aircraft for which any of the following is in force:
a special certificate of airworthiness mentioned in regulation 21.186, 21.189 or 21.190;
an experimental certificate;
a special flight permit;
a provisional certificate of airworthiness.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aircraft is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

For a large aeroplane that was originally certificated on or after 1 January 1958, each seat in the flight crew compartment must be fitted with an approved safety harness that meets the requirements in subregulations (4) and (6).
For any other aircraft, each seat that is:
a flight crew seat; or
a seat in the front row of seats in the aircraft’s cockpit;
must be fitted with an approved safety harness that meets the requirements in subregulations (5) and (6).
For subregulation (2), the safety harness must consist of:
an approved symmetrical type harness; or
a single shoulder strap harness that was approved and installed before 6 March 1980; or
for an aircraft of a type prescribed by the Part 90 Manual of Standards—a single shoulder strap harness.
For subregulation (3), the safety harness must consist of a lap belt and at least 1 shoulder strap.
For subregulations (2) and (3), the safety harness must:
allow any flight crew member who is occupying the seat and has the harness correctly fastened to perform his or her functions; and
when not in use, be able to be secured so it does not:
prevent the proper operation of the aircraft; or
hinder a person in the aircraft if he or she must leave the aircraft in an emergency.
Source FARs sections 91.205, 91.521 and 121.311 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a small aeroplane that:
is an aircraft to which this Subpart applies; and
was manufactured on or after 13 December 1986;
other than a multi-engine aeroplane that has 10 or more passenger seats.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in subregulation (3) is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A seat (other than a side-facing seat) in the aeroplane that does not have an approved seat belt and shoulder harness:
must not be used during take-off or landing; and
must carry a placard to that effect.
Source FARs section 91.205 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a helicopter that:
is an aircraft to which this Subpart applies; and
was manufactured on or after 17 September 1992.
The registered operator of the helicopter commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the helicopter; or
permits a person to operate the helicopter; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the helicopter is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A seat in the helicopter that does not have an approved seat belt and shoulder harness:
must not be used during take-off or landing; and
must carry a placard to that effect.
There must be a means to secure each seat belt and harness when it is not in use so that it does not:
prevent the proper operation of the helicopter; or
hinder a person in the helicopter if he or she must leave the helicopter in an emergency.
Source FARs section 91.205 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aircraft is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
In the aircraft, a side-facing seat that is to be used during take-off or landing must be fitted with:
an approved lap belt and an energy-absorbing rest that would support the arms, shoulders, head and spine of the occupant during an emergency landing; or
an approved safety harness that would prevent the occupant’s head being injured by striking an object during an emergency landing.
Source FARs section 121.311 modified.
A side-facing seat in the aircraft that is not fitted with an approved lap belt or an approved safety harness as mentioned in subregulation (2):
must not be used during take-off or landing; and
must carry a placard to that effect.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
while the aircraft is operating, a cabin crew seat or any related equipment does not meet the standard set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs sections 91.521 and 121.311 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation does not apply in relation to an external door that is only used for cargo.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aircraft is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An external door in the aircraft must be of a kind that can be opened from both inside and outside the aircraft, unless:
the aircraft is an unpressurised small aeroplane; and
in the aircraft’s type design the door can be opened from the inside only.
The information mentioned in subregulation (4) must be clearly marked:
on the inside of each external door; and
if an external door can be opened from the outside—on the outside of the external door.
For subregulation (3), the information is:
the location of the handle; and
the operating instructions for the handle; and
the position of the handle when the door is properly locked, or another way of showing when the door is properly locked.

In a large aeroplane or a pressurised small aeroplane, the design of an external door that, in use, initially opens outwards must allow for the locking mechanism to be visible from inside the aircraft to check whether the locking pins or latches are fully engaged.
An external door must also meet the requirements in this Part for an emergency exit.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aircraft is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subject to paragraph (6)(b), each passenger and crew member in the aircraft must have access to at least 1 emergency exit that meets the requirements prescribed by the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
The location of each emergency exit must be marked so that each seated passenger can see the location of the exit nearest to the passenger.
Each passenger compartment in the aircraft must have a sign showing the way to any emergency exit that is not located in the passenger compartment.
Instructions showing how to open the emergency exit must be clearly marked on:
the inside of each emergency exit; and
if an emergency exit can be opened from the outside—on the outside of the emergency exit.
If an aircraft has 7 or more seats, including crew seats:

each emergency exit sign and the instructions for operating each emergency exit must be self-illuminated or provided with lighting so that, if the cabin is in darkness and the cabin lighting is not operating, the sign and instructions can be read by a person attempting to open the emergency exit; and
subject to regulation 90.215, access to an emergency exit must not be blocked by a seat back, stretcher or other item of equipment fitted to the aircraft unless:
the seat back, stretcher or other item of equipment can easily be moved out of the way; and
instructions for moving the seat back, stretcher or other item of equipment are clearly marked on or near the seat, stretcher or item of equipment.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
a requirement in subregulation (2) is not met while the aircraft is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If the aircraft has lighting within a cargo or baggage compartment, the lamps:
must be protected against the possibility of accidental damage; and
must be designed so that any baggage placed adjacent to the lamp is not subjected to excessive heat.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a large transport category aeroplane.
However, this regulation does not apply to an aeroplane of a particular type if a certificate of airworthiness was issued in respect of at least 1 aeroplane of that type before 1 January 1958.
The registered operator of an aeroplane to which this regulation applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If:
the aeroplane was manufactured before 2 September 2005; and
thermal/acoustic insulation materials have been installed in the fuselage as replacements on or after 2 September 2005; and
the materials are:
of a blanket construction; or
installed around air ducting;
the materials must meet the flame propagation standards of FARs paragraph 25.856(a), as in force on 2 September 2003.

If the aeroplane was manufactured on or after 2 September 2005, any thermal/acoustic insulation materials installed in the fuselage must meet the flame propagation standards of FARs paragraph 25.856(a), as in force on 2 September 2003.
Source FARs section 121.312 modified.
An offence against subregulation (3) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of an aircraft to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aircraft; or
permits a person to operate the aircraft; and
a fire extinguisher fitted to or carried on the aircraft contains a fire extinguishing agent of a kind prescribed by the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 90.C—Large aeroplanes engaged in air transport operations
This Subpart applies to large aeroplanes engaged in air transport operations.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If:
the aeroplane has an emergency exit; and
the exit:
is higher than 1.83 m above the ground when the aeroplane’s landing gear is extended; and
is not positioned over the wing;
the aeroplane must be fitted with an escape device to help passengers and members of the crew reach the ground from the aeroplane’s cabin in an emergency.
The escape device must meet the standard for escape devices set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
However, subregulation (2) does not apply to the rear window emergency exit of a DC-3 aeroplane that is being operated with 35 occupants or fewer.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a passenger-carrying aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
is required under its type certification basis to have 2 or more emergency exits on each side of the fuselage.
Note: For the definition of type certification basis, see the Dictionary.
However, this regulation does not apply to an aeroplane that:
was in operation before 16 October 1987; and
had an emergency exit configuration installed and approved before 16 October 1987.
The registered operator of an aeroplane to which this regulation applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
the requirement in subregulation (4) is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The distance between any 2 adjacent emergency exits that lead from the same deck in the aeroplane must be no more than 18.3 m.
For subregulation (4), the distance between 2 adjacent emergency exits is measured between the closest edges of the 2 doors, parallel to the aeroplane’s longitudinal axis.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (3) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, a passageway leading to, or an area providing access to, an emergency exit does not meet the standard for access to emergency exits set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, the identification marking for an emergency exit on the aeroplane, or a location sign or instruction for opening such an emergency exit, does not meet the standard for interior emergency exit marking set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying transport category aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
while the aeroplane is operating, the interior emergency lighting system of the aeroplane does not meet the standard for interior emergency lighting set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a passenger-carrying transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
was originally certificated on or after 1 January 1958; and
has 20 or more passenger seats.
The registered operator of an aeroplane to which this regulation applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, the aeroplane does not have a floor proximity emergency escape path that meets the standard for floor proximity emergency escape paths set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, the outside of an emergency exit on the aeroplane is not marked so that it meets the standard for exterior emergency exit marking set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying transport category aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, an over-wing exit on the aeroplane, or an escape device fitted to the aeroplane for regulation 90.205, is not fitted with an exterior emergency lighting system that meets the standard for exterior emergency lighting set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, an over-wing emergency exit on the aeroplane does not have an over-wing escape route that meets the standard for over-wing escape routes set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.310 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
has 20 or more passenger seats.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
while the aeroplane is operating, the materials used in the interior of the cabin of the aeroplane do not meet the standard for cabin interiors set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.312 modified.
Subregulation (2) does not apply to a material used for a passenger seat cushion in an aeroplane to which regulation 90.255 applies.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
has 31 or more passenger seats; and
was originally certificated on or after 1 January 1958.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
while the aeroplane is operating, a seat cushion, other than a flight crew seat cushion, in the aeroplane does not comply with FARs paragraph 25.853(c), as in force on 26 November 1984.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.312 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
was originally certificated on or after 1 January 1958.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in subregulation (3) is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If the aeroplane has a Class C cargo or baggage compartment, or a Class D cargo or baggage compartment, larger than 5.66 m³, the ceiling and wall liner panels of the compartment must be:
constructed of glass fibre reinforced resin; or
constructed of 1 or more materials that meet:
the flame penetration test requirements of FARs Part 25, Appendix F, Part III, as in force on 16 June 1986; or
another approved test; or
an aluminium liner installation approved before 20 March 1989.
Source FARs section 121.314 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Cargo compartments for aeroplanes engaged in scheduled air transport operations

content.p: This regulation applies to a transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
was originally certificated on or after 1 January 1958; and
is engaged in scheduled air transport operations.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in subregulation (3) is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If the aeroplane has a Class D cargo or baggage compartment, the compartment must meet:
for a passenger-carrying aeroplane—the standards for a Class C cargo or baggage compartment set out in FARs paragraph 25.857(c) and section 25.858; or
for any other aeroplane—the standards for a Class E cargo compartment set out in FARs paragraph 25.857(e).
Source FARs section 121.314 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of a passenger-carrying aeroplane to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Both sides of the door of each toilet in the aeroplane must have, installed above the door knob or near the door, a placard showing:
the words ‘NO SMOKING IN TOILET’ or ‘NO SMOKING’; or
a symbol with the same meaning.
Each waste receptacle in each toilet in an aeroplane must have installed, on or near the waste receptacle, a placard showing:
the words ‘NO CIGARETTE DISPOSAL’; or
a symbol with the same meaning.
Each toilet in an aeroplane that has 20 or more passenger seats must be fitted with:
a smoke detector that gives a warning signal that can be seen or heard by a flight crew member or cabin crew member; and
1 or more fire extinguishers that will, in the event of a fire in a waste receptacle in the toilet, discharge into the receptacle.
Source FARs section 121.308 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
was manufactured on or after 2 September 2009; and
has 20 or more passenger seats; and
is engaged in scheduled air transport operations.
However, this regulation does not apply to an aeroplane of a particular type if a certificate of airworthiness was issued in respect of at least 1 aeroplane of that type before 1 January 1958.
The registered operator of an aeroplane to which this regulation applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, any thermal/acoustic insulation materials installed in the lower half of the aeroplane’s fuselage do not meet the flame penetration resistance standards of FARs paragraph 25.856(b), as in force on 2 September 2003.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.312 modified.
An offence against subregulation (3) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
was originally certificated on or after 1 January 1958; and
is manufactured on or after 27 October 2009; and
is engaged in scheduled air transport operations.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
while the aeroplane is operating, a seat for a passenger or cabin crew member does not meet the standards of FARs section 25.562, as in force on 16 June 1988.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.311 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to a turbine-powered transport category aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
has a flight instrument pitot heating system; and
is engaged in scheduled air transport operations.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The aeroplane must have an indication system to indicate to the flight crew if the flight instrument pitot heating system is not operating.
The indication system must comply with the following requirements:
the indication system must incorporate an amber light that is in clear view of a flight crew member;
the indication system must be designed to alert the flight crew if either of the following conditions exists:
the flight instrument pitot heating system is switched off;
the flight instrument pitot heating system is switched on and any pitot tube heating element is inoperative.
Source FARs section 121.342 modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
The registered operator of an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies, other than an aeroplane that complies with FARs section 25.729 as in force on 6 January 1992, commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, the aeroplane does not have a landing gear aural warning system and associated devices that meet the standard for landing gear aural warning systems and associated devices set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs section 121.289 modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 90.D—Small aeroplanes engaged in air transport operations
This Subpart applies to small aeroplanes engaged in air transport operations.
The registered operator of an aeroplane that has 10 or more passenger seats and to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the aeroplane is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
(2) Each compartment for cargo, baggage or both (goods) in the aeroplane must:
display a placard showing the maximum load for which the compartment has been designed; and
have a means to prevent goods creating a hazard by shifting, or by damaging the aeroplane; and

(c) have a means to restrain goods to protect the aeroplane’s occupants from injury in the event of the aeroplane being subjected to a forward inertial load of up to 9 g when the compartment is carrying the maximum weight of goods.

If goods are in the passenger compartment of the aeroplane, the compartment must have a means to prevent the passengers being injured by the goods during the emergency landing conditions mentioned in the aeroplane’s type certification basis.
Source FARs Part 135 Appendix A modified.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to an aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
has 10 or more passenger seats; and
is engaged in scheduled air transport operations.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and
while the aeroplane is operating, the aeroplane’s emergency exits do not meet the standard for emergency exits set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs Part 135 Appendix A modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to an aeroplane that:
is an aeroplane to which this Subpart applies; and
has 10 or more passenger seats; and
has wing flaps and retractable landing gear; and
is not an amphibian.
The registered operator of the aeroplane commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the aeroplane; or
permits a person to operate the aeroplane; and

while the aeroplane is operating, the aeroplane does not have a landing gear aural warning system and associated devices that meet the standard for landing gear aural warning systems and associated devices set out in the Part 90 Manual of Standards.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Source FARs Part 135 Appendix A modified.
An offence against subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 90.E—Helicopters engaged in scheduled air transport operations
This Subpart applies to helicopters engaged in scheduled air transport operations.
The registered operator of a helicopter to which this Subpart applies commits an offence if:
the registered operator:
operates the helicopter; or
permits a person to operate the helicopter; and
a requirement in this regulation is not met while the helicopter is operating.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Each emergency exit must be marked so that its location can be seen from a distance equal to the width of the cabin.
There must be a sign on or near each exit that:
shows the location of the exit handle; and
gives the operating instructions for the handle; and
can be read by a person attempting to open the exit.
The light for each emergency exit sign must:
operate independently of the helicopter’s main lighting system; and
be able to be switched on manually; and
remain illuminated when the helicopter makes an emergency landing, regardless of whether the light switches on automatically or must be switched on manually.
The outside of the fuselage must be marked to show:
each emergency exit; and
if an exit can be opened from outside—the means by which it can be opened.
An offence against subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
