Subpart 119.A—General
This Part makes provision for applicants for, and holders of, AOCs that authorise the operation of aeroplanes or rotorcraft for Australian air transport operations.
Note 1: See also Division 2 (Air Operators’ Certificates (AOCs)) of Part III of the Act in relation to AOCs generally.
Note 2: A person must hold an AOC under this Part to conduct any of the following:
Part 121 operations;
Part 133 operations;
Part 135 operations.

section.heading: Definition of Australian air transport operation

content.p: (1) An operation is an Australian air transport operation if the operation is any of the following:
an air transport operation conducted by an Australian operator using a registered aeroplane or rotorcraft;
an air transport operation:
that is a flight into or out of Australian territory or an operation in Australian territory; and
that is conducted by an Australian operator using an aeroplane or rotorcraft that is a foreign registered aircraft;
an air transport operation:
that is conducted by an Australian operator using an aeroplane or rotorcraft; and
that is provided for under the ANZA mutual recognition agreements;
an air transport operation conducted by a foreign operator:
using an aeroplane or rotorcraft that is a foreign registered aircraft; and
undertaken wholly within Australia; and
not undertaken as part of a flight into or out of Australian territory;
an operation, conducted using an aeroplane or rotorcraft, of a kind prescribed by the Part 119 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.
(2) However, each of the following is not an Australian air transport operation:
the operation of an aeroplane or rotorcraft under a permission under:
section 25 (non-scheduled flights by foreign registered aircraft) of the Act; or
section 27A (permission for operation of foreign registered aircraft without AOC) of the Act;
an air transport operation authorised by a New Zealand AOC with ANZA privileges that is in force for Australia;
an operation of an aircraft to which Part 129 (foreign air transport operations) of these Regulations applies;
an operation, conducted using an aeroplane or rotorcraft, of a kind prescribed by the Part 119 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.

Note: See Part 129 for provisions relating to foreign operators conducting flights into or out of Australian territory, or flights wholly within Australian territory that are conducted as part of flights into or out of Australian territory.

section.heading: Definitions of Australian air transport AOC and Australian air transport operator

content.p: (1) An Australian air transport AOC is an AOC that authorises the operation of an aeroplane or rotorcraft for an Australian air transport operation.
(2) An Australian air transport operator is a person who holds an Australian air transport AOC.
a change in relation to any of the following:
the location and operation of the operator’s main operating bases, including the opening or closing of main operating bases;
the operator’s key personnel;
a person authorised to carry out the responsibilities of any of the key personnel if the position holder is absent from the position or cannot carry out the responsibilities of the position;
the formal reporting lines for a managerial or operational position with safety functions and responsibilities that reports directly to any of the key personnel;
the operator’s process for making changes that relate to the safe conduct and management of the operator’s air transport operations;
the kinds of Australian air transport operations the operator is authorised to conduct under the operator’s Australian air transport AOC;
the operator’s areas of operation or routes, including beginning to operate in a new area or on a new route (but not including ceasing to operate in an area or on a route);

the types and models of aeroplanes or rotorcraft used in the operator’s Australian air transport operations, including the addition of a new type or model (but not including ceasing to operate a type or model); or
a change in relation to any of the following that does not maintain or improve, or is not likely to maintain or improve, aviation safety:
the plans, processes, procedures, programs and systems for the safe conduct and management of the operator’s Australian air transport operations;
the qualifications, experience and responsibilities required by the operator for any of the operator’s key personnel;
any other aeronautical or aviation safety related services provided to the operator by third parties;
any change to the registration of an aeroplane or rotorcraft used in the operator’s Australian air transport operations;
any leasing or other arrangements for the supply of an aeroplane or rotorcraft used in the operator’s Australian air transport operations; or

a change required to be approved by CASA under these Regulations, other than a change that results in the reissue or replacement of an instrument previously issued by CASA in which the conditions or other substantive content of the instrument are unchanged.
If a provision of this Part, or of the Part 119 Manual of Standards, refers to a person holding an approval under this regulation, the person may apply to CASA, in writing, for the approval.
Subject to regulation 11.055, CASA must grant the approval.
Subregulation 11.055(1B) applies to the granting of an approval under this regulation for either of the following provisions:
paragraph 119.135(3)(a);
paragraph 119.145(3)(a).
For the purposes of subsection 27(9) of the Act, the flying or operation of an aeroplane or rotorcraft for an Australian air transport operation is a prescribed purpose.
An Australian air transport operator must have a safety manager.
(2) For the purposes of paragraph (e) of the definition of key personnel in subsection 28(3) of the Act, the position of safety manager is prescribed for Australian air transport operators.

section.heading: Required position—head of training and checking

content.p: An Australian air transport operator must have a position (however described) that is the head of the training and checking part of the organisation.
For the purposes of paragraph 28BH(2)(b) of the Act, the following material is required for an Australian air transport operator:
the civil aviation legislation that is relevant to the operator’s Australian air transport operations;
the parts of the AIP that are relevant to the operations;
if the operator conducts operations in one or more foreign countries—the document for each of those countries that is equivalent to the AIP;

all information about the flight operations of each type and model of aeroplane or rotorcraft operated by the operator for the operations that is necessary to ensure the safe conduct of the operations;
any other publications, information or data required for the reference library by the operator’s exposition.
To avoid doubt, if material is required under subregulation (1), the requirement is taken to be satisfied if an electronic copy of the material is readily available.

section.heading: Issue of Manual of Standards for Part 119

content.p: For the purposes of subsection 98(5A) of the Act, CASA may issue a Manual of Standards for this Part prescribing matters:
required or permitted by these Regulations to be prescribed by the Part 119 Manual of Standards; or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Part.
Note: A Manual of Standards is a legislative instrument: see subsection 98(5AA) of the Act.
A person contravenes this subregulation if:
the person conducts an Australian air transport operation; and
the person does not hold an Australian air transport AOC that authorises the person to conduct the Australian air transport operation.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Compliance with Australian air transport AOCs

content.p: A person contravenes this subregulation if:
the person conducts an Australian air transport operation; and
the person holds an Australian air transport AOC that authorises the person to conduct the Australian air transport operation; and
the person conducts the operation in a way that contravenes the AOC.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Compliance with conditions of Australian air transport AOCs

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if the operator contravenes a condition of the operator’s Australian air transport AOC.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 119.B—Australian air transport AOCs
A person may apply to CASA for the issue of an Australian air transport AOC.
The application must include the following:
the applicant’s name (including any operating or trading name), contact details and ABN (if any);
if the address of the applicant’s operational headquarters is different from the applicant’s mailing address—the address of the applicant’s operational headquarters;
if the applicant is an individual—a statement that the individual is, or proposes to be, the applicant’s chief executive officer;
if the applicant is a corporation—the name of each of the directors of the corporation;
if the applicant is a corporation registered in Australia that has an ACN—the applicant’s ACN and the address of the applicant’s registered office;
if the applicant is a corporation not registered in Australia—the place the applicant was incorporated or formed;
details of the Australian air transport operations covered by the application;
a written undertaking from the person appointed, or proposed to be appointed, as the applicant’s chief executive officer that, if CASA issues the AOC, the applicant will:
be capable of operating in accordance with the applicant’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation; and
operate in accordance with the applicant’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation.
Note: See also sections 27AB (lodgment of manuals) and 27AC (CASA may require information etc. and inspections etc.) of the Act.
The application must be:
accompanied by a copy of the applicant’s proposed exposition; and
signed by the person appointed, or proposed to be appointed, as the applicant’s chief executive officer.
(1) It is a condition for the issue to the applicant of an Australian air transport AOC that CASA is satisfied of each of the following:
the applicant’s proposed exposition complies with regulation 119.205;
the applicant can conduct Australian air transport operations safely and in accordance with the applicant’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation;
if the applicant is an individual—the applicant:
is a fit and proper person to be issued an Australian air transport AOC; and
is, or proposes to be, the applicant’s chief executive officer;
if the applicant is a corporation—each director of the corporation is a fit and proper person to be a director of a corporation that is issued an Australian air transport AOC;
(e) each of the applicant’s proposed key personnel:
is a fit and proper person to be appointed to the position; and
has the qualifications and experience required under Subpart 119.D for the position; and
has the additional qualifications and experience required by CASA under regulation 119.165 for the position (if any); and
has the qualifications and experience required by the applicant under subparagraph 119.205(1)(e)(i) for the position (if any);

the applicant’s arrangements for managing the continuing airworthiness of each type and model of aeroplane or rotorcraft the applicant proposes to operate in the applicant’s Australian air transport operations comply with these Regulations.
Note 1: These matters are in addition to the matters specified in section 28 (CASA must issue AOC if satisfied about certain matters) of the Act.

Note 2: For Australian air transport AOCs with ANZA privileges, these matters are also in addition to the matters specified in section 28B (Additional conditions for issue of an Australian AOC with ANZA privileges) of the Act and subregulation (4) of this regulation.
For the purposes of paragraph (1)(b), without limiting the matters that CASA may consider, CASA must consider the following:
the applicant’s proposed exposition;
whether the applicant can comply with the proposed exposition;
the content of the undertaking mentioned in paragraph 119.065(2)(h);
details of, and reasons for, any suspension or cancellation of:
a civil aviation authorisation issued to the applicant; or
an equivalent authorisation issued to the applicant under the law of a foreign country or by a multinational aviation authority;
the suitability of the applicant’s corporate and organisational structures for the operations;
any other information:
accompanying the application; or
in any other document given to CASA by the applicant for the application, including any document requested by CASA in relation to the application.
For the purposes of paragraphs (1)(c) to (e), the matters CASA may consider in deciding whether a person is a fit and proper person include the following:
the person’s criminal record (if any), whether in Australia or a foreign country;
the person’s bankruptcy (if any), whether in Australia or a foreign country;
the person’s history (if any) of serious behavioural problems;
any information held or obtained by CASA that the person has contravened:
the civil aviation legislation; or
another law, whether in Australia or a foreign country, relating to transport (including aviation) safety or safety in any other safety-critical industry;
the person’s demonstrated attitude towards compliance with regulatory requirements, in Australia or a foreign country, relating to transport (including aviation) safety;
the record of compliance with regulatory requirements, in Australia or a foreign country, relating to transport (including aviation) safety of any corporation or other body in which the person:
is or was a director or partner (however described); or
holds or held a position equivalent to any of the applicant’s key personnel;
for any corporation in which the person is or was a director, or holds or held a position equivalent to any of the applicant’s key personnel, in Australia or a foreign country—the following records:
the corporation’s criminal record (if any);
the corporation’s record of insolvency, bankruptcy, receivership or winding up (if any);
the corporation’s record (if any) as a body subject to investigation or comment by a statutory authority that regulates the share dealings by, or financial affairs of, corporations;
any other matter relating to the fitness of the person to:
for an applicant—hold an Australian air transport AOC; or
for a director or proposed director—be a director of a corporation that holds an Australian air transport AOC.
Additional conditions—Australian air transport AOC with ANZA privileges

For the purposes of paragraph 28B(1)(e) of the Act, it is also a condition for the issue of an Australian air transport AOC with ANZA privileges that CASA must be satisfied that each aeroplane the applicant proposes to operate under the AOC for ANZA activities in New Zealand complies with the following requirements:
the aeroplane either:
has a maximum take-off weight of more than 15,000 kg; or
is permitted by its type certificate or foreign type certificate to have a passenger seating capacity of more than 30 seats;
the aeroplane is registered in Australia or New Zealand.
If CASA issues an Australian air transport AOC to the applicant, CASA is taken to have also approved the applicant’s proposed exposition.

section.heading: Conditions of an Australian air transport AOC

content.p: For the purposes of paragraph 28BA(1)(b) of the Act, each of the following is a condition of an Australian air transport AOC issued to an operator:
the operator must comply with each direction given to the operator, or obligation imposed on the operator, by CASA under a provision of these Regulations;
each of the operator’s key personnel must comply with:
each provision of this Part that applies to the person; and
each direction given to the person, or obligation imposed on the person, by CASA under a provision of these Regulations; and
each other provision of the civil aviation legislation that applies to the operator’s operations under the AOC;
each of the positions of the operator’s key personnel must be filled;
each of the operator’s personnel must comply with each provision of the civil aviation legislation that applies to the operator’s operations under the AOC;
if the operator is an individual—the individual must be the operator’s chief executive officer;
the positions of chief executive officer and safety manager may be occupied by the same person only:
in an unforeseen circumstance; and
for the period mentioned in subregulation (2);
the positions of head of flying operations and safety manager may be occupied by the same person:
if there is an unforeseen circumstance—for the period mentioned in subregulation (2); or
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 119.025 for the positions to be occupied by the same person—for the period specified in the approval;
for each registered aeroplane or rotorcraft operated by the operator under the AOC, the operator must:
be the registered operator of the aeroplane or rotorcraft; or
hold an approval under regulation 119.025 for the aeroplane or rotorcraft.

Note 1: These matters are in addition to the matters specified in section 28BA (general conditions) and subsection 28BAA(1) (certain conditions for grant of AOC also have effect as ongoing conditions on the AOC) of the Act.

Note 2: For Australian air transport AOCs with ANZA privileges, these matters are also in addition to the matters specified in subsection 28BAA(2) (certain conditions for grant of AOC also have effect as ongoing conditions on the AOC) of the Act and subregulation (3) of this regulation.
For the purposes of subparagraphs (1)(f)(ii) and (g)(i), the period is:
no more than 7 consecutive days for each unforeseen circumstance; or
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 119.025 in relation to an unforeseen circumstance—the period mentioned in the approval for the unforeseen circumstance.
Additional conditions—Australian air transport AOC with ANZA privileges

For the purposes of paragraph 28BA(1)(b) of the Act, it is also a condition of an Australian air transport AOC with ANZA privileges that each aeroplane operated by the AOC holder under the AOC for ANZA activities in New Zealand must comply with the following requirements:
the aeroplane either:
has a maximum take-off weight of more than 15,000 kg; or
is permitted by its type certificate or foreign type certificate to have a passenger seating capacity of more than 30 seats;
the aeroplane is registered in Australia or New Zealand.
Subpart 119.C—Changes relating to Australian air transport operators
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if the operator:
makes a change mentioned in subregulation (2); and
does not, before making the change:
amend the operator’s exposition to reflect the change; and
give CASA written notice of the change and a copy of the amended part of the exposition clearly identifying the change.
For the purposes of paragraph (1)(a), the changes are the following:
a change to the operator’s name (including any operating or trading name) or contact details;
if the address of the operator’s operational headquarters is different from the operator’s mailing address—a change to the address of the operator’s operational headquarters.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Application for approval of significant changes

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator makes a significant change other than a significant change mentioned in subregulation (2); and
CASA has not approved the significant change.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:

the operator makes a significant change that is the permanent appointment, or the acting appointment (for a period of greater than 35 days), as any of the operator’s key personnel of a person previously authorised to carry out the responsibilities of the position in a circumstance mentioned in subparagraph 119.205(1)(e)(iv); and
the operator does not apply to CASA for approval of the change, in accordance with subregulation (4), within 7 days after the change is made.
An application for approval of a significant change must:
be in writing; and
set out the change; and
be accompanied by a copy of the part of the operator’s exposition affected by the change, clearly identifying the change.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

CASA may approve a significant change for an Australian air transport operator only if satisfied that the requirements mentioned in section 28 of the Act and subregulation 119.070(1) will continue to be met.
If CASA approves the significant change, CASA is taken to have also approved the changes to the operator’s exposition covered by the application for the change.

section.heading: Changes must be made in accordance with process in exposition

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator makes a change; and
the change is not made in accordance with the process included in the operator’s exposition in accordance with paragraph 119.205(1)(m).
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: CASA directions relating to exposition or key personnel

content.p: If CASA is satisfied that it is necessary in the interests of aviation safety, CASA may, by written notice given to an Australian air transport operator, direct the operator to change the operator’s exposition:
to remove particular information, procedures or instructions from the exposition; or
to include particular information, procedures or instructions in the exposition; or
to revise or vary the information, procedures or instructions in the exposition.

CASA may, by written notice given to an Australian air transport operator, direct the operator to remove any of the operator’s key personnel from the person’s position if satisfied that the person is not:
carrying out the safety responsibilities of the position under Subpart 119.D; or
if the person is the chief executive officer—properly managing safety matters for which the person is accountable under Subpart 119.D.
A notice under this regulation must state the time within which the direction must be complied with.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
CASA gives the operator a direction under this regulation; and
the operator does not comply with the direction within the time stated in the notice.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 119.D—Organisation and personnel

An Australian air transport operator must maintain an organisational structure that effectively manages the operator’s Australian air transport operations, taking into account the size, nature and complexity of the operations.

An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if any of the operator’s key personnel carries out a responsibility of the person’s position in a way that contravenes the operator’s exposition or this Subpart.
A person commits an offence if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: When key personnel cannot carry out responsibilities

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator becomes aware that any of the operator’s key personnel cannot carry out, or is likely to be unable to carry out, the person’s responsibilities for a period of longer than 35 days; and
the operator does not tell CASA of the matter mentioned in paragraph (a) within the time mentioned in subregulation (2).
The time is:
if there is not another person authorised to carry out the responsibilities for all or part of the period—24 hours after the operator becomes aware of the matter; or
if there is another person authorised to carry out the responsibilities for all or part of the period—3 days after the operator becomes aware of the matter.
A person commits an offence if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

An Australian air transport operator must ensure that, before a person appointed as any of the operator’s key personnel begins to carry out the responsibilities of the position, the person has completed any training that is necessary to familiarise the person with the responsibilities.
The chief executive officer of an Australian air transport operator must have the experience required under subregulation (2).
The experience required is:
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 119.025—the experience mentioned in the approval; or
if paragraph (a) does not apply—the experience mentioned in paragraphs (3)(a) and (b).
The experience is the following:

sufficient relevant experience in organisational, operational, financial and people management of air operations to capably lead, manage and set standards to enable the operator to conduct safe operations in accordance with the operator’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation;
a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations.
The chief executive officer of an Australian air transport operator is responsible for the following:

ensuring that, for the safe conduct of the operator’s Australian air transport operations in accordance with the operator’s Australian air transport AOC and exposition and the civil aviation legislation, the operator:
has sufficient suitably experienced, qualified and competent personnel; and
has a suitable management structure; and
is adequately financed and resourced;
ensuring that the operator:
complies with the civil aviation legislation; and
complies with the aviation safety laws of each foreign country (if any) where the operator conducts Australian air transport operations; and
implements and manages the operator’s safety management system; and
has procedures that ensure that all of the operator’s personnel understand the operator’s safety policy; and
has an organisational structure that ensures that the safety manager is independent and not subject to undue influence; and
sets and maintains standards for flight and ground operations; and

tells CASA if the operator becomes aware that a leasing, financing or other arrangement for the supply of an aeroplane or rotorcraft that the operator operates under the operator’s Australian air transport AOC may affect the operator’s safe conduct of the operator’s Australian air transport operations; and

tells CASA if the operator becomes aware that an arrangement mentioned in subparagraph (vii) may contravene a provision of the civil aviation legislation or the law of the country in which the aeroplane or rotorcraft is registered; and

for each foreign registered aircraft (if any) used in the operator’s Australian air transport operations—maintains the aircraft in accordance with the law of the country in which the aircraft is registered (subject to any applicable 83 bis agreement);
establishing and regularly reviewing the operator’s safety performance indicators and targets;
ensuring that the operator’s exposition is monitored and managed for continuous improvement;

ensuring that training and checking of the operator’s operational safety-critical personnel (other than flight crew) conducted by or for the operator is conducted in accordance with the operator’s exposition;
ensuring that key personnel satisfactorily carry out the responsibilities of their positions in accordance with the operator’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation.

The chief executive officer of an Australian air transport operator is accountable to the operator and CASA for ensuring the responsibilities mentioned in subregulation (1) are carried out effectively.

section.heading: Head of flying operations—qualifications and experience

content.p: The head of flying operations of an Australian air transport operator must:
hold the pilot licence required under subregulation (2); and

hold a pilot type or class rating (within the meaning of Part 61) for a type or class of aeroplane or rotorcraft that is used to conduct a significant proportion of the operator’s Australian air transport operations; and
have the experience required under subregulation (3); and
have a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations; and

have sufficient safety and regulatory knowledge to enable the operator to conduct the operator’s Australian air transport operations safely and in accordance with the operator’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation.
The licence required is:
if the operator conducts only single-pilot operations—a commercial pilot licence or an air transport pilot licence; or
in any other case—an air transport pilot licence.
The experience required is:
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 119.025—the experience mentioned in the approval; or
if paragraph (a) does not apply—the experience mentioned in paragraphs (4)(a) and (b).
The experience is the following:

at least 500 hours flight time on a type of aeroplane or rotorcraft that is the same as, or substantially similar to, a type of aeroplane or rotorcraft used to conduct a significant proportion of the operator’s Australian air transport operations;
at least 6 months experience in the conduct or management of air operations conducted under an AOC or equivalent foreign authorisation.

CASA may, by written notice given to the head of flying operations, or proposed head of flying operations, of an Australian air transport operator, direct the person to undertake an assessment mentioned in subregulation (6).
The assessment:

is an assessment conducted by CASA, or a person nominated by CASA, to demonstrate the head of flying operation’s or proposed head of flying operation’s suitability as head of flying operations for the operator; and
may include assessment in an aeroplane, rotorcraft or flight simulation training device.
The head of flying operations of an Australian air transport operator must safely manage the flying operations of the operator.
Without limiting subregulation (1), the responsibilities of the head of flying operations include the following:

monitoring and maintaining, and reporting to the chief executive officer on, the operator’s compliance with the provisions of the civil aviation legislation and the operator’s exposition that apply to flying operations;
ensuring that the operator’s flight crew are provided with the information and documentation necessary to properly carry out their responsibilities;
ensuring the proper allocation and deployment of the operator’s aeroplanes or rotorcraft, and the operator’s personnel, for use in the operator’s Australian air transport operations;
ensuring that the operator complies with section 28BH (reference library) of the Act in relation to flight crew.

section.heading: Head of training and checking—qualifications and experience

content.p: The head of training and checking of an Australian air transport operator must:
hold the pilot licence required under subregulation (2); and

hold a pilot type or class rating (within the meaning of Part 61) for a type or class of aeroplane or rotorcraft used to conduct a significant proportion of the operator’s Australian air transport operations; and
have the experience required under subregulation (3); and
have a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations; and
have a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of training and checking in relation to air operations; and

have sufficient safety and regulatory knowledge to enable the operator to conduct the operator’s Australian air transport operations safely and in accordance with the operator’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation.
The licence required is:
if the operator conducts only single-pilot operations—a commercial pilot licence or an air transport pilot licence; or
in any other case—an air transport pilot licence.
The experience required is:
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 119.025—the experience mentioned in the approval; or
if paragraph (a) does not apply—the experience mentioned in paragraphs (4)(a) and (b).
The experience is the following:

at least 500 hours flight time on a type of aeroplane or rotorcraft that is the same as, or substantially similar to, a type of aeroplane or rotorcraft used to conduct a significant proportion of the operator’s Australian air transport operations;
at least 6 months experience in the conduct or management of air operations conducted under an AOC or equivalent foreign authorisation.

CASA may, by written notice given to a head of training and checking, or proposed head of training and checking, of an Australian air transport operator, direct the person to undertake an assessment mentioned in subregulation (6).
The assessment:

is an assessment conducted by CASA, or a person nominated by CASA, to demonstrate the heading of training or checking’s or proposed heading of training or checking’s suitability as head of training and checking for the operator; and
may include assessment in an aeroplane, rotorcraft or flight simulation training device.
The head of training and checking of an Australian air transport operator must safely manage the training and checking activities of the operator for the operator’s flight crew.
Without limiting subregulation (1), the responsibilities of the head of training and checking include the following:
ensuring that the operator complies with each provision of the civil aviation legislation that relates to the qualifications, training or checking of the operator’s flight crew;
reporting to the head of flying operations on the operator’s compliance with the provisions mentioned in paragraph (a);
ensuring that training and checking of flight crew conducted by or for the operator is conducted in accordance with the operator’s exposition;
if the operator has a contract with a Part 142 operator for the Part 142 operator to conduct training or checking for the operator’s flight crew:
ensuring that each person who conducts the training or checking for the Part 142 operator is authorised under Part 61 to conduct the activities involved in the training or checking; and

telling the Part 142 operator, in writing, of any change in the Australian air transport operator’s exposition relating to the training and checking activities the Part 142 operator conducts under the contract.
A safety manager required under regulation 119.035 for an Australian air transport operator must have:

sufficient relevant safety management experience to capably lead, manage and set standards to enable the operator to safely implement the operator’s safety management system in accordance with the operator’s exposition; and
a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations; and

sufficient safety and regulatory knowledge to enable the operator to conduct the operator’s Australian air transport operations safely and in accordance with the operator’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation.
A safety manager required under regulation 119.035 for an Australian air transport operator must manage the operator’s safety management system.
Without limiting subregulation (1), the responsibilities of the safety manager include:
managing the operation of the safety management system including managing corrective, remedial and preventative action in relation to the system; and
regularly reporting to the chief executive officer on the effectiveness of the safety management system; and
managing the maintenance and continuous improvement of the following systems:
safety management system;
fatigue risk management system (if any).

section.heading: Key personnel—additional qualification and experience requirements

content.p: This regulation applies to:
an applicant for an Australian air transport AOC; and
an Australian air transport operator.

CASA may, by written notice given to the applicant or operator, direct that any of the key personnel of the applicant or operator must have stated additional qualifications or experience to those otherwise required under this Subpart.

If CASA is satisfied that it is necessary in the interests of aviation safety, CASA may, by written notice given to a person who is, or is proposed to be, any of the key personnel of the applicant or operator, direct the person:
to undertake a stated examination; or
to be interviewed by CASA; or
to complete a stated training course.
In deciding whether to give a direction under this regulation, CASA must have regard to, but is not limited to considering, the following:
the need to ensure that the applicant or operator can conduct Australian air transport operations safely and in accordance with the operator’s exposition and the civil aviation legislation;
the nature and complexity of the operations;
the leadership, management and standards-setting skills required by the person for the operations;
how recently the person has used the person’s aviation skills;
whether the person is able to exercise the privileges of each civil aviation authorisation held by the person.
Subpart 119.E—Training and checking for operational safety-critical personnel
An Australian air transport operator must have a training and checking system.
The training and checking system must include the following in relation to flight crew and cabin crew:
a description of how training and checking, including recurrent training and line checking, is conducted by or for the operator;
an auditable system for maintaining records of the results of training and checking;
procedures that ensure that each of the operator’s flight crew and cabin crew:
completes training and checking in accordance with the training and checking system; and
is supervised effectively during training and checking;
a description of how the operator assesses the competence of a flight crew member or cabin crew member to perform the duties assigned to the member for a flight;
if the operator has a contract with a person for the person to conduct training or checking for the operator:
details of the person; and
details of the training or checking covered by the contract; and
details of how the operator ensures that the person is complying with the operator’s training and checking system.
The training and checking system must also include the following in relation to cabin crew:
the circumstances in which training is required to familiarise a cabin crew member with their duties;
if any of the training or checking of cabin crew is conducted by a member of the operator’s personnel—a description of the operator’s system for training and assessing such personnel.

If subregulation (5) applies in relation to the operator, the training and checking system must include the following in relation to operational safety-critical personnel who are not flight crew or cabin crew:
a description of how training and checking, including recurrent training, for the personnel is conducted by or for the operator;
an auditable system for maintaining records of the results of the training and checking;
the circumstances in which training is required to familiarise a member of the personnel with their duties;
if the operator has a contract with a person for the person to conduct the training or checking for the operator:
details of the person; and
details of the training or checking covered by the contract; and
details of how the operator ensures that the person is complying with the operator’s training and checking system;
if any of the training or checking is conducted by a member of the operator’s personnel—a description of the operator’s system for training and assessing such personnel.
This subregulation applies to the operator if the operator conducts one or more of the following operations:
operations in an aeroplane to which either or both of the following apply:
the aeroplane has a maximum take-off weight of more than 8,618 kg;
the aeroplane has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 9 seats;
operations in a rotorcraft to which either or both of the following apply:
the rotorcraft has a maximum take-off weight of more than 3,175 kg;
the rotorcraft has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 9 seats;
medical transport operations;
operations of a kind prescribed by the Part 119 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.
The operator must conduct checking for flight crew in relation to the flying of the aeroplane or rotorcraft if the operator operates:
an aeroplane or rotorcraft that is used for passenger transport operations and has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 30 seats; or
an aeroplane or rotorcraft that is used for cargo transport operations and has a maximum payload capacity of at least 3,410 kg.
The operator must only use individuals employed by the operator to conduct the checking required by subregulation (6).
This regulation does not apply to:
training that is authorised Part 141 flight training for the operator; or
training or checking that is an authorised Part 142 activity for the operator.

section.heading: Program for training and assessment in human factors principles and non-technical skills

content.p: An Australian air transport operator must have a program for training and assessing operational safety-critical personnel in human factors principles and non-technical skills.

section.heading: Training in human factors principles and non-technical skills for flight crew etc.

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if a person who is a member of the operator’s personnel mentioned in subregulation (2) contravenes subregulation (3).
The personnel are the following:
a flight crew member;
a cabin crew member;
an air crew member;
a medical transport specialist;
a flight dispatcher.

The person must not carry out a duty of the person’s position unless the person meets the requirements in the operator’s exposition about training in human factors principles and non-technical skills.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Training in human factors principles and non-technical skills for other operational safety-critical personnel

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if a person who is a member of the operator’s personnel mentioned in subregulation (2) contravenes subregulation (3).
The personnel are operational safety-critical personnel other than personnel mentioned in subregulation 119.180(2).
The person must meet the requirements in the operator’s exposition about training in human factors principles and non-technical skills within 3 months after being appointed to the person’s position.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a person who is a member of the operator’s personnel mentioned in subregulation (2) performs a duty of the person’s position; and

the duty is described in the operator’s exposition as a duty that may be performed only by a person who meets the requirements in the operator’s exposition about training in human factors principles and non-technical skills; and
the person does not meet the requirements in the operator’s exposition about training in human factors principles and non-technical skills.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 119.F—Safety management
An Australian air transport operator must have a safety management system that is appropriate for the size, nature and complexity of the operator’s Australian transport operations.
The safety management system must include the following matters:
a statement of the operator’s safety policy and objectives, including details of the following:
the management commitment to, and responsibility for, safety;
the safety accountabilities of managers (including key personnel);
the appointment of safety management personnel;
coordination of an emergency response plan;
safety management system documentation;
a safety risk management process, including:
hazard identification processes; and
safety risk assessment and mitigation processes;
a safety assurance system, including details of processes for:
safety performance monitoring and measurement; and
management of change; and
continuous improvement of the safety management system;
a safety training and promotion system, including details of the following:
safety management system training and education;
safety management system safety communication;
if regulation 119.195 applies in relation to the Australian air transport operator—a flight data analysis program that meets the requirements of that regulation.
This regulation applies in relation to an Australian air transport operator if the operator conducts Australian air transport operations in either or both of the following:
an aeroplane with a maximum take-off weight of more than 27,000 kg;
a rotorcraft:
with a maximum take-off weight of more than 7,000 kg; or
with a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 9 seats and that is required, under these Regulations, to be fitted with a flight data recorder.
The Australian air transport operator must have a flight data analysis program.
The flight data analysis program must:
regularly record and analyse the operational flight data of individual and aggregated operations for the purpose of improving the safety of flight operations; and
be provided by:
the operator; or
another appropriate person; and
(c) ensure that, except as mentioned in subregulation (5), the identity of a person (the identified person) who is the source of data is protected from disclosure to anyone other than the following:
a person whose duties require that person to analyse operational flight data;
a person who has access to the identified person’s identity solely for the purpose of analysing operational flight data;
a pilot appointed by the operator to liaise with flight crew in relation to matters arising from the flight data analysis program; and
ensure that no punitive action in relation to the data may be taken by the operator against the identified person.

For the purposes of subparagraph (3)(b)(ii), the provision of the flight data analysis program by an appropriate person does not in any way compromise the operator’s responsibility to provide, and ensure the effectiveness of, the program.
For the purposes of paragraph (3)(c), the identity of the identified person may be disclosed:
with the written consent of the person; or
as required by CASA; or
as otherwise required or authorised by law.
Subpart 119.G—Personnel fatigue management
Subpart 119.H—Expositions for Australian air transport operators
Note: This Subpart reserved for future use.
An exposition for an Australian air transport operator must include the following:
the operator’s name (including any operating or trading name), contact details and ABN (if any);
the address of:
the operator’s operational headquarters; and
each of the operator’s main operating bases; and
each of the operator’s operational facilities;
a description and diagram of the operator’s organisational structure showing formal reporting lines, including the formal reporting lines for each of the key personnel;
if the operator is a corporation—a description of the operator’s corporate structure;
for each of the key personnel, the following information:
the qualifications and experience (if any) required by the operator for the position in addition to the qualifications and experience required under Subpart 119.D for the position;
each matter (if any) for which the holder of the position is responsible in addition to the responsibilities mentioned in Subpart 119.D for the position;
the name of the person appointed to the position;
the name of each person authorised to carry out the responsibilities of the position when the position holder is absent from the position or cannot carry out the responsibilities;
a description of how the operator will manage the responsibilities of the position during a circumstance mentioned in subparagraph (iv);
each matter (if any) for which the chief executive officer is responsible and accountable in addition to the matters mentioned in regulation 119.130;
an outline of the Australian air transport operations conducted by the operator under the operator’s Australian air transport AOC, including the areas of operation and routes;

details of each plan, process, procedure, program and system implemented by the operator to safely conduct and manage their Australian air transport operations in compliance with the civil aviation legislation;
for each registered aeroplane or rotorcraft operated by the operator under the AOC—its type and model and registration mark;
for each foreign registered aircraft operated by the operator under the AOC—its type and model, nationality and registration mark;
a description of the arrangements for managing the continuing airworthiness of the operator’s aeroplanes or rotorcraft;

a description of any leasing or other arrangements for the supply of the aeroplanes or rotorcraft as the arrangements relate to the operational control or continuing airworthiness of the aeroplanes or rotorcraft, or to any other safety matter;
a description of the operator’s process for making changes, including:
identifying changes that are significant changes; and
identifying changes that are not significant changes; and
telling CASA and the operator’s personnel of the changes;
a description of anything else required to be approved by CASA under these Regulations in relation to the operations mentioned in paragraph (g);
any other matter required to be included in the exposition under these Regulations.
Note: The plans, processes, procedures, programs and systems mentioned in paragraph (h) may be set out in one or more operator manuals.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if the operator’s exposition does not comply with subregulation (1).
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if the operator does not meet a requirement of the operator’s exposition.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
(1) An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a person who is a member of the operator’s personnel is subject to a requirement under the operator’s exposition; and

the operator does not make the part of the exposition that relates to the requirement available to the person before the person first begins carrying out the person’s duties relating to the requirement.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A member of an Australian air transport operator’s personnel contravenes this subregulation if:
the member is subject to a requirement under the operator’s exposition in relation to the safe conduct of the operator’s Australian air transport operations; and
the member does not meet the requirement.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a member of the operator’s personnel is subject to a requirement under the operator’s exposition in relation to the safe conduct of the operator’s Australian air transport operations; and
the member does not meet the requirement.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 119.J—Records and documents

section.heading: Personnel training and checking records—making records

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a person who is a member of the operator’s personnel undertakes an activity, obtains a qualification or certificate or gains flying experience; and
the activity, qualification, certificate or flying experience is mentioned for the person in subregulation (2); and
the following records are not made within 21 days after the person undertakes the activity, obtains the qualification or certificate or gains the flying experience:
when the activity was undertaken, the qualification or certificate obtained or the flying experience gained;
if the activity was training or a check, flight test, flight review or assessment of competency—whether the training, check, flight test, flight review or assessment was successfully completed.
The activities, qualifications, certificates and flying experience for the person are the following:
for a flight crew member of the operator’s personnel:
training, or a check, flight test, flight review or assessment of competency, mentioned in Subpart 121.N, 133.N or 135.N; or
a qualification or certificate mentioned in Subpart 121.N, 133.N or 135.N; or
flying experience mentioned in Subpart 121.N, 133.N or 135.N; or
training in human factors principles or non-technical skills; or
training or education in the operator’s safety management system;
for a cabin crew member of the operator’s personnel:
training, or a check or assessment of competency, mentioned in Subpart 121.P or Division 133.P.1; or
training in human factors principles or non-technical skills; or
training or education in the operator’s safety management system;
for an air crew member of the operator’s personnel:
training, or a check or assessment of competency, mentioned in Division 133.P.2 or 135.P.1; or
training in human factors principles or non-technical skills; or
training or education in the operator’s safety management system;
for a medical transport specialist of the operator’s personnel:
training, or a check or assessment of competency, mentioned in Division 133.P.3 or 135.P.2; or
training in human factors principles or non-technical skills; or
training or education in the operator’s safety management system;
for a member of the operator’s operational safety-critical personnel (other than a flight crew or cabin crew member):
training in human factors principles or non-technical skills; or
training or education in the operator’s safety management system;
for a member of the operator’s personnel who performs ground support duties—any training;
for a member of the operator’s personnel not mentioned in paragraph (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) or (f)—training or education in the operator’s safety management system.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Personnel training and checking records—availability of records

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator makes a record about a person under regulation 119.225; and
the person requests that the record be made available to the person; and
the operator does not make the record available to the person within 7 days after receiving the request.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a record is made under regulation 119.225; and
the operator receives a request from another Australian air transport operator for a copy of the record; and
the operator holds a written authority from the person to whom the record relates to provide a copy of the person’s records to another Australian air transport operator if requested; and
the operator does not give a copy of the record to the other Australian air transport operator within 7 days after receiving the request.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Copies of flight crew licences and medical certificates

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a person who is a flight crew member of the operator’s personnel exercises a privilege of the person’s flight crew licence for the operator; and
the operator does not have the following:
a copy of the person’s flight crew licence;
a copy of the person’s medical certificate.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:

the operator is required, under this Part or Part 121, 133 or 135, to make or have a record of a kind mentioned in column 1 of an item of the following table about a person who is a member of the operator’s personnel; and
the operator does not keep the record for at least the period mentioned in column 2 of the item.

tr.td: Column 2 Minimum period for which the record must be kept
A record required under regulation 119.225 for a flight crew member
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 5 years after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel
A record required under regulation 119.225 for a cabin crew member
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 1 year after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel
A record required under regulation 119.225 for an air crew member
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 5 years after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel
A record required under regulation 119.225 for a medical transport specialist
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 1 year after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel
A record required under regulation 119.225 for a member of the operator’s personnel who performs ground support duties
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 1 year after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel
A copy of a flight crew member’s flight crew licence and medical certificate required by regulation 119.235
The period during which the member is exercising the privileges of the licence for the operator
A record of a flight crew member’s cosmic radiation dose required under Part 121 or 135
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 5 years after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel
A record of a cabin crew member’s cosmic radiation dose required under Part 121
The period beginning when the record is created and ending 5 years after the member ceases to be a member of the operator’s personnel

content.p: A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
under Part 91, 121, 133 or 135, a document mentioned in subregulation (2) is required for a flight of an aeroplane or rotorcraft conducted under the operator’s Australian air transport AOC; and
the operator does not keep the document for at least 3 months after the end of the flight.
The documents are the following for the flight:
an operational flight plan;
any authorised weather forecasts;
the authorised aeronautical information;
a weight and balance document;
a statement or information about cargo that may require special or unusual handling;
a passenger list;
a notice of action, taken in an emergency by the pilot flying the aeroplane or rotorcraft, that involves a contravention of these Regulations.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Retention periods for other flight-related records

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
a person is required under Part 121, 133 or 135 to make a record that is a journey log for a flight of an aeroplane or rotorcraft conducted under the operator’s Australian air transport AOC; and
the record is made other than in the flight technical log for the aeroplane or rotorcraft; and
the operator does not keep the record for at least 6 months after the end of the flight.
Note: See regulation 42.260 (retention of continuing airworthiness records) for the retention period for records made in the flight technical log for the aeroplane or rotorcraft.
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:

the operator is required under Part 121 to make a record of the results of the verification of the accuracy of the weight and balance data generated by a computerised system that is not fitted to the aeroplane; and
the operator does not keep the record for at least 6 months after it is made.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 119.K—Miscellaneous offences

section.heading: Dealings in relation to cancelled, suspended, varied, pending or refused civil aviation authorisations

content.p: Requirement for approval
An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator enters into an agreement with another person; and
the operator does an act mentioned in subregulation (2), (4), (6) or (8); and
the operator does not hold an approval under regulation 119.025 to do the act.
Acts in relation to cancelled authorisations
The acts are the following:
to use, in an Australian air transport operation, an aeroplane or rotorcraft the operation of which was authorised by a cancelled authorisation held by the other person;

to employ, in connection with an Australian air transport operation, a person who was, at the time of the cancellation of a cancelled authorisation held by the other person, employed in connection with an operation the conduct of which was authorised by the cancelled authorisation;
to conduct an operation, or part of an operation, the conduct of which was authorised by a cancelled authorisation.
Acts in relation to suspended or varied authorisations
Subregulation (4) applies in relation to a suspended or varied authorisation held by the other person.
The acts are the following:
to use, in an Australian air transport operation, an aeroplane or rotorcraft the operation of which:
was, immediately before the suspension or variation, authorised by the authorisation; but
is no longer authorised by the authorisation as suspended or varied;
to employ, in connection with an Australian air transport operation, a person who was, at the time of the suspension or variation, employed in connection with an operation the conduct of which:
was, immediately before the suspension or variation, authorised by the authorisation; but
is no longer authorised by the authorisation as suspended or varied;
to conduct an operation, or part of an operation, the conduct of which:
was, immediately before the suspension or variation, authorised by the authorisation; but
is no longer authorised by the authorisation as suspended or varied.
Note: See section 28BB (CASA may impose and vary AOC conditions) of the Act in relation to varying AOC conditions.
Pending applications for authorisations
Subregulation (6) applies in relation to an application by the other person for a civil aviation authorisation that has not been finally determined by CASA.
The acts are the following:
to use, in an Australian air transport operation, an aeroplane or rotorcraft the operation of which would be authorised by the authorisation;
to employ, in an Australian air transport operation, a person employed, or proposed to be employed, in connection with an operation the conduct of which would be authorised by the authorisation;
to conduct an operation, or part of an operation, the conduct of which would be authorised by the authorisation.
Application for authorisation refused
Subregulation (8) applies in relation to an application by the other person for a civil aviation authorisation that has been refused by CASA.
The acts are the following:
to use, in an Australian air transport operation, an aeroplane or rotorcraft the use of which would have been authorised by the authorisation;

to employ, in an Australian air transport operation, a person employed, or proposed to be employed, in connection with an operation the conduct of which would have been authorised by the authorisation;
to conduct an operation, or part of an operation, the conduct of which would have been authorised by the authorisation.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
In this regulation:
cancelled authorisation means a civil aviation authorisation that has been cancelled otherwise than on the application or request of the holder of the authorisation.
employ includes engage, whether by contract or other arrangement.
suspended authorisation means a civil aviation authorisation that has been suspended otherwise than on the application or request of the holder of the authorisation.
varied authorisation means a civil aviation authorisation that has been varied otherwise than on the application or request of the holder of the authorisation.

section.heading: Maximum period for use of foreign registered aircraft in Australian territory

content.p: An Australian air transport operator contravenes this subregulation if, in any 12 month period, the operator uses a foreign registered aircraft to conduct Australian air transport operations for a total of more than the number of days mentioned in subregulation (2).
The number of days is:
90; or
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 119.025 in relation to the aircraft—the number mentioned in the approval for the aircraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

Subpart 121.A—Preliminary

This Part (other than Subpart 121.Z) applies to the operation of a multi-engine aeroplane for an Australian air transport operation if either or both of the following apply in relation to the aeroplane:
it has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 9;
it has a maximum take-off weight of more than 8,618 kg.
Note: For the additional application of Subpart 121.N, see regulation 121.470.
Subpart 121.Z applies to the operation of a single-engine aeroplane for an Australian air transport operation if both of the following apply in relation to the aeroplane:
it has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 9;
it has a maximum take-off weight of not more than 8,618 kg.
If a provision of this Part, or of the Part 121 Manual of Standards, refers to a person holding an approval under this regulation, a person may apply to CASA, in writing, for the approval.
Subject to regulation 11.055, the approval must be granted.
Subregulation 11.055(1B) applies to the granting of an approval under this regulation.

section.heading: Issue of Manual of Standards for Part 121

content.p: For the purposes of subsection 98(5A) of the Act, CASA may issue a Manual of Standards for this Part prescribing matters:
required or permitted by these Regulations to be prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards; or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Part.
Note: A Manual of Standards is a legislative instrument: see subsection 98(5AA) of the Act.
Subpart 121.C—General
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the aeroplane begins the flight; and
the aeroplane is not type certificated in any of the following categories:
transport;
commuter;
(iii) normal (within the meaning of Special Federal Aviation Regulation 41 of the United States of America, as in force on 12 September 1983).
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Aeroplane to be flown under the IFR

content.p: The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, during a stage of the flight, the aeroplane is flown under the VFR.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Flights further than the 60 minute distance

content.p: Flying further than the 60 minute distance
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the aeroplane is mentioned in an item in column 1 of the following table; and
the aeroplane is flown:
(i) further from an adequate aerodrome for the aeroplane than the distance (the 60 minute distance) the aeroplane can fly if flying at the speed mentioned in column 2 of that item for 60 minutes; but

(ii) no further than the distance (the threshold distance) from an adequate aerodrome for the aeroplane that the aeroplane can fly if flying at the speed mentioned in column 2 of that item for the time mentioned in column 3 of that item; and
a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met.
Note: This provision will not apply in relation to items 1, 2 and 3 of the following table as, in those cases, the 60 minute distance is equal to the threshold distance.

content.p: Requirements to be met
The requirements are that:
the aeroplane operator’s exposition includes procedures for conducting flights further than the 60 minute distance, including procedures for:
dispatching such flights; and
providing updated information relating to the adequate aerodrome to the flight crew during such flights; and
(b) the operator estimates there will be an adequate aerodrome for the flight when the aeroplane is flown further than that distance; and

for a 2-engine aeroplane—the operator estimates that the landing minima for the adequate aerodrome at the estimated time of use of the aerodrome are not less than the landing minima required to comply with the requirements under Division 121.D.4 for the aerodrome; and
the operator has operational control for the flight in accordance with the operator’s exposition procedures mentioned in regulation 121.160.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Flights further than the threshold distance

content.p: Flying further than the threshold distance
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the aeroplane is flown further from an adequate aerodrome for the aeroplane than the threshold distance mentioned in subparagraph 121.030(1)(b)(ii) for the aeroplane; and
the operator does not hold an approval under regulation 121.010 to do so.
Requirements in the Manual of Standards
The Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe:
criteria for the grant of an approval mentioned in paragraph (1)(b); and
the form in which an application for such an approval must be made; and
factors to be considered by CASA in deciding whether or not to grant such an approval.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:

a requirement prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards in relation to conducting flights further from an adequate aerodrome than the threshold distance applies to the aeroplane for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
Exposition procedures

If an aeroplane is flown further from an adequate aerodrome for the aeroplane than the threshold distance mentioned in subparagraph 121.030(1)(b)(ii) for the aeroplane, the aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for conducting flights further than that distance.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
This regulation applies in relation to an aeroplane:
that has a maximum operational passenger seat configuration of more than 30; and
that does not comply with the ditching requirements of the relevant airworthiness standards for the aeroplane.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, during the flight:
the aeroplane is flown over water; and
the aeroplane is flown further than the distance mentioned in subregulation (3) from land.
The distance is the lesser of:
the distance the aeroplane can fly in 2 hours at its normal cruising speed in International Standard Atmosphere conditions and in still air; and
400 nautical miles.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Simulation of emergency or abnormal situations, or IMC

content.p: The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if an emergency or abnormal situation is simulated during the flight.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if IMC are simulated during the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Ferrying an aeroplane with one engine inoperative

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, during the flight, the aeroplane is ferried with one engine inoperative.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, during the flight, the aeroplane is operated in a way that does not meet a requirement or limitation that:
is set out in the aircraft flight manual instructions for the aeroplane; and
relates to the operation of the aeroplane.
Note: The pilot in command of the aeroplane must also ensure the aeroplane is operated in accordance with the aircraft flight manual instructions: see regulation 91.095.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Operator to have minimum equipment list for certain flights

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, there is no minimum equipment list for the aeroplane.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Duty statement to be available to crew

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a crew member is assigned to duty for the flight; and
the operator has not made a statement of the crew member’s duties for the flight available to the crew member; and
the crew member begins to carry out the crew member’s duties for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the flight.

The requirement is that, before a crew member for the flight begins to carry out a duty for the flight, the operator must make available to the member each checklist of normal, abnormal and emergency procedures for the aeroplane that is relevant to the duty.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

To avoid doubt, if a document is required to be carried on a flight of an aircraft under this Division, that requirement is taken to be satisfied if an electronic copy of the document is carried on the flight.
Note: Electronic copies may not satisfy the requirements of the law of a foreign country for flights that begin or end at an aerodrome outside Australian territory.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the following parts of the aeroplane operator’s exposition are not available to a crew member for the flight:
a part that is relevant to the duties of the crew member;
a part that is required for the conduct of the flight; and
the aeroplane begins the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Documents required by Part 121 Manual of Standards
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
a document prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph is not carried on the aeroplane; and
the aeroplane begins the flight.
Flight crew medical certificates
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a flight crew member’s medical certificate is not carried on the aeroplane for the flight; and
the flight crew member does not give CASA written notice that the certificate is not being carried on the aeroplane for the flight:
before the flight begins; or
if it is not practicable to give the notice before the flight begins—within 24 hours after the flight ends.
Flight crew licences
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a flight crew member’s flight crew licence is not carried on the aeroplane for the flight; and
the flight crew member does not give CASA written notice that the licence is not being carried on the aeroplane for the flight:
before the flight begins; or
if it is not practicable to give the notice before the flight begins—within 24 hours after the flight ends.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
under regulation 121.085, a document is required to be carried on the aeroplane for the flight; and
when the flight begins, the document is not readily accessible to the aeroplane’s crew.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Carriage of documents—flights that begin or end outside Australian territory

content.p: This regulation applies to a flight of an aeroplane that begins or ends at an aerodrome outside Australian territory.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
a document prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph is not carried on the aeroplane; and
the aeroplane begins the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following for a flight of the aeroplane:
procedures for keeping the documents prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards accessible to a person on the ground for the duration of the flight;
procedures for providing updated information to such a person during the flight if the information in the document requires updating during that time.
Operator—preparation of journey log
