The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the operator has not prepared a journey log for the flight:
that is capable of containing the information mentioned in subregulations (3) and (5); and
with a place for the pilot in command to verify the entries for the flight.
Pre-flight completion of journey log

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the information about the flight mentioned in subregulation (3) is not recorded in the journey log.
The information is the following:
the aeroplane’s registration mark or flight number;
the date of the flight;
for each crew member assigned to the flight:
the crew member’s name or another means to identify the crew member; and
the duties assigned to the crew member for the flight;
for the flight:
the place of departure; and
the time the flight begins;
the amount of fuel added to the aeroplane’s fuel tanks before the flight begins (if any);
the amount of fuel in the aeroplane’s fuel tanks when the flight begins.
Post-flight completion of journey log

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if the information about the flight mentioned in subregulation (5) is not recorded in the journey log for the flight as soon as practicable after the flight ends.
The information is the following:
the place of arrival;
the time the flight ends;
the duration of the flight;
the amount of fuel in the aeroplane’s fuel tanks when the flight ends;
incidents and observations (if any) relevant to the flight.
Exception to completion of journey log

Subregulations (1), (2) and (4) do not apply to the operator or the pilot in command in relation to information mentioned in those subregulations if, by the time it is required to be recorded, the information is:
recorded in another document kept by the operator; or
readily available to the operator from another source.
Note: An example for paragraph (a) is an operational flight plan kept by the operator for the flight.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (6): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

The operator of an aeroplane for a flight that is a passenger transport operation or a medical transport operation contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the operator has not prepared a passenger list for the flight that contains the information mentioned in subregulation (2).
The information is the following:
the aeroplane’s registration mark or flight number;
the name of each passenger;
the places of departure and destination for each passenger;
the number of infants carried;
the date, and estimated time of departure, of the flight.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to the operator in relation to information mentioned in that subregulation if, by the time it is required to be recorded, the information is:
recorded in another document kept by the operator; or
readily available to the operator from another source.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (3): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

section.heading: Flight preparation forms for flights that begin or end outside Australian territory

content.p: This regulation applies to a flight of an aeroplane that begins or ends at an aerodrome outside Australian territory.

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the pilot in command has not signed a flight preparation form certifying that the pilot in command is satisfied of the matters mentioned in subregulation (3).
The matters are the following:
the aeroplane can be operated during the flight in accordance with its configuration deviation list (if any);
the parts of the operator’s exposition required to be available to the aeroplane’s crew before the flight by regulation 121.080 are available;
the requirements and limitations in the operator’s exposition relating to the flight can be complied with for the flight;
regulations 121.085 and 121.095 are being complied with for the flight;
equipment required to be fitted to, or carried on, the aeroplane for the flight by Subpart 121.K is fitted to, or carried on, the aeroplane in accordance with that Subpart;
equipment mentioned in paragraph (e) is:
operative; or
inoperative, and permitted to be inoperative for the flight under these Regulations;
the aeroplane’s take-off, en-route and landing performance capabilities meet the performance requirements for the circumstances and conditions expected during the flight;
the aeroplane’s weight and balance will remain within the aeroplane’s weight and balance limits throughout the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

division.heading: Reporting and recording defects and incidents etc.

section.heading: Procedures for reporting and recording defects etc.

content.p: An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the reporting and recording by a flight crew member for a flight of the aeroplane of any of the following that occur during the flight:
an abnormal instrument indication;
abnormal behaviour by the aeroplane;
exceedence of an operating limit specified in the aircraft flight manual instructions for the aeroplane;
a defect in the aeroplane.

section.heading: Procedures for reporting and recording incidents

content.p: An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the reporting and recording by crew members of incidents relating to a flight of the aeroplane that endanger, or could endanger, the safe operation of the aeroplane.

division.heading: Search and rescue services and emergency and survival equipment

section.heading: Information about search and rescue services

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, information about the search and rescue services relevant to the flight is not readily accessible to the flight crew members for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Information about emergency and survival equipment

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the Part 121 Manual of Standards prescribes an item of equipment for the purposes of this regulation; and
when the flight begins, the information prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards for that equipment is not available for immediate communication by the operator to a rescue coordination centre.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Crew activities necessary for safe operation

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator requires a crew member for the flight to perform an activity during take-off, initial climb, final approach or landing of the aeroplane for the flight; and
the activity is not necessary for the safe operation of the aeroplane.
A crew member for a flight of an aeroplane contravenes this subregulation if:
the crew member performs an activity during take-off, initial climb, final approach or landing of the aeroplane for the flight; and
the activity is not necessary for the safe operation of the aeroplane.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, before a member of the operator’s personnel carries out a ground support duty for the flight, the member has not met a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2).
The requirements are the following:
the member must have successfully completed training for the duty;
the member must have been assessed as competent to carry out the duty.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Duty statement to be available to ground support personnel

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a member of the operator’s personnel is assigned to carry out a ground support duty for the flight; and
the operator has not made a statement of the member’s duties for the flight available to the member; and
the member begins to carry out the duty for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
(1) This regulation applies to an aeroplane that is required to be equipped with a cockpit door under regulation 4.68 of the Aviation Transport Security Regulations 2005.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
during the flight, a person enters the cockpit; and
the person is not a person mentioned in subregulation (3).
The persons are the following:
an authorised officer who is carrying out an audit, check, examination, inspection or test under these Regulations;
(b) a person who is permitted to enter the cockpit by regulation 4.67 of the Aviation Transport Security Regulations 2005.
Note: A person is not allowed to enter the cockpit after take-off unless the person holds appropriate identification: see paragraph 4.67(4)(b) of the Aviation Transport Security Regulations 2005.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
during the flight, a person other than a crew member for the flight enters the cockpit; and
the person is not briefed by the pilot in command or the co-pilot on the safety procedures that are relevant to the cockpit:
before the person enters the cockpit; or
as soon as practicable after the person enters the cockpit.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 121.D—Operational procedures
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for determining how operational control for a flight of the aeroplane is to be exercised and by whom.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for complying with the following for a flight of the aeroplane:
the flight preparation (weather assessments) requirements;
the flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirements.
(1) The Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements relating to flight preparation and alternate aerodromes (the flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirements).
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if a flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirement is not met for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, an operational flight plan that meets the requirements mentioned in subregulation (2) has not been prepared for the flight.
The requirements are the following:
the flight plan must be prepared having regard to:
the safety of the aeroplane, and of the people on board the aeroplane, during the flight; and
the aeroplane’s performance; and
the expected aeroplane operating limitations and conditions for the flight; and
meteorological conditions for the flight;
the flight plan must contain the information prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the Part 121 Manual of Standards prescribes information about the flight for the purposes of this subregulation; and
that information is not recorded in the operational flight plan for the flight:
unless subparagraph (ii) applies—before the flight ends; or
if it is not practicable to record the information before the flight ends—as soon as practicable after the flight ends.

Subregulation (1) or (3) does not apply to the operator or the pilot in command in relation to information required to be included in the operational flight plan under that subregulation if, by the time it is required to be recorded, the information is:
recorded in another document kept by the operator; or
readily available to the operator from another source.
Note: An example for paragraph (a) is a journey log kept by the operator for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (4): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the flight.
The requirements are the following:
the pilot in command of the aeroplane must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) before and during the flight;
each person in the operator’s organisation who is responsible for flight planning for the flight must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) before the flight;
each person in the operator’s organisation who is responsible for flight replanning for the flight must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) during the flight;
each person in the operator’s organisation who exercises operational control for the flight must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) before and during the flight.
The information is the following:
authorised weather forecasts and authorised weather reports:
in relation to the flight; and
if a destination alternate aerodrome is required for the flight by the flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirements—in relation to the destination alternate aerodrome;
NOTAMs for the flight;
the suitability for a take-off or landing by the aeroplane of:
the departure and planned destination aerodromes for the flight; and
(ii) if a destination alternate aerodrome is required for the flight by the flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirements—the destination alternate aerodrome.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Take-off and landing minima for aerodromes

content.p: If an aeroplane conducts an IFR flight to or from an aerodrome, the aeroplane operator’s exposition must include:
procedures for determining take-off minima that meet the requirements mentioned in subregulation (2); and
procedures for determining landing minima that meet the requirement mentioned in subregulation (3).
The requirements are the following:
the take-off minima must not be less than the take-off minima prescribed by the take-off minima requirements for the aerodrome;
the take-off minima must be sufficient to enable the pilot in command to control the aeroplane if it is necessary to conduct a discontinued take-off in adverse circumstances;
for a multi-engine aeroplane—the take-off minima must be sufficient to enable the pilot in command to control the aeroplane if it is necessary to conduct a continued take-off after:
failure of the aeroplane’s critical engine; or
if the aeroplane does not have a critical engine—the failure of an engine.
The requirement is that the landing minima must not be less than the landing minima prescribed by the landing minima requirements for the aerodrome, including for an approach with visual circling.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the operator has not established:
for each route or route segment for the flight for which there is a published lowest safe altitude—the published lowest safe altitude for the route or route segment; and
for each route or route segment for the flight for which there is no published lowest safe altitude—the lowest safe altitude for the route or route segment.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
each type of low-visibility operation conducted using the aeroplane;
the aircraft systems required to be used for each type of those operations;
the aerodrome facilities required to conduct each type of those operations;
the training and qualifications required for the aeroplane’s flight crew members for each type of those operations;
the requirements to be met by the aeroplane’s flight crew members during each of those operations.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures about conducting stabilised approaches to land at an aerodrome.

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if the aeroplane takes off from, or lands at, an aerodrome that does not meet a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2).
The requirements are the following:
the aerodrome must be suitable for the aeroplane to take-off and land;
the aerodrome must be:
a certified aerodrome that complies with the standards mentioned in the Part 139 Manual of Standards; or
an aerodrome for which the operator’s exposition includes the matters required by subregulation 121.210(1).
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the aeroplane has a maximum certificated passenger seating capacity of 20 or more; and
the aeroplane is a turbine-engine aeroplane (other than a turbine-engine propeller-driven aeroplane); and
the aeroplane lands on an aerodrome runway; and
the aerodrome is the planned destination aerodrome; and
the aerodrome runway does not meet the requirement mentioned in subregulation (4).
The requirement is that:
the runway is equipped with an approved visual approach slope indicator system in accordance with Part 139; or
both of the following are satisfied:
the runway is equipped with an approved visual approach slope indicator system in accordance with Part 139 that has been inoperative for no more than 7 days before the aeroplane lands on the runway;
the operator’s exposition includes procedures for conducting an approach and landing on a runway with such a system inoperative; or
the aeroplane is equipped or fitted with an approach slope indicator system mentioned in the operator’s exposition that is suitable for use for the runway; or
the operator holds an approval for the aeroplane and the runway under regulation 121.010.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Procedures to determine information about aerodromes

content.p: An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
if the information mentioned in subregulation (2) for an aerodrome mentioned in subregulation (3) is not published in the AIP—procedures to determine the information for the aerodrome;
the special procedures and restrictions (if any) that the operator requires the flight crew of the aeroplane to use at an aerodrome mentioned in subregulation (3), including:
engine failure procedures; and
obstacle clearance procedures;

procedures for the pilot in command to plan a take-off from, or a landing at, an aerodrome not mentioned in subregulation (3), including a procedure to determine the kinds of information mentioned in subregulation (2) for the aerodrome.
The information is the following:
runway or strip lengths, widths, directions, slopes and surface types for the aerodrome;
the location of taxiways and turning nodes (if any);
the aerodrome’s elevation;
the location on the aerodrome of the aerodrome reference point (if any);
the location of the aerodrome’s windsocks;
the aids to navigation and communication facilities available at the aerodrome (if any);
the limitations (if any) on the use of the aerodrome;
the special procedures (if any) in use at the aerodrome, in flight or on the ground or water;
a contact person capable of providing information about the condition of the aerodrome.
The aerodromes are the following for a flight of the aeroplane:
the departure aerodrome;
the planned destination aerodrome;
any alternate aerodromes required for the flight by the flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirements.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures to ensure the safety of persons in the vicinity of an aeroplane when any of the following circumstances apply:
a person is embarking or disembarking the aeroplane;
a passenger is embarking or disembarking, or on board, the aeroplane while an engine of the aeroplane is operating but the aeroplane is not being flown or fuelled;
the aeroplane is being loaded or unloaded;
the aeroplane is being operated at an aerodrome.

section.heading: Taking off from and landing on narrow runways

content.p: This regulation applies in relation to an aeroplane if:
the aeroplane takes off from, or lands on, a runway; and
(b) the width of the runway (a narrow runway) is less than the width for the aeroplane worked out in the manner prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph; and
the aeroplane has a maximum certificated take-off weight of more than 5,700 kg; and
the aeroplane is of a type first type certificated in its country of manufacture on or after 1 March 1978.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the aeroplane takes off from, or lands on, a narrow runway; and
the aircraft flight manual instructions for the aeroplane do not include requirements for the operation of the aeroplane on a narrow runway.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for taking off from, or landing on, a narrow runway.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures relating to the training required for the aeroplane’s flight crew to conduct a take-off from, or a landing on, a narrow runway.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures to ensure that a flight of the aeroplane is conducted in accordance with the requirements mentioned in subregulation 121.235(1).

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the aeroplane is not carrying sufficient oil to complete the flight safely.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements relating to fuel for aeroplanes, including (but not limited to) the following:
matters that must be considered when determining whether an aeroplane has sufficient fuel to complete a flight safely;
the amounts of fuel that must be carried on board an aeroplane for a flight;
procedures for monitoring amounts of fuel during a flight;
procedures to be followed if fuel reaches specified amounts during a flight.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the pilot is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1) for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1) for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures to ensure the aeroplane is fuelled safely;

procedures relating to the safety of passengers for a flight of the aeroplane who are embarking or disembarking, or on board, the aeroplane during fuelling, including the normal, emergency and communication procedures to be followed by the following persons:
any cabin crew for the flight;
any flight crew members for the flight who are on duty in the cockpit;
any of the operator’s personnel who carry out a ground support duty for the flight;

if the operator permits a person to operate low-risk electronic devices inside the cabin of the aeroplane while the aeroplane is being fuelled—procedures to ensure that, before an engine of the aeroplane is started, any effects of radio frequency emissions from those devices have been corrected.
This Division applies in relation to the operation of an aeroplane for a passenger transport operation or a medical transport operation.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures for carrying a restricted person on the aeroplane for a flight;
procedures to inform the pilot in command of the aeroplane for a flight about the carriage of a restricted person for a flight.
Note: For other requirements for the carriage of restricted persons who are deportees, removees and other persons in custody, see Division 4.5 of the Aviation Transport Security Regulations 2005.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the following:
securely stowing carry-on baggage;
determining the maximum weight and size of baggage that can be taken on the aeroplane as carry-on baggage;
determining the locations on the aeroplane where carry-on baggage can be stowed;
giving instructions to passengers about securely stowing carry-on baggage at the following times:
before take-off;
before landing;
any other time that the pilot in command directs.
This regulation applies in relation to a flight of an aeroplane for which regulation 121.630 requires the aeroplane to carry a cabin crew member.
The operator of the aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if an aisle of the aeroplane is obstructed during the flight, other than:
by a person; or
by cabin service equipment while cabin service is being provided to passengers.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Stowage of passenger service equipment etc.

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the aeroplane is:
taxiing; or
taking off; or
landing; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met.
The requirement is that any piece of passenger service equipment that could interfere with an evacuation of the aeroplane in an emergency must be secured in its stowed position.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the aeroplane is taxiing, taking off or landing; and
an item of galley equipment or a serving cart is not secured so as to prevent it from moving in the emergency landing conditions set out in the aeroplane’s type certification basis.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Passengers in emergency exit row seats

content.p: This regulation applies in relation to a flight of an aeroplane if regulation 121.630 requires a cabin crew member to be carried on the aeroplane for the flight.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the assigning of passengers to seats in an emergency exit row for a flight of the aeroplane.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the aeroplane is taxiing, taking off or landing, the requirement mentioned in subregulation (4) is not met.
The requirement is that at least one crew member for the flight must be satisfied that each person occupying an emergency exit row seat is a suitable person.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a person occupying an emergency exit row seat has not given the person’s agreement to a crew member to assist the crew members with the evacuation of the aeroplane in an emergency; and
the aeroplane begins the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3) or (5).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Carriage of passengers with reduced mobility

content.p: The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, during the flight, a passenger with reduced mobility occupies a seat where the passenger could:
hinder the crew in their safety duties; or
obstruct access to emergency equipment; or
hinder the evacuation of the aeroplane in an emergency.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a passenger with reduced mobility is carried on the flight; and
before the flight begins, the operator does not tell at least one of the following that the passenger is carried on the flight:
the pilot in command of the aeroplane for the flight;
if one cabin crew member is carried on the flight—the cabin crew member;
if more than one cabin crew member is carried on the flight—the person assigned to duty as the senior cabin crew member for the flight under regulation 121.660.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, a safety briefing card for the aeroplane is not available to each passenger on the aeroplane.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, a safety briefing card does not meet the requirements mentioned in subregulation (3).
The requirements are the following:
the safety briefing card must include any information prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards;
the only other information that may be included in the safety briefing card is the following:
information that is relevant to the type and model of aeroplane;
information that is relevant to the safety of the aeroplane and its passengers.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if a passenger is not given a safety briefing, instructions or demonstrations in accordance with the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this regulation.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if a safety briefing, instruction or demonstration includes:
information that is not relevant to the type and model of the aeroplane; or
information that is not relevant to the safety of the aeroplane and its passengers.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a passenger with reduced mobility will be carried on the flight; and

(b) before the aeroplane takes off for the flight, the passenger, or a person accompanying or assisting the passenger, is not asked by a crew member for the flight about the best way of helping the passenger if an emergency evacuation of the aeroplane is necessary.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Additional safety briefing for passengers in emergency exit rows

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a passenger is seated in an emergency exit row for the flight; and
the passenger will be required to operate the emergency exit if it becomes necessary to use the exit during the flight; and
before the flight begins, the passenger is not briefed by a crew member for the flight about what to do if it becomes necessary to use the exit.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Safety briefing in the event of an emergency

content.p: An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for briefing passengers on what to do if an emergency occurs during a flight of the aeroplane.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures for using airborne weather radar equipment;
procedures for conducting a flight without airborne weather radar equipment, for use if the equipment is inoperative.

section.heading: Head-up displays, enhanced vision systems and synthetic vision systems

content.p: This regulation applies in relation to an aeroplane if it is fitted with any of the following systems:
a head-up display;
an enhanced vision system;
a synthetic vision system.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following in relation to a flight of the aeroplane:
procedures for using each system mentioned in subregulation (1) that is fitted to the aeroplane during the flight;
procedures for conducting the flight without an element of the system, for use if the element is inoperative.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the use of protective breathing equipment that is required, under Subpart 121.K, to be fitted to, or carried on, the aeroplane.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include, for each configuration of the aeroplane operated by the operator, a description of the following:
the location of each hand-held fire extinguisher that is required, under Subpart 121.K, to be fitted to, or carried on, the aeroplane;
the extinguishing agent in each of the fire extinguishers.
This regulation applies to an aeroplane that is, or will be, used to conduct a flight for which the aeroplane is required, under Subpart 121.K, to carry one or more first-aid kits.
The aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures to ensure that the first-aid kits required under Subpart 121.K:
contain sufficient supplies for the number of persons to be carried on a flight of the aeroplane; and
are readily recognisable as first-aid kits; and
are readily accessible by each crew member for a flight when the aeroplane is on the ground or water and not in operation;
procedures for inspecting the first-aid kits;
procedures for replacing items in the first-aid kits.
The operator’s exposition must also include a list of the minimum contents of each first-aid kit for the aeroplane.

section.heading: Procedures relating to universal precaution kits

content.p: This regulation applies to an aeroplane that is, or will be, used to conduct a flight for which the aeroplane is required, under Subpart 121.K, to carry one or more universal precaution kits.
The aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures for inspecting the universal precaution kits required under Subpart 121.K;
procedures for replacing items in the universal precaution kits.
The operator’s exposition must also include a list of the minimum contents of each universal precaution kit for the aeroplane.

section.heading: Procedures relating to emergency medical kits

content.p: This regulation applies to an aeroplane that is, or will be, used to conduct a flight for which the aeroplane is required, under Subpart 121.K, to carry an emergency medical kit.
The aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures for inspecting the emergency medical kit;
procedures for replacing items in the emergency medical kit;

procedures for the administration and supply of prescription medicines in the emergency medical kit, including procedures to ensure that prescription medicines are administered only under the authority of a medical practitioner.
The operator’s exposition must also include a list of the minimum contents of the emergency medical kit.
This regulation applies to an aeroplane that is, or will be, used to conduct a flight for which the aeroplane is required, under Subpart 121.K, to carry one or more life rafts.
The aeroplane operator’s exposition must include a list of the minimum life-saving equipment carried on the aeroplane for each life raft.
This regulation applies to a flight of an aeroplane if:
the flight is in or through an area prescribed as a remote area by the Part 91 Manual of Standards; or
the aeroplane is required, under Subpart 121.K, to carry a life raft for the flight.
If an aeroplane is, or will be, used to conduct a flight to which this regulation applies, the operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures for determining the survival equipment required for the area in or through which the flight will be conducted;

(b) for a flight mentioned in paragraph (1)(b)—procedures for determining the pyrotechnic signalling devices required to ensure the distress signals, set out in Appendix 1 to Annex 2, Rules of the Air, to the Chicago Convention, can be made.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following in relation to a flight of the aeroplane:
procedures for the inspection of the aeroplane by the pilot in command before the flight if frost or icing conditions exist;
if ground de-icing and ground anti-icing measures are required for the flight—procedures for carrying out these measures before the flight;
procedures for using de-icing and anti-icing equipment (where fitted) during the flight.

section.heading: Procedures relating to portable electronic devices

content.p: An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the operation of portable electronic devices for a flight of the aeroplane.

section.heading: Procedures relating to carriage of animals

content.p: An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the carriage of animals for a flight of the aeroplane.
This regulation applies in relation to a flight of an aeroplane if, during the flight, the aeroplane enters the polar region.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the aeroplane is flown in the polar region during the flight; and
the operator does not hold an approval under regulation 121.010 to fly in the polar region.
The aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures for the following:
monitoring and dealing with fuel freezing;
ensuring communication capability for the duration of an operation that includes a flight in the polar region;
training the aeroplane’s flight crew in polar operations;
mitigating crew member and passenger exposure to cosmic radiation during solar flare activity;

if the aeroplane conducts a flight for which an alternate aerodrome in the polar region is required at a time of year when extreme climatic conditions are expected at the aerodrome—the carrying of at least 2 serviceable, cold weather, anti-exposure suits.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator’s exposition does not set a limit for the total cosmic radiation receivable inside the aeroplane’s cabin during the flight; and
the aeroplane is flown above flight level 490.
The operator of an aeroplane contravenes this subregulation if:

a flight crew member or cabin crew member of the operator’s personnel has, in the previous 12 month period, flown on a flight of an aeroplane operated by the operator during which the aeroplane was flown above flight level 490; and
the operator does not have a record of the total cosmic radiation dose received by the member during that period on such flights.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the aeroplane is flown above flight level 490; and
the aeroplane operator’s exposition sets a limit for the total cosmic radiation receivable inside the aeroplane’s cabin during the flight; and
the limit is exceeded during the flight; and
the pilot in command does not, as soon as practicable after the limit is exceeded, descend to the lowest altitude at which it is practicable to complete the flight safely.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if an emergency exit is obstructed at any of the following times:
while the aeroplane is taxiing;
while the aeroplane is taking off;
while the aeroplane is landing;
at any time that the pilot in command directs that the exit not be obstructed.
For the purposes of subregulation (1), an emergency exit is not taken to be obstructed by a passenger occupying a seat adjacent to the exit or a seat in a row of seats adjacent to the exit.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the flight.

The requirement is that the assignment of cabin crew seats to crew members for the flight must be in accordance with the emergency evacuation procedures for the aeroplane required by regulation 121.755.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a person, other than a crew member, is assigned to a cabin crew seat; and
the cabin crew seat is in a row of cabin crew seats adjacent to a floor level exit; and
the person is not a person to whom subregulation (4), (5) or (6) applies.
This subregulation applies to a person if:
the person is a crew member employed by the operator who has not been assigned to the flight by the operator; and
a passenger seat is not available for the person; and
the person is identified as an employee of the operator; and
the person is briefed by a cabin crew member for the flight on the following before the aeroplane takes off:
the operation and use of the seat and its restraint system;
the location and use of the oxygen system at the seat (if any);
the location and use of the life jacket for the seat;
the person’s responsibilities during an emergency.
This subregulation applies to a person if:
(a) the person is an authorised officer carrying out an in-flight passenger cabin inspection; and
a passenger seat is not available for the person; and
the person is briefed by a cabin crew member on the following before the aeroplane takes off:
the operation and use of the seat and its restraint system;
the location and use of the oxygen system at the seat (if any);
the location and use of the life jacket for the seat;
the person’s responsibilities during an emergency.
This subregulation applies to a person if:
the pilot in command:
declares an emergency; or
directs the cabin crew that abnormal circumstances exist for the flight; and
the person is an able-bodied person; and
a cabin crew member assigns the person to the cabin crew seat; and
the person is briefed by a cabin crew member on the person’s responsibilities while occupying the cabin crew seat.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: CASA approvals relating to take-offs and landings

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the aeroplane takes off or lands in circumstances mentioned in subregulation (2); and
the requirement in subregulation (3) is not met.
The circumstances are the aeroplane conducts a 3D instrument approach operation with an approach path angle of 4.5 degrees or more.
The requirement is that the operator must hold an approval under regulation 121.010 to conduct the take-off or landing in those circumstances.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 121.F—Performance
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the performance data in the aircraft flight manual instructions for the aeroplane does not comply with Annex 8 to the Chicago Convention; and
the aeroplane begins the flight.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
a calculation relating to the aeroplane’s performance for the flight is made for the purposes of this Subpart; and
data other than either of the following is used to make that calculation:
performance data set out in the aircraft flight manual instructions for the aeroplane;
performance data for which the aeroplane operator holds an approval under regulation 121.010.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements relating to take-off performance for a flight of an aeroplane.
Without limiting subregulation (1), the Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements that relate to one or more of the following:
the kinds of operations to be carried out during the flight;
characteristics of the aerodrome at which the aeroplane takes off;
characteristics of the route flown by the aeroplane;
characteristics of the aerodrome at which the aeroplane lands.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the pilot is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1) for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1) for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements relating to landing performance for a flight of an aeroplane.
Without limiting subregulation (1), the Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements relating to one or more of the following:
the aeroplane’s configuration;
the operation of any equipment for the flight;
characteristics of the aerodrome at which the aeroplane lands;
safety factor percentages to be applied.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the pilot is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1) for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1) for the flight; and
the requirement is not met for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Computerised performance data systems not fitted to aeroplanes

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:

a computerised system that is not fitted to the aeroplane is used as the primary means to make calculations relating to the aeroplane’s performance for the flight for the purposes of this Subpart; and
the system does not meet the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include procedures to allow the aeroplane’s flight path to meet the requirements mentioned in subregulation (2) if one engine becomes inoperative during take-off and the take-off is continued.
The requirements are that the aeroplane’s flight path must provide a safe route, clearing all obstacles along the flight path, for the aeroplane to land at either of the following aerodromes:
the departure aerodrome for the flight;
if the operational flight plan for the flight includes a take-off alternate aerodrome—the take-off alternate aerodrome.
The operator of a 3-engine or 4-engine aeroplane must include, in the operator’s exposition, procedures to follow if 2 engines become inoperative during the flight.
Subpart 121.J—Weight and balance

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the aeroplane is loaded in a way that contravenes the aeroplane’s weight and balance limits.

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, during the flight, the aeroplane ceases to be loaded in accordance with the aeroplane’s weight and balance limits.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include the following:
procedures for loading the aeroplane for a flight to comply with regulation 121.435;
procedures for working out the following weights for a flight of the aeroplane:
the total weight of the crew members and the carry-on baggage of the crew members;
the total weight of the passengers and the carry-on baggage of the passengers;
the total weight of the cargo (other than carry-on baggage);
the total weight of the usable fuel to be carried;
procedures to ensure that the aeroplane is loaded:
in accordance with the information for the loading of the aeroplane for the flight prepared by the person responsible for planning the loading of the aeroplane for the flight; and
by, or under the supervision of, the person responsible for supervising the loading of the aeroplane for the flight;

procedures setting out the circumstances in which a last-minute change to a load may be made, including procedures to ensure that a last-minute change to a load does not cause the aeroplane to exceed its weight and balance limits;
procedures for confirming the weight and balance documents;
procedures for offloading passengers or cargo to ensure that the aeroplane does not exceed its weight and balance limits.
For the purposes of subparagraphs (1)(b)(i) and (ii), the procedures must provide that the weights mentioned in those subparagraphs must be worked out:
by actual weighing; or
in accordance with a method for which the operator holds an approval under regulation 121.010; or
in accordance with the standard weights prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards.
For the purposes of subparagraph (1)(b)(iv), the procedures must provide that the weight of the usable fuel must be worked out as follows:
if the density of the fuel is known—by reference to its density and in accordance with a method set out in the procedures;
if the density of the fuel is not known—in accordance with a method set out in the procedures.

section.heading: Pilot in command must have information about aeroplane’s weight and balance

content.p: The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the pilot in command does not have the information about the aeroplane’s weight and balance that is prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Computerised weight and balance systems not fitted to aeroplanes

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
a computerised system that is not fitted to the aeroplane is used as the primary means to calculate the weight and balance of the aeroplane for the flight; and
the system does not meet the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the weight and balance documents for the flight do not meet the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 121.K—Equipment
The Part 121 Manual of Standards may prescribe requirements relating to:
the fitment and non-fitment of equipment to an aeroplane; and
the carrying of equipment on an aeroplane; and
equipment that is fitted to, or carried on, an aeroplane.
A person contravenes this subregulation if:
the person is subject to a requirement mentioned in subregulation (1); and
the requirement is not met.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 121.N—Flight crew
This Subpart also applies to the operation of a multi-engine aeroplane if:
either or both of paragraphs 121.005(1)(a) and (b) apply in relation to the aeroplane; and
the operator of the aeroplane holds an Australian air transport AOC that authorises the conduct of Part 121 operations; and
the operation is of a kind specified in the operator’s exposition.
Composition, number, qualifications and training
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met.
The requirements are as follows:
the composition of the aeroplane’s flight crew for the flight must comply with the aeroplane’s flight manual;
the flight crew must include at least 2 pilots;
at least one pilot occupying a pilot seat must have the experience required by regulation 121.480 for a flight crew member for the operator and the aeroplane;
if the flight is a kind of operation for which the operator’s exposition requires the carriage of additional flight crew members—the flight crew must include the additional flight crew members;
if the flight is a kind of operation for which these Regulations require the carriage of additional flight crew members—the flight crew must include the additional flight crew members;
each flight crew member must be qualified under regulation 121.490, 121.495 or 121.500 to carry out the duties assigned to the flight crew member by the operator for the flight;

if the operator’s exposition includes requirements, in accordance with regulation 121.515, in relation to knowledge that the pilot in command must have of the route of, and aerodromes for, the flight—the pilot in command must meet the requirements;
each flight crew member must have the recent experience for the flight required by Division 121.N.4;
each flight crew member must meet the initial training requirements under regulation 121.555 for the operator;
each flight crew member must meet the conversion training requirements under subregulation 121.560(1) for the operator and the aeroplane;
each flight crew member assigned to duty for unsupervised line flying for the flight must meet the conversion training requirement under subregulation 121.560(2) for the operator and the aeroplane;
each flight crew member must meet the recurrent training and checking requirements under subregulation 121.570(1) for the flight;
each flight crew member assigned to duty for unsupervised line flying for the flight must meet the recurrent training and checking requirements under subregulation 121.570(2) for the flight;
each flight crew member for whom, under the operator’s exposition, differences training for the aeroplane is required, must have successfully completed the differences training:
for the aeroplane; and
for equipment that is required under Subpart 121.K to be fitted to, or carried on, the aeroplane and may be used by the flight crew member in connection with operating the aeroplane.
For the purposes of paragraph (2)(d), the operator’s exposition must include the kinds of operation (if any) for which additional flight crew members must be carried.
Training or checking involving safety or emergency equipment

The operator of an aeroplane contravenes this subregulation if training or checking mentioned in subregulation (2), to the extent that it involves safety equipment or emergency equipment, is conducted other than by a person who holds an approval under regulation 121.010.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
For the purposes of paragraph 121.475(2)(c), the experience required for a flight crew member for an aeroplane operator and an aeroplane is that:
the flight crew member:
holds a rating that covers the aeroplane; or
has successfully completed command training that complies with regulation 121.565 for the operator and an aeroplane; and
the flight crew member has completed the flying experience mentioned in subregulation (2).
For the purposes of paragraph (1)(b), the flying experience:
must be the number of hours and sectors mentioned in subregulation (3) in aeroplanes of that kind; and
must be completed as part of line operations; and
may include experience while the flight crew member is flying under supervision.
For the purposes of paragraph (2)(a), the number of hours and sectors is:
at least 100 hours and 10 sectors; or

if the aeroplane operator by whom the flight crew member is employed holds an approval under regulation 121.010 for a different numbers of hours and sectors for the flight crew member—at least that number of hours and sectors.
CASA may grant the approval mentioned in paragraph (3)(b) only if satisfied that there are special circumstances in relation to the operator’s operation that justify the grant of the approval.
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator assigns a person to duty as a flight crew member for the flight; and
the person has not been assessed by the operator, in accordance with the operator’s training and checking system, as competent to perform the duties assigned to the person for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Assignment to duty as pilot in command

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, none of the pilots assigned as flight crew members for the flight is assigned to duty as the pilot in command of the aeroplane for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A pilot is qualified as pilot in command for a flight of an aeroplane if:
the pilot meets the minimum flying experience requirements specified, in accordance with subregulation (2), in the aeroplane operator’s exposition for the aeroplane; and
the pilot has successfully completed command training that complies with regulation 121.565 for the aeroplane operator and an aeroplane; and
the pilot is:
if the aeroplane is an Australian aircraft—authorised to pilot the aeroplane during the flight as pilot in command under Part 61; or
if the aeroplane is a foreign registered aircraft—authorised to pilot the aeroplane during the flight as pilot in command by the aeroplane’s State of registry.
For the purposes of paragraph (1)(a), the aeroplane operator’s exposition must include minimum flying experience requirements for all aeroplanes operated by the operator for Part 121 operations.
A pilot is qualified as co-pilot for a flight of an aeroplane if:
the pilot is:
if the aeroplane is an Australian aircraft—authorised to pilot the aeroplane during the flight as co-pilot under Part 61; or
if the aeroplane is a foreign registered aircraft—authorised to pilot the aeroplane during the flight as co-pilot by the aeroplane’s State of registry; and
the pilot has completed supervised line flying on an aeroplane of that kind as co-pilot for the number of sectors or flight hours mentioned in the aeroplane operator’s exposition.
A pilot is qualified as co-pilot for a flight of an aeroplane if the pilot is qualified under regulation 121.495 as pilot in command for the flight.
A pilot is qualified as cruise relief co-pilot for a flight of an aeroplane if:
the pilot is:
if the aeroplane is an Australian aircraft—authorised to pilot the aeroplane during the flight as cruise relief co-pilot under Part 61; or
if the aeroplane is a foreign registered aircraft—authorised to pilot the aeroplane during the flight as cruise relief co-pilot by the aeroplane’s State of registry; and
the pilot has completed supervised line flying on an aeroplane of that kind as cruise relief co-pilot for the number of sectors or flight hours mentioned in the aeroplane operator’s exposition.
A pilot is qualified as cruise relief co-pilot for a flight of an aeroplane if the pilot is:
qualified under regulation 121.495 as pilot in command for the flight; or
qualified under regulation 121.500 as co-pilot for the flight.

section.heading: Use of approved flight simulators for training or checking

content.p: Seating capacity of more than 19 and certain other aeroplanes
Subregulation (2) applies to:
an aeroplane with a maximum certificated passenger seating capacity of more than 19; or
an aeroplane of a kind prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards.
The operator of the aeroplane contravenes this subregulation if:
a flight crew member of the operator’s personnel undertakes training or checking, in accordance with this Subpart, for the aeroplane; and
the training or checking involves a simulated engine or system failure that affects, or is likely to affect, the aeroplane’s performance or handling characteristics; and

there is an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane (whether in Australia, or in a recognised foreign State within the meaning of regulation 61.010) that is available for use, within the meaning of subregulation (5), by the operator for the training or checking; and
the training or checking is conducted other than in the flight simulator.
Seating capacity of 19 or less
Subregulation (4) applies to an aeroplane with a maximum certificated passenger seating capacity of 19 or less, other than an aeroplane to which subregulation (2) applies.
The operator of the aeroplane contravenes this subregulation if:
a flight crew member of the operator’s personnel undertakes training or checking, in accordance with this Subpart, for the aeroplane; and
the training or checking involves a simulated engine or system failure that affects, or is likely to affect, the aeroplane’s performance or handling characteristics; and
there is an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane in Australia that is available for use, within the meaning of subregulation (5), by the operator for the training or checking; and
the training or checking is conducted other than in the flight simulator.
Available for use
For the purposes of paragraphs (2)(b) and (4)(b), an approved flight simulator is available for use by an operator if the flight simulator:
is available for the operator to use, or to reserve for use; and
is offered for use on a commercial basis; and
is serviceable.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An aeroplane operator’s exposition must include requirements in relation to the knowledge that a pilot in command of the aeroplane for a flight must have of:
the route of the flight; and
the departure aerodrome and the planned destination aerodrome for the flight; and
any alternate aerodrome required for the flight by the flight preparation (Part 121 alternate aerodromes) requirements.

division.heading: Operation of aeroplanes of different type ratings

content.p: This Division applies in relation to the operator of an aeroplane if:
under the operator’s AOC, the operator operates aeroplanes of more than one type rating for Part 121 operations; and
the operator assigns, or is likely to assign, a flight crew member employed by the operator to duty on aeroplanes of more than one type rating.

section.heading: Assignment of flight crew to aeroplanes of different type ratings

content.p: The operator’s exposition must include the following:
a description of the circumstances in which the operator may assign a flight crew member to duty on aeroplanes of more than one type rating;
the combinations of aeroplanes with different type ratings that a single flight crew member may be assigned to duty on by the operator;

the flying experience, checks and training that a flight crew member must gain or complete, while the flight crew member is employed by the operator, before being assigned to duty on aeroplanes of more than one type rating;

procedures to ensure that, if a flight crew member is assigned to duty on aeroplanes with different type ratings within one tour of duty, the flight crew member has adequate time between flights on aeroplanes with different ratings for the flight crew member to prepare for duty.

section.heading: Credit for checks, qualifications, training and experience

content.p: Subregulation (2) applies if an operator holds an approval under regulation 121.010 in relation to:
a particular check or qualification, or particular training or experience, mentioned in this Subpart; and
(b) aeroplanes of 2 particular type ratings (the first type rating and the second type rating).
Note: See also regulation 121.575 in relation to Part 121 proficiency checks completed for a previous operator.

For the purposes of these Regulations, the successful completion, by a flight crew member of the operator’s personnel, of the check, qualification, training or experience for an aeroplane of the first type rating is taken to also be the successful completion by the flight crew member of the check, qualification, training or experience for an aeroplane of the second type rating.
CASA may grant an approval mentioned in subregulation (1) only if satisfied that:

the check, qualification, training or experience for an aeroplane of the first type rating is sufficiently similar to the check, qualification, training or experience for an aeroplane of the second type rating; and
an aeroplane of the first type rating and second type rating are sufficiently similar in relation to:
their level of technology; and
their operational procedures; and
their handling characteristics.
Example: For the purposes of subparagraph (b)(i), the level of technology for an aeroplane might involve the following:
the aeroplane’s flight management system;
the aeroplane’s auto-pilot system;
the aeroplane’s flight instrumentation.
The operator and the pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the pilot in command delegates the conduct of the flight; and
the delegation is not permitted by either subregulation (2) or (3).
General
The pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight may delegate the conduct of the flight to a pilot who is qualified under regulation 121.495 as pilot in command for the flight.
Flight above flight level 200
The pilot in command of an aeroplane for a flight may delegate the conduct of the flight above flight level 200 to a pilot who meets the requirements mentioned in subregulation (4).
The requirements are as follows:
the pilot must hold an air transport pilot licence;
the pilot must be qualified under regulation 121.500 as co-pilot for the flight;
the pilot must have the flying experience required by regulation 121.480 for the flight;
the pilot must have the knowledge of the route of the flight required by the operator’s exposition.
For the purposes of paragraph (4)(d), the operator’s exposition must include the knowledge the pilot must have of the route of the flight.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Pilot in command and co-pilot—recent experience requirements

content.p: Operator
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator assigns a pilot to duty as pilot in command or co-pilot of the aeroplane for the flight; and
the pilot does not have the recent experience required for the flight by subregulation (3).
Pilot
A pilot of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the pilot operates the aeroplane as pilot in command or co-pilot for the flight; and
the pilot does not have the recent experience required for the flight by subregulation (3).
Recent experience requirements
The recent experience required for a flight is:
within 90 days before the flight, the pilot must meet at least one of the requirements mentioned in subregulation (4); or
if it is not practicable for the pilot to comply with paragraph (a)—the flight experience required under the aeroplane operator’s exposition.
For the purposes of paragraph (3)(a), the requirements are as follows:
the pilot has carried out, in an aeroplane of that kind or an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane:
at least 3 take-offs that comply with subregulation (5) while controlling the aeroplane or simulator; and
at least 3 landings while controlling the aeroplane or simulator;
the pilot has passed a flight test for the grant of a pilot licence or a rating on a pilot licence in an aeroplane of that kind or an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane;
the pilot has successfully completed a Part 121 proficiency check for the operator and an aeroplane of that kind.
For the purposes of subparagraph (4)(a)(i), each take-off must be followed by a climb to at least 500 ft AGL.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Operator
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator assigns a pilot to duty as cruise relief co-pilot for the flight; and
the pilot has not, within 90 days before the flight, done at least one of the following:
completed at least 2 hours of simulated flight time as co-pilot in an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane;
passed a flight test for the grant of a pilot licence or a rating on a pilot licence in an aeroplane of that kind or an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane;
exercised the privileges of a pilot licence or a rating on a pilot licence that covers the aeroplane.
Pilot
A pilot of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the pilot operates the aeroplane as cruise relief co-pilot for the flight; and
the pilot has not, within 90 days before the flight, done at least one of the following:
completed at least 2 hours of simulated flight time as co-pilot in an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane;
passed a flight test for the grant of a pilot licence or a rating on a pilot licence in an aeroplane of that kind or an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane;
exercised the privileges of a pilot licence or a rating on a pilot licence that covers the aeroplane.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Operator
The operator of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator assigns a flight engineer to duty as flight engineer of the aeroplane for the flight; and
the flight engineer does not have the recent experience required under regulation 61.1335 (limitations on exercise of privileges of flight engineer licences—recent experience) for the flight.
Flight engineer
A flight engineer of an aeroplane for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the flight engineer performs a duty that is essential to the operation of the aeroplane for the flight; and
the flight engineer does not have the recent experience required under regulation 61.1335 (limitations on exercise of privileges of flight engineer licences—recent experience) for the flight.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
For the purposes of paragraph 121.475(2)(i), a flight crew member meets the initial training requirements for an operator of an aeroplane if:
the flight crew member has completed the operator’s initial training for a flight crew member; and
the initial training meets the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards; and
the flight crew member has successfully completed an initial training check in accordance with the operator’s exposition.
Without limiting paragraph (1)(b), the requirements may relate to training facilities or devices.
For the purposes of paragraph 121.475(2)(j), a flight crew member meets the conversion training requirements under this subregulation for an operator of an aeroplane and the aeroplane if:
the flight crew member has completed training, for an aeroplane of that kind, that meets the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards; and
the training is conducted by:
an individual employed by the operator to conduct the training; or
a Part 142 operator with which the operator has a contract for the Part 142 operator to conduct the training for the operator.

(2) For the purposes of paragraph 121.475(2)(k), a flight crew member meets the conversion training requirement under this subregulation for an operator of an aeroplane and the aeroplane if the flight crew member has completed supervised line flying in an aeroplane of that kind.
The supervised line flying mentioned in subregulation (2) must have been completed after the flight crew member has successfully completed all of the following:
a Part 121 proficiency check for the operator and the aeroplane;
a valid annual emergency and safety equipment check for the operator and the aeroplane under regulation 121.605;
a valid 3 yearly emergency and safety equipment check for the operator and the aeroplane under regulation 121.615.
Command training for a pilot for an aeroplane operator and an aeroplane must include the following:
either:
flying training conducted in an aeroplane of that kind; or
if there is an approved flight simulator for the aeroplane—training conducted in the approved flight simulator;
successful completion of a Part 121 proficiency check, for the operator and the aeroplane, for a pilot in command of the aeroplane;
training in the responsibilities of the pilot in command of an aeroplane of that kind;
training in relation to pilot incapacitation;
supervised line flying on an aeroplane of that kind as pilot in command under supervision for at least the number of sectors required by the operator’s exposition;
successful completion of a line check that complies with regulation 121.590 for a pilot in command for an aeroplane of that kind.
For the purposes of paragraph 121.475(2)(l), a flight crew member meets the recurrent training and checking requirements for a flight of an aeroplane if the flight crew member:
holds the following for the aeroplane operator and the aeroplane:
a valid Part 121 proficiency check under regulation 121.575;
a valid refresher check under regulation 121.595;
a valid annual emergency and safety equipment check under regulation 121.605;
a valid 3 yearly emergency and safety equipment check under regulation 121.615; and
has completed, within the previous 12 months, recurrent flight training, in accordance with the requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards, for an aeroplane of that kind.

For the purposes of paragraph 121.475(2)(m), a flight crew member meets the recurrent training and checking requirements for a flight of an aeroplane if the flight crew member holds a valid line check under regulation 121.585 for the aeroplane operator and the aeroplane.
Holding a valid check
(1) If a person successfully completes a Part 121 proficiency check for the operator of an aeroplane and an aeroplane on a day (the completion day), the check is valid for the period:
beginning on the completion day; and
ending at the earliest of the following times:
the beginning of the day the person successfully completes another Part 121 proficiency check for the operator and the aeroplane;
the end of the 8 month period beginning on the completion day;

(iii) if the person has, within the 12 month period ending immediately before the completion day, successfully completed one or more Part 121 proficiency checks (the previous checks) for the operator and the aeroplane—the end of the 12 month period beginning on the day the most recent of the previous checks was successfully completed.
When a check completed for a previous operator is valid
If:

(a) an operator (the current operator) of an aeroplane of a particular kind that has a maximum certificated passenger seating capacity of 19 or less holds an approval under regulation 121.010 in relation to Part 121 proficiency checks completed for another particular operator (the previous operator) and an aeroplane of that kind; and
a person holds a valid Part 121 proficiency check for the previous operator and an aeroplane of that kind;
the person is taken, for the purposes of these Regulations, to hold a valid Part 121 proficiency check for the current operator and an aeroplane of that kind.
Pilots

A proficiency check for a pilot for an aeroplane must, in accordance with any requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards, check the competence of the pilot in carrying out normal, abnormal and emergency procedures in relation to the flying of an aeroplane of that kind while performing duties at their normal pilot seat.
The check for the pilot must be conducted by an individual:
who is either:
employed by the operator to conduct the check; or
employed by a Part 142 operator with which the operator has a contract for the Part 142 operator to conduct the check for the operator; and
who meets the requirements mentioned in subregulation (3).
For the purposes of paragraph (2)(b), the individual must:
hold:
a flight examiner rating for an aeroplane of that kind; or
an approval under regulation 121.010 to conduct a Part 121 proficiency check for an aeroplane of that kind; and
have successfully completed training in human factors principles and non-technical skills.
Flight engineers

A proficiency check for a flight engineer for an aeroplane must, in accordance with any requirements prescribed by the Part 121 Manual of Standards, check the competence of the flight engineer in carrying out the duties of a flight engineer in relation to the operation of an aeroplane of that kind while acting as part of a normal flight crew for the aeroplane.
The check for the flight engineer must be conducted by an individual:
who is either:
employed by the operator to conduct the check; or
employed by a Part 142 operator with which the operator has a contract for the Part 142 operator to conduct the check for the operator; and
who meets the requirements mentioned in subregulation (6).
For the purposes of paragraph (5)(b), the individual must:
hold:
a flight engineer examiner rating for an aeroplane of that kind; or
an approval under regulation 121.010 to conduct a Part 121 proficiency check for an aeroplane of that kind; and
have successfully completed training in human factors principles and non-technical skills.
A flight crew member holds a valid line check for the operator of an aeroplane and the aeroplane if:
