Subpart 132.A—Preliminary
Subpart 132.A sets out preliminary matters, including the relationship of Part 132 to other requirements for operating limited category aircraft.
Subpart 132.B sets out the general requirements for flying limited category aircraft.
Subpart 132.C sets out the requirements for conducting adventure flights.
Subpart 132.D sets out the certification and airworthiness requirements for limited category aircraft.
In these Regulations:
administering authority, for a limited category aircraft, means:
a limited category organisation in relation to the aircraft; or
if there is no limited category organisation in relation to the aircraft—CASA.

adventure flight procedures, for a limited category aircraft, means procedures for conducting an adventure flight using the aircraft for which the operator of the aircraft holds an approval granted by the administering authority for the aircraft under regulation 132.035.
approved airframe life, for a limited category aircraft, means the airframe life stated in the most recent of the following:
the aircraft’s approved design;
a variation (if any) of the airframe life by the national aviation authority of the country of the aircraft’s manufacture;
if the aircraft is an ex-armed forces aircraft—a variation (if any) of the airframe life by the armed force that operated the aircraft or for which the aircraft was manufactured;
a certificate (if any) stating an airframe life for the aircraft’s airframe given by the administering authority for the aircraft.
Note: Airframe life may be expressed in a number of ways, including the amount of operating time, the number of operating cycles or a calendar period.
ex-armed forces aircraft means:

a version of an aircraft that has been manufactured in accordance with the requirements of, and accepted for use by, an armed force of any country (whether or not it has been used by such a force); or
a particular aircraft:
to which paragraph (a) does not apply; and
that has been operated by an armed force of any country.
historic aircraft means:
an aircraft that was manufactured before 1 January 1960; or
an Australian-manufactured aircraft of a type that is no longer being manufactured; or
a replica of an aircraft mentioned in paragraph (a) or (b); or
an aircraft prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards for this paragraph.
limited category aircraft means an aircraft for which a special certificate of airworthiness mentioned in regulation 21.189 is in force.
limited category certificate means a special certificate of airworthiness to which an applicant is entitled under regulation 21.189.
limited category organisation means an organisation that is approved under regulation 262AN of CAR to perform functions in relation to limited category aircraft.

permit index number, for an aircraft for which a limited category certificate has been issued, means the permit index number most recently assigned to the aircraft under subregulation 21.176(5) or Division 132.D.2.

section.heading: Definition of adventure flight for limited category aircraft

content.p: A flight of a limited category aircraft is an adventure flight if it is a flight:
on which a passenger is carried; and
that is:
conducted for hire or reward; or
publicly available.

section.heading: Definition of major for modifications and repairs for limited category aircraft

content.p: (1) A modification or repair to a limited category aircraft is a major modification or repair if the modification or repair has a significant effect on a characteristic affecting the aircraft’s airworthiness, including any of the following:
its weight or balance;
its structural strength;
its reliability;
its performance;
its operational characteristics.

(2) However, a modification or repair to a limited category aircraft is taken not to be a major modification or repair if advice has been given under regulation 132.175 that the modification or repair is not a major modification or repair.
In this regulation:
modification includes a combination of modifications.
repair includes a combination of repairs.

section.heading: Definition of safety-critical aeronautical product for limited category aircraft

content.p: (1) An aeronautical product for a limited category aircraft is a safety-critical aeronautical product for the aircraft if the aircraft cannot be operated safely if the product is inoperative or missing.

(2) However, an aeronautical product for a limited category aircraft is taken not to be a safety-critical aeronautical product for the aircraft if advice has been given under regulation 132.175 that the aeronautical product is not a safety-critical aeronautical product for the aircraft.

section.heading: Approval of modifications and repairs for limited category aircraft

content.p: A modification or repair to a limited category aircraft is approved for the purposes of this regulation if the modification or repair has been approved (however described, and whether before, on or after the commencement of this regulation) by any of the following:
the aircraft’s manufacturer;
CASA;
the national aviation authority of a foreign country under a law of the foreign country;
if the aircraft is an ex-armed forces aircraft—an armed force that operated the aircraft or for which the aircraft was manufactured;
the administering authority for the aircraft.

A modification or repair to a limited category aircraft is approved for the purposes of this regulation if the modification or repair, or the design for the modification or repair, has been approved (however described, and whether before, on or after the commencement of this regulation) under Part 21 by:
an authorised person; or
an approved design organisation.

A modification or repair to a limited category aircraft is approved for the purposes of this regulation if an approval (however described) for the modification or repair, or the design for the modification or repair, is in force in accordance with regulation 202.054 or 202.055.

section.heading: Approvals by CASA or administering authority for Part 132

content.p: If a provision of this Part refers to a person holding an approval granted by CASA under this regulation, a person may apply to CASA, in writing, for the approval.

If a provision of this Part refers to a person holding an approval granted by the administering authority for a limited category aircraft under this regulation, a person may apply to the administering authority, in writing, for the approval.
Subject to regulation 11.055, CASA or the administering authority must grant the approval.
Subregulation 11.055(1B) applies to the granting of an approval under this regulation for any of the following provisions:
paragraph 132.055(1)(i) (authorised operations for limited category aircraft);
subregulation 132.060(1) (maximum number of persons to be carried);
paragraph 132.075(4)(a) or subregulation 132.075(6) (flights over populous areas).

section.heading: Issue of Manual of Standards for Part 132

content.p: For subsection 98(5A) of the Act, CASA may issue a Manual of Standards for this Part prescribing matters:
required or permitted by these Regulations to be prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards; or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Part.

section.heading: Relationship of Part 132 to other requirements for operating limited category aircraft

content.p: To avoid doubt:

a provision of CAR or of Part 91 that applies to the operation of a limited category aircraft and is inconsistent with this Part has no effect, in relation to the operation of the limited category aircraft, to the extent of the inconsistency, but the provision is taken to be consistent with this Part to the extent that it is capable of operating concurrently with this Part; and

if this Part, or a provision of a document mentioned in subregulation (2), imposes a more stringent requirement (however described) on the operation of a limited category aircraft than the comparable requirement mentioned in paragraph (a), the more stringent requirement prevails.
Example: For paragraph (c), more stringent requirements might include the following:
the aircraft must be operated only under the VFR by day;
the aircraft must be flown only by a named pilot;
the aircraft must not be flown faster than a stated speed, higher than a stated height or have a take-off weight of more than a stated weight.
For paragraph (1)(c), the documents are the following, as in force from time to time:
the aircraft’s limited category certificate;
a document that states the aircraft’s approved airframe life;
a document that states the life limit of a safety-critical aeronautical product fitted to the limited category aircraft;
the approval of a modification or repair to the aircraft;
an approval under regulation 132.035 in relation to the aircraft;
the aircraft’s flight manual;
for an adventure flight of the aircraft—the adventure flight procedures for the aircraft;
an instrument issued under regulation 11.068 (conditions imposed on class of authorisations) that applies to the aircraft;
a direction under Subpart 11.G that applies to the aircraft;
if the administering authority for the aircraft is a limited category organisation—the organisation’s operations manual.
Note: The aircraft must be operated in accordance with the requirements in a document mentioned in subregulation (2): see regulation 132.050.
Subpart 132.B—Flying limited category aircraft—general requirements
Aircraft without a special flight permit
The operator and the pilot in command of a limited category aircraft each contravene this subregulation if:
a special flight permit is not in force for the aircraft; and
the aircraft is operated for a flight; and
a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the flight.
The requirements are the following:
the flight must be an authorised operation for the aircraft under regulation 132.055;
a maintenance release must be in force for the aircraft;
the flight must be conducted in accordance with each requirement (however described) in a document mentioned in subregulation 132.045(2);
the total number of persons on board the aircraft for the flight must be not more than the number of persons allowed under regulation 132.060;

if the aircraft is capable of carrying a passenger—a placard that complies with the requirements prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards must be displayed inside the aircraft so that it is conspicuous to, and can be easily read by, each passenger on board the aircraft, including a passenger sitting in a flight control seat;
before beginning the flight, the pilot in command must make himself or herself aware of all relevant information about the aircraft, including the following:
each requirement (however described) in a document mentioned in subregulation 132.045(2);
the matters mentioned in subregulation (3);
the pilot in command must be authorised under Part 61 (flight crew licensing) to conduct the flight.
Note: For example, for paragraph (e): an aircraft with dual controls that may be flown by a single pilot is capable of carrying a passenger.
For subparagraph (2)(f)(ii), the matters are the following:
each authorisation (within the meaning of Part 11) that relates to the operation of the aircraft and is in force;
each condition imposed under Subpart 11.BA on an authorisation mentioned in paragraph (a) that is in force;
each exemption granted by CASA under Subpart 11.F that relates to the operation of the aircraft and is in force;
each direction issued by CASA under these Regulations that relates to the operation of the aircraft and is in force.
Aircraft with a special flight permit
The operator and the pilot in command of a limited category aircraft each contravene this subregulation if:
a special flight permit is in force for the aircraft; and
the aircraft is operated for a flight; and
either:
the operation of the aircraft for the flight is not in accordance with the special flight permit; or
a requirement mentioned in paragraph (2)(d) or (e), subparagraph (2)(f)(ii) or paragraph (2)(g) is not met for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Authorised operations for limited category aircraft

content.p: For paragraph 132.050(2)(a), each of the following is an authorised operation for a limited category aircraft:
a personal use of the aircraft;
a cost-sharing flight;
flight training for:
a flight crew endorsement for a type or class rating for the aircraft; or
the competency standards mentioned in regulation 61.385 (limitations on exercise of privileges of pilot licences—general competency requirement);
a flight review or test for a flight crew licence, rating or endorsement that authorises the person to pilot, or act as the flight engineer for, the aircraft;
a special purpose operation for which the aircraft’s limited category certificate was issued;
an activity necessary to conduct the special purpose operation, including training for the operation;

if the administering authority for the aircraft is a limited category organisation—an activity that is stated, in the organisation’s operations manual, to be an activity in support of the special purpose operation for the aircraft;
an operation prescribed as an authorised operation by the Part 132 Manual of Standards;
a flight conducted in accordance with an approval, held by the operator, granted by CASA under regulation 132.035 for this paragraph.
(2) For paragraph (1)(a), a flight of an aircraft is a personal use of the aircraft if the flight:
is not publicly available; and
is a flight for which no payment or reward is made or given to the aircraft’s registered operator, operator or flight crew.

section.heading: Maximum number of persons to be carried

content.p: Approval from administering authority

For paragraph 132.050(2)(d), if the operator holds an approval granted by the administering authority for the aircraft under regulation 132.035 for the aircraft to be flown with a stated number of persons (that is greater than 6) on board, the number of persons allowed is the number stated in the approval.
However, for subregulation (1), the number of persons stated in the approval must not be more than the number of persons the aircraft was designed to carry.
Approval of modification
For paragraph 132.050(2)(d), if:
the aircraft has been modified for it to be flown with a number of persons (that is greater than the number of persons the aircraft was designed to carry) on board; and
the modification to the aircraft is approved for the purposes of regulation 132.030; and
the approval states the number of persons that the aircraft may carry;
the number of persons allowed is the number stated in the approval.
Other cases
For paragraph 132.050(2)(d), in any other case the number of persons allowed is the lower of the following numbers:
the number of persons the aircraft was designed to carry;

section.heading: Passenger briefing for flights other than adventure flights

content.p: This regulation applies to a flight of a limited category aircraft if:
a passenger is to be carried on the flight; and
the flight is not an adventure flight.
Note: For the passenger briefing requirement for adventure flights, see regulation 132.155.
The operator of the aircraft contravenes this subregulation if the requirement mentioned in subregulation (3) is not met for the passenger for the flight.
For subregulation (2), the requirement is that, on the day of the flight, before the passenger is taken to the aircraft, a briefing that complies with subregulation (4) must be given to:
the passenger; and
if the passenger is under 18—the passenger’s parent or guardian; and
if the person giving the briefing reasonably believes that the passenger will not be able to understand the briefing—a person who has care of the passenger.
For subregulation (3), the briefing must:
include the content mentioned in subregulation 132.070(1); and
be in a language that the passenger (and, if applicable, the passenger’s parent, guardian or carer) understands.
Subregulation (2) does not apply to the operator if:
the passenger was carried on an earlier flight of the aircraft on the same day; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (3) was met for the passenger for the earlier flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (5): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

section.heading: Content of safety briefing for flights other than adventure flights

content.p: For paragraph 132.065(4)(a), the briefing must include the following:
statements to the effect that:
the design, manufacture and airworthiness of the aircraft are not required to meet any standard recognised by CASA; and
the aircraft is not required by CASA to be operated to the same safety standards as an aircraft used for air transport operations; and
travel in the aircraft is done at the passenger’s own risk;
if subregulation (2) applies to the aircraft—a statement of how the subregulation applies to the aircraft.
For paragraph (1)(b), this subregulation applies to the aircraft if:
the aircraft has reached its approved airframe life; or
a safety-critical aeronautical product fitted to the aircraft has reached its life limit; or
the aircraft has a major modification or repair that is not approved for the purposes of regulation 132.030.
The operator and the pilot in command of a limited category aircraft each contravene this subregulation if:
the aircraft is flown over a populous area; and
the flight is not permitted by this regulation.
A limited category aircraft for which there is no permit index number is not permitted to be flown over a populous area.
A limited category aircraft with a permit index number of 0 may be flown over a populous area.
A limited category aircraft with a permit index number of 1 may be flown over a populous area only:
in accordance with an approval, held by the operator of the aircraft, granted by the administering authority for the aircraft under regulation 132.035 for this paragraph; or
for the purpose of taking off from, or landing at, a landing area other than a landing area prescribed as an unsuitable landing area for this paragraph by the Part 132 Manual of Standards.
In deciding whether to grant an approval mentioned in paragraph (4)(a), the administering authority must take into account:
the aircraft’s permit index number; and
anything else relevant to the safety of other airspace users or persons on the ground or water.

A limited category aircraft with a permit index number of 2 may be flown over a populous area only in accordance with an approval, held by the operator of the aircraft, granted by CASA under regulation 132.035 for this subregulation.
In deciding whether to grant an approval mentioned in subregulation (6), CASA must take into account:
the aircraft’s permit index number; and
anything else relevant to the safety of other airspace users or persons on the ground or water.
Despite subregulations (3), (4) and (6), an aircraft is not permitted to be flown over a populous area if:
the aircraft:
has reached its approved airframe life; or
would reach its approved airframe life during the flight; or
an aeronautical product fitted to the aircraft that is a safety-critical aeronautical product:
has reached its life limit; or
would reach its life limit during the flight; or
a modification or repair to the aircraft:
is a major modification or repair; and
is not approved for the purposes of regulation 132.030.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator and the pilot in command of a limited category aircraft each contravene this subregulation if:
the aircraft is flown in a foreign country’s airspace; and
either:
the country’s national aviation authority has not granted an approval to the operator for the flight; or
the country’s national aviation authority has granted an approval to the operator for the flight subject to a condition and the condition is contravened for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
Subpart 132.C—Flying limited category aircraft—adventure flights

The operator and the pilot in command of a limited category aircraft each contravene this subregulation if, when the aircraft begins an adventure flight, there are no adventure flight procedures for the aircraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Limited category certificate must include adventure flights as special purpose operation

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if, when the aircraft begins an adventure flight, a limited category certificate that includes conducting adventure flights in historic or ex-military aircraft as a special purpose operation for the aircraft is not in force for the aircraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: When adventure flights prohibited—aircraft airframe life and life-limited safety-critical aeronautical products

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if, when the aircraft begins an adventure flight:
the aircraft has reached its approved airframe life; or
an aeronautical product fitted to the aircraft:
is a safety-critical aeronautical product; and
has reached its life limit.

Note: An aeronautical product is not a safety-critical aeronautical product if advice has been given under regulation 132.175 that the aeronautical product is not a safety-critical aeronautical product: see subregulation 132.025(2).
The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if, during an adventure flight of the aircraft:
the aircraft reaches its approved airframe life; or
an aeronautical product fitted to the aircraft:
is a safety-critical aeronautical product; and
reaches its life limit.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: When adventure flights prohibited—major modifications or repairs

content.p: This regulation applies to the operator of a limited category aircraft if:
the aircraft has a modification or repair; and
the modification is a major modification or repair.
Approval of modifications and repairs
The operator contravenes this subregulation if, when the aircraft begins an adventure flight, the modification or repair is not approved for the purposes of regulation 132.030.
Certificate from administering authority

The operator contravenes this subregulation if, when the aircraft begins an adventure flight, the operator does not hold a certificate, given by the administering authority for the aircraft, to the effect that the modified or repaired aircraft may be operated for an adventure flight subject to the limitations (however described) stated in the certificate.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: When adventure flights prohibited—certain aircraft that are not ex-armed forces or historic aircraft

content.p: This regulation applies to a limited category aircraft that is not an ex-armed forces aircraft or historic aircraft.
The operator of the aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the aircraft is used to conduct an adventure flight; and
the aircraft meets the airworthiness requirements for the issue of a standard certificate of airworthiness.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: When adventure flights prohibited—aircraft with special flight permit

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if, when the aircraft begins an adventure flight, a special flight permit is in force for the aircraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Requirements for pilot in command of adventure flights

content.p: The operator and the pilot in command of a limited category aircraft each contravene this subregulation if, when an adventure flight of the aircraft begins, the pilot in command does not meet a requirement (if any) mentioned in the adventure flight procedures for the aircraft for the pilot in command for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: The pilot in command must also be otherwise authorised under Part 61 to conduct the flight: see paragraph 132.050(2)(g).
The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if an adventure flight of the aircraft contravenes subregulation (2).
For subregulation (1), the flight must begin and end at the same landing area and must not involve a landing anywhere else.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if an adventure flight of the aircraft is marketed or represented as a sightseeing flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Clothes and equipment supplied by operator

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator supplies clothing or equipment to a passenger for an adventure flight of the aircraft; and
the clothing or equipment is supplied to the passenger before the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2) is given to the passenger.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Passengers who cannot understand safety briefing to be accompanied on adventure flights

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the aircraft is used to conduct an adventure flight; and
the person giving a passenger on the flight the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2) reasonably believes that the passenger is not able to understand the briefing; and
the passenger is not accompanied on the flight by a parent, guardian or carer.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Requirement for passenger safety briefing when booking

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
a booking for the carriage of a passenger for an adventure flight of the aircraft is taken by:
the operator or an employee or agent of the operator; or
a booking vendor for the aircraft; and
before the booking is finalised, the person making the booking is not given a briefing that:
complies with regulation 132.150; and
is in a language the person understands.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to the operator in relation to a booking taken by an agent of the operator or a booking vendor for the aircraft if, before the agent or vendor took the booking:

the operator, or the administering authority for the aircraft, had instructed the agent or vendor that the agent or vendor must ensure that a briefing that complies with paragraph (1)(b) is given to a person making a booking for the carriage of a passenger on an adventure flight of the aircraft before finalising the booking; and

the operator or the administering authority (as applicable) had given the agent or vendor the information that is necessary for the agent or vendor to give a briefing that complies with regulation 132.150.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (2): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

(4) For the purposes of this regulation, a person is a booking vendor for a limited category aircraft if the person takes bookings for the carriage of passengers on adventure flights for the aircraft, but is not the operator of the aircraft or an employee or agent of the operator.

section.heading: Content of passenger safety briefing when booking

content.p: For subparagraph 132.145(1)(b)(i), the briefing must include the following:
statements to the effect that:
the design, manufacture and airworthiness of the aircraft are not required to meet any standard recognised by CASA; and
the aircraft is not required by CASA to be operated to the same safety standards as an aircraft used for air transport operations; and
travel in the aircraft is done at the passenger’s own risk; and
a more detailed briefing about the safety of the aircraft will be given to the passenger before the passenger boards the aircraft;
if the person making the booking is not the passenger—information on the effect of regulation 132.155 (requirement for passenger safety briefing before boarding aircraft);
information on the effect of regulation 132.140 (passengers who cannot understand safety briefing to be accompanied on adventure flights).

section.heading: Requirement for passenger safety briefing before boarding aircraft

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the aircraft is used to conduct an adventure flight; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for a passenger for the flight.
For paragraph (1)(b), the requirement is that, on the day of the flight, before the passenger is taken to the aircraft, the passenger must be given a briefing that:
complies with subregulation (4); and
is in a language the passenger understands.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to the operator if:
the passenger was carried on an earlier flight of the aircraft on the same day; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) was met for the passenger for the earlier flight.
For paragraph (2)(a), the briefing must include the following:

information comparing the safety of the aircraft with aircraft used for air transport operations, including that CASA does not require the aircraft to be operated to the same degree of safety as an aircraft used for air transport operations;

information about the design, airworthiness and type certification of the aircraft, including that the design, manufacture and airworthiness of the aircraft are not required to meet any standard recognised by CASA;
a statement of the risks associated with undertaking the flight;
a statement to the effect that travel in the aircraft is done at the passenger’s own risk;
if the operator requires the passenger to wear safety equipment (other than a seat belt) during the flight—a statement that the safety equipment must be worn and information about its purpose.
Note: For other provisions about the safety of aircraft occupants, see Division 91.D.7.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (3): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

section.heading: Acknowledgement by passengers who are at least 18 and who can understand passenger safety briefing

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the aircraft is used to conduct an adventure flight; and
a passenger for the flight is at least 18; and
the person giving the passenger the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2) reasonably believes that the passenger is able to understand the briefing; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the passenger for the flight.
For paragraph (1)(d), the requirement is that, on the day of the flight, before the passenger is taken to the aircraft:
the passenger must be given a written copy of the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2) in a language the passenger understands; and
the passenger must sign an acknowledgement, in a language that the passenger understands, that the passenger has received and understood:
the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2); and
the written copy of the briefing.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Acknowledgement for passengers under 18 or who cannot understand passenger safety briefing

content.p: The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the aircraft is used to conduct an adventure flight; and
either or both of the following apply to a passenger for the flight:
the passenger is under 18;
the person giving the passenger for the flight the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2) reasonably believes that the passenger will not be able to understand the briefing; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the passenger for the flight.
For paragraph (1)(c), the requirement is that, before the passenger is taken to the aircraft:
a parent, guardian or carer of the passenger must have been given a written copy of the briefing mentioned in subregulation 132.155(2) in a language the parent, guardian or carer understands; and

the parent, guardian or carer of the passenger must have signed an acknowledgement, in a language that the parent, guardian or carer understands, that he or she has received and understood the written copy of the briefing.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of a limited category aircraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the aircraft is used to conduct an adventure flight; and
a signed acknowledgement mentioned in paragraph 132.160(2)(b) or 132.165(2)(b) for a passenger for the flight is not retained by the operator for at least 3 months after the day the flight ends.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 132.D—Limited category aircraft—certification and airworthiness requirements

section.heading: Advice about modifications, repairs, damage, defects and life-limited aeronautical products

content.p: Giving advice on request from aircraft operator
The operator of a limited category aircraft may, in writing, ask the administering authority for the aircraft for its advice about any of the following matters in relation to the aircraft:
whether a modification or repair is a major modification or repair;
whether damage is major damage;
whether a defect is a major defect;
whether a life-limited aeronautical product for the aircraft is a safety-critical aeronautical product for the aircraft.

If the administering authority for a limited category aircraft receives a request from the operator of the aircraft under subregulation (1) about a matter in relation to the aircraft, the authority must give the operator of the aircraft, in writing, its advice about the matter.
Giving advice on administering authority’s initiative

The administering authority for a limited category aircraft may, on its own initiative, give the operator of the aircraft, in writing, the authority’s advice about a matter mentioned in subregulation (1) in relation to the aircraft.
Note: Under regulation 47 of CAR:
damage to a limited category aircraft is taken not to be major damage if, under this regulation, advice has been given that the damage is not major damage; and
a defect in a limited category aircraft is taken not to be a major defect if, under this regulation, advice has been given that the defect is not a major defect.

section.heading: Requirements for giving approvals, certificates and advice—individuals

content.p: Individuals must be authorised to give approvals, certificates and advice
An individual contravenes this subregulation if:
the individual gives, on behalf of a limited category organisation, an approval, certificate or advice covered by subregulation (4) for a limited category aircraft; and
the individual is not authorised under subregulation 132.185(1) by the organisation to give the advice, approval or certificate for the aircraft.
Individuals must comply with relevant requirements when giving approvals, certificates and advice
An individual contravenes this subregulation if:
the individual gives, on behalf of a limited category organisation, an approval, certificate or advice covered by subregulation (4); and
a procedure included in the organisation’s manual for the purposes of paragraph 262AN(3)(d) of CAR applies to the individual and the approval, certificate or advice; and
the individual does not comply with the procedure in relation to the giving of the approval, certificate or advice.
An individual contravenes this subregulation if:
the individual gives, on behalf of a limited category organisation, an approval, certificate or advice covered by subregulation (4); and
the approval, certificate or advice is covered by a requirement prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards; and
the individual does not comply with the requirement.
Kinds of approvals, certificates and advice
The approvals, certificates and advice covered by this subregulation are:
certificates of airworthiness;
an approval mentioned in regulation 132.030 (approval of modifications and repairs);
a certificate mentioned in subregulation 132.105(3) (operation of an aircraft that has a major modification or repair for an adventure flight subject to limitations);
a certificate stating an airframe life for the aircraft’s airframe given by the administering authority for the aircraft;
advice under regulation 132.175 (advice about modifications, repairs, damage etc.);
an approval or certificate prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards under subparagraph 262AN(3)(d)(vi) of CAR.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Authorisations to give approvals, certificates and advice for limited category aircraft

content.p: How individuals become authorised to give approvals, certificates and advice

An individual is authorised under this subregulation to give, on behalf of a limited category organisation, an approval, a certificate or advice of a kind covered by subregulation 132.180(4) for a limited category aircraft if the individual holds a written authorisation, issued by the limited category organisation, to give the approval, certificate or advice for the aircraft.
Individuals must have relevant qualifications and experience

A limited category organisation must not issue an authorisation to an individual for the purposes of subregulation (1) unless the organisation is satisfied that the individual has the qualifications and experience prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards.
Approvals, certificates and advice given on behalf of limited category organisations

If an individual is authorised under subregulation (1) by a limited category organisation, approvals, certificates and advice given by the individual in accordance with the approval are taken, for the purposes of these Regulations (other than regulation 132.180), to have been given by the limited category organisation.

section.heading: Requirements for giving approvals, certificates and advice—limited category organisations

content.p: A limited category organisation contravenes this subregulation if:
the organisation gives an approval, certificate or advice covered by subregulation 132.180(4); and
a procedure included in the organisation’s manual for the purposes of paragraph 262AN(3)(d) of CAR is not complied with in relation to the giving of the approval, certificate or advice.
A limited category organisation contravenes this subregulation if:
the organisation gives an approval, certificate or advice covered by subregulation 132.180(4); and
the approval or certificate is covered by a requirement prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards; and
the organisation does not comply with the requirement.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A permit index number assigned to a limited category aircraft must:
meet the requirements prescribed by the Part 132 Manual of Standards for the assignment of the number; and
not be likely to have an adverse effect on the safety of other airspace users or persons on the ground or water.
A permit index number must be a whole number from 0 to 3.
Note: For the assignment of a permit index number with the issue of a limited category certificate, see subregulation 21.176(5).

section.heading: Assignment of new permit index numbers on initiative of administering authority

content.p: The administering authority for a limited category aircraft must assign a new permit index number to the aircraft if satisfied that the aircraft’s existing permit index number does not comply with regulation 132.195.
Note: See also regulation 132.230 (Notice to CASA—certain proposed actions by limited category organisation).

section.heading: Assignment of new permit index numbers at CASA direction

content.p: This regulation applies if:
there is a limited category organisation in relation to a limited category aircraft; and
CASA is satisfied that the aircraft’s existing permit index number does not comply with regulation 132.195.
CASA must direct the organisation to assign a new permit index number to the aircraft.
The organisation contravenes this subregulation if it does not comply with the direction.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Assignment of new permit index numbers on application by registered operator

content.p: The registered operator of a limited category aircraft may apply, in writing, to the administering authority for the aircraft for the assignment of a new permit index number for the aircraft.
Part 11 applies to an application mentioned in subregulation (1) as if a permit index number were an authorisation (within the meaning of Part 11).
Subject to regulation 11.055, the administering authority must assign a new permit index number to the aircraft.
Note: See also regulation 132.230 (notice to CASA—certain proposed actions by limited category organisation).

section.heading: When assignment of new permit index number takes effect

content.p: An assignment of a new permit index number for a limited category aircraft takes effect when the aircraft’s registered operator is given, under regulation 132.200, 132.205 or 132.210, a reissued limited category certificate for the aircraft, or a reissued attachment to the certificate, that includes the new number.
Note: The permit index number initially assigned to the aircraft must be included in the limited category certificate or an attachment to the certificate: see paragraph 21.176(5A)(b).

section.heading: Notice to operator if new permit index number assigned

content.p: If a new permit index number is assigned to a limited category aircraft, and the registered operator is not the aircraft’s operator, the administering authority for the aircraft must give written notice of the assignment of the new permit index number to the aircraft’s operator.

division.heading: Certification and airworthiness—notice to CASA of certain matters

section.heading: Notice to CASA—permit index numbers assigned by limited category organisation for aircraft

content.p: This regulation applies if a permit index number is assigned to a limited category aircraft under subregulation 21.176(5) or Division 132.D.2 by a limited category organisation.
The limited category organisation contravenes this subregulation if the organisation does not give CASA written notice of the assignment of the number in accordance with subregulation (3).
The notice must:
include the aircraft’s registration mark and the permit index number assigned to the aircraft; and
be given not later than 14 days after the day the number is assigned.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 10 penalty units.

section.heading: Notice to CASA—certain proposed actions by limited category organisation

content.p: This regulation applies if a limited category organisation proposes to:
refuse to issue a limited category certificate;
refuse to vary a limited category certificate.
This regulation also applies if:
a limited category organisation proposes to assign a new permit index number to a limited category aircraft under Division 132.D.2; and
the aircraft’s existing permit index number was assigned by CASA.
The limited category organisation contravenes this subregulation if it does not give CASA notice of the proposed action in accordance with the organisation’s operations manual.
CASA may give the limited category organisation any advice or comments it considers appropriate in relation to the proposed action within the period mentioned in the manual.

The limited category organisation contravenes this subregulation if it does not have regard to any advice or comments given to it by CASA under subregulation (4) when deciding whether to take the action.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3) or (5).
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
This regulation applies if a limited category organisation reasonably believes that:
a matter exists in relation to a limited category aircraft; and
CASA might want to exercise its powers under subregulation 21.181(6) to suspend or cancel the aircraft’s limited category certificate because of the matter.
The organisation must give CASA notice of the matter in accordance with the organisation’s operations manual.
Subpart 132.M—Limited category aircraft—airworthiness and maintenance

Subpart 133.A—Preliminary
This Part applies in relation to the operation of a rotorcraft for an Australian air transport operation.

section.heading: Definition of suitable forced landing area for rotorcraft flights

content.p: Areas of ground

(1) An area of ground is a suitable forced landing area for a flight of a rotorcraft if the rotorcraft could make a forced landing in the area with a reasonable expectation that there would be no injuries to persons in the rotorcraft or on the ground.
Areas of water
(2) An area of water that meets the requirements mentioned in subregulation (3) is a suitable forced landing area for a flight of a rotorcraft if the rotorcraft:
is equipped with emergency flotation equipment; or
has a type certificate or supplemental type certificate for landing on water.
For the purposes of subregulation (2), the requirements are the following:
the rotorcraft must be able to ditch in the area of water with a reasonable expectation that there would be no injuries to persons in the rotorcraft or on the water;
there must be a reasonable expectation that persons in the rotorcraft would survive in the area of water for the time that it would take to rescue the persons;
if the flight is a passenger transport operation or a medical transport operation—the area of water must be:
adjacent to land; or
adjacent to an offshore installation with search and rescue capabilities; or
in a location, set out in the rotorcraft operator’s exposition, that has search and rescue capabilities.
Factors that affect whether there is a reasonable expectation about the matters mentioned in paragraphs (3)(a) and (b) include the following:
the surface condition of the area of water, including the wave height, wind conditions and swell;
the limits of the capability of the rotorcraft’s emergency flotation system to stay upright and floating in certain sea states.
If a provision of this Part, or of the Part 133 Manual of Standards, refers to a person holding an approval under this regulation, a person may apply to CASA, in writing, for the approval.
Subject to regulation 11.055, the approval must be granted.
Subregulation 11.055(1B) applies to the granting of an approval under this regulation.

section.heading: Issue of Manual of Standards for Part 133

content.p: For the purposes of subsection 98(5A) of the Act, CASA may issue a Manual of Standards for this Part prescribing matters:
required or permitted by these Regulations to be prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards; or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Part.
Note: A Manual of Standards is a legislative instrument: see subsection 98(5AA) of the Act.
Subpart 133.C—General
The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the rotorcraft begins the flight; and
the rotorcraft is not type certificated in any of the following categories:
transport;
normal;
a category prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, during the flight, the rotorcraft is operated in a way that does not meet a requirement or limitation that:
is set out in the aircraft flight manual instructions for the rotorcraft; and
relates to the operation of the rotorcraft.
Note: The pilot in command of the rotorcraft must also ensure the rotorcraft is operated in accordance with the aircraft flight manual instructions: see regulation 91.095.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to a requirement or limitation if:
circumstances prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards exist for the flight; and
the requirement or limitation is of a kind prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards for those circumstances.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (2): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

section.heading: Operator to have minimum equipment list for certain flights

content.p: The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the flight is either or both of the following:
an IFR flight;
a flight that begins or ends at an aerodrome outside Australian territory; and
there is a master minimum equipment list for the rotorcraft; and
when the flight begins, there is no minimum equipment list for the rotorcraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if the requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the flight.

The requirement is that, before a crew member for the flight begins to carry out a duty for the flight, the operator must make available to the member each checklist of normal, abnormal and emergency procedures for the rotorcraft that is relevant to the duty.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

To avoid doubt, if a document is required to be carried on a flight of a rotorcraft under this Division, that requirement is taken to be satisfied if an electronic copy of the document is carried on the flight.
Note: Electronic copies may not satisfy the requirements of the law of a foreign country for flights that begin or end at an aerodrome outside Australian territory.

The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if the following parts of the rotorcraft operator’s exposition are not available to a crew member for the flight before the flight begins:
a part that is relevant to the duties of the crew member for the flight;
a part that is required for the conduct of the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Documents required by the Part 133 Manual of Standards
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
a document prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph is not carried on the rotorcraft; and
the rotorcraft begins the flight.
Flight crew medical certificates
The operator and a flight crew member for a flight of a rotorcraft each contravene this subregulation if:
the flight crew member’s medical certificate is not carried on the rotorcraft for the flight; and
the flight crew member does not give CASA written notice that the certificate is not being carried on the rotorcraft for the flight:
before the flight begins; or
if it is not practicable to give the notice before the flight begins—within 24 hours after the flight ends.
Flight crew licences
The operator and a flight crew member for a flight of a rotorcraft each contravene this subregulation if:
the flight crew member’s flight crew licence is not carried on the rotorcraft for the flight; and
the flight crew member does not give CASA written notice that the licence is not being carried on the rotorcraft for the flight:
before the flight begins; or
if it is not practicable to give the notice before the flight begins—within 24 hours after the flight ends.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Availability or carriage of documents for certain flights

content.p: Flights for which documents must be carried
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the flight is:
an IFR flight; or
a VFR flight at night; or
a flight during which the rotorcraft will not remain within 50 nautical miles of the departure aerodrome; and
when the flight begins, a document mentioned in subregulation (4) is not carried on the rotorcraft.
Flights for which documents must be available or carried
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the rotorcraft begins a VFR flight by day during which the rotorcraft will remain within 50 nautical miles of the departure aerodrome; and
the requirement mentioned in subregulation (3) is not met.
The requirement is that each document mentioned in subregulation (4) must be:
available to the pilot in command immediately before the flight; or
carried on the rotorcraft.
Required documents
The documents are the following:
if a flight notification is required for the flight under Part 91—the flight notification;
weight and balance documents for the flight;
NOTAMs and AIS briefing documents for the flight;
authorised weather forecasts for:
the planned route of the flight; and
the planned area of operation for the flight; and
if a destination alternate aerodrome is required for the flight by the flight preparation (alternate aerodromes) requirements—the destination alternate aerodrome;
if there is a person on board who may require special consideration during the flight or during an evacuation of the rotorcraft—a statement identifying the person and the special consideration;
forms to comply with the reporting requirements under the operator’s safety management system;
if the rotorcraft is fitted with computerised navigation equipment—the operating instructions for the equipment;
each other document (if any) required by a foreign country within whose territory the flight is conducted.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Carriage of documents—flights that begin or end outside Australian territory

content.p: This regulation applies to a flight of a rotorcraft that begins or ends at an aerodrome outside Australian territory.
However, this regulation does not apply to a flight of a rotorcraft if:
the flight:
begins in Australia and ends at a helideck outside Australian territory; or
begins at a helideck outside Australian territory and ends in Australia; and
the flight is not part of a multi-flight journey that begins or ends at an aerodrome that is outside Australian territory.
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
a document prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph is not carried on the rotorcraft; and
the rotorcraft begins the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include the following for a flight of the rotorcraft:
procedures for keeping the documents prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards accessible to a person on the ground for the duration of the flight;
procedures for providing updated information in relation to the flight to a person on the ground if:
the flight is part of a multi-flight journey; and
a copy of a document for the flight has been kept on the ground in relation to an earlier flight that is part of the multi-flight journey; and
the information in the document requires updating; and
it is not practicable to keep a copy of the updated document on the ground;
the circumstances in which a person on the ground who has access to the information about the flight mentioned in paragraphs (a) and (b) may provide that information to another person;
procedures for providing information in a circumstance mentioned in paragraph (c).
Operator—preparation of journey log
The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the operator has not prepared a journey log for the flight:
that is capable of containing the information mentioned in subregulations (3) and (6); and
with a place for the pilot in command to verify the entries for the flight.
Pre-flight completion of journey log

The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the information about the flight mentioned in subregulation (3) is not recorded in the journey log.
The information is the following:
the rotorcraft’s registration mark and flight number (if any);
the date of the flight;
for each crew member assigned to the flight:
the crew member’s name; and
the duties assigned to the crew member for the flight;
for the flight:
the place of departure; and
the time the flight begins;
the amount of fuel added to the rotorcraft’s fuel tanks before the flight begins (if any);
the amount of fuel in the rotorcraft’s fuel tanks when the flight begins.
(4) Subregulation (2) does not apply if:
the flight is a medical transport operation; and
the information mentioned in that subregulation is not recorded in the journey log before the flight begins because of the urgent nature of the medical transport operation; and
the pilot in command is satisfied, when the flight begins, that the failure to record the information in the journey log before the flight begins will not affect the safety of the rotorcraft; and
the information is recorded in the journey log as soon as practicable after the flight ends.
Post-flight completion of journey log

The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if the information about the flight mentioned in subregulation (6) is not recorded in the journey log for the flight as soon as practicable after the flight ends.
The information is the following:
the place of arrival;
the time the flight ends;
the duration of the flight;
the amount of fuel in the rotorcraft’s fuel tanks when the flight ends;
incidents and observations (if any) relevant to the flight.
Offence
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (5).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (4): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight that is a passenger transport operation contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the operator has not prepared a passenger list for the flight that contains the information mentioned in subregulation (2).
The information is the following:
the rotorcraft’s registration mark and flight number (if any);
the name of each passenger;
the places of departure and destination for each passenger;
the number of infants carried;
the date, and estimated time of departure, of the flight.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to the operator in relation to information mentioned in that subregulation if, by the time it is required to be recorded, the information is:
recorded in another document kept by the operator; or
readily available to the operator from another source.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (3): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

section.heading: Flight preparation forms for flights that begin or end outside Australian territory

content.p: This regulation applies to a flight of a rotorcraft that begins or ends at an aerodrome outside Australian territory.
However, this regulation does not apply to a flight of a rotorcraft if:
the flight:
begins in Australia and ends at a helideck outside Australian territory; or
begins at a helideck outside Australian territory and ends in Australia; and
the flight is not part of a multi-flight journey that begins or ends at an aerodrome that is outside Australian territory.

The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if, when the flight begins, the pilot in command has not signed a flight preparation form certifying that the pilot in command is satisfied of the matters mentioned in subregulation (4).
The matters are the following:
the rotorcraft can be operated during the flight in accordance with its configuration deviation list (if any);
the parts of the operator’s exposition required to be available to the rotorcraft’s crew before the flight by regulation 133.050 are available;
the requirements and limitations in the operator’s exposition relating to the flight can be complied with for the flight;
regulations 133.055, 133.060 and 133.065 are being complied with for the flight;
equipment required, under Subpart 133.K, to be fitted to, or carried on, the rotorcraft for the flight is fitted to, or carried on, the rotorcraft in accordance with that Subpart;
equipment mentioned in paragraph (e) is:
operative; or
inoperative, and permitted to be inoperative for the flight under these Regulations;
the rotorcraft’s take-off, en-route and landing performance capabilities meet the performance requirements for the circumstances and conditions expected during the flight;
the rotorcraft’s weight and balance will remain within the rotorcraft’s weight and balance limits throughout the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

division.heading: Reporting and recording defects and incidents etc.

section.heading: Procedures for reporting and recording defects etc.

content.p: A rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include procedures for the reporting and recording, by a flight crew member for a flight of the rotorcraft, of any of the following that occur during the flight:
an abnormal instrument indication;
abnormal flight conditions;
abnormal behaviour by the rotorcraft;
exceedence of an operating limit specified in the aircraft flight manual instructions for the rotorcraft;
a defect in the rotorcraft.

section.heading: Procedures for reporting and recording incidents

content.p: A rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include procedures for the reporting and recording by crew members of incidents relating to a flight of the rotorcraft that endanger, or could endanger, the safe operation of the rotorcraft.

division.heading: Search and rescue services and emergency and survival equipment

section.heading: Information about search and rescue services

content.p: The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, when the flight begins, information about the search and rescue services relevant to the flight is not readily accessible to the flight crew members for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Information about emergency and survival equipment

content.p: The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the Part 133 Manual of Standards prescribes an item of equipment for the purposes of this regulation; and
when the flight begins, the information prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards for that equipment is not available for immediate communication by the operator to a rescue coordination centre.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Crew activities necessary for safe operation

content.p: The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator requires a crew member for the flight to perform an activity during take-off, initial climb, final approach or landing of the rotorcraft for the flight; and
the activity is not necessary for the safe operation of the rotorcraft.
A crew member for a flight of a rotorcraft contravenes this subregulation if:
the crew member performs an activity during take-off, initial climb, final approach or landing of the rotorcraft for the flight; and
the activity is not necessary for the safe operation of the rotorcraft.
Subregulations (1) and (2) do not apply if:
the flight is a medical transport operation; and
the crew member is a medical transport specialist; and
the activity relates to providing care to a medical patient; and
the crew member is satisfied that:
it is essential to perform the activity; and
performing the activity will not affect the safe operation of the rotorcraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (3): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.

The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if, before a member of the operator’s personnel carries out a ground support duty for the flight, the member has not met a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2).
The requirements are the following:
the member must have successfully completed training for the duty;
the member must have been assessed as competent to carry out the duty.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
during the flight, a person occupies a crew station; and
the person is not a person mentioned in subregulation (2).
The persons are the following:
a flight crew member assigned to duty for the flight by the operator;
another crew member authorised by the operator and the pilot in command to occupy the crew station during the flight;
an authorised officer who is carrying out an audit, check, examination, inspection or test under these Regulations;
a person who is permitted by the operator’s exposition to occupy the crew station.
The pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
during the flight, a person other than a member of the rotorcraft’s crew occupies a crew station; and
before the person occupies the crew station, the pilot in command does not cause the person to be briefed on the safety procedures that are relevant to the crew station.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Subpart 133.D—Operational procedures
A rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include procedures for determining how operational control for a flight of the rotorcraft is to be exercised and by whom.
A rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include procedures for complying with the following for a flight of the rotorcraft:
the flight preparation (weather assessments) requirements;
the flight preparation (alternate aerodromes) requirements.
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the flight is:
an IFR flight; or
a VFR flight at night; or
a flight during which the rotorcraft will not remain within 50 nautical miles of the departure aerodrome; and
when the flight begins, an operational flight plan that meets the requirements mentioned in subregulation (2) has not been prepared for the flight.
The requirements are the following:
the flight plan must be prepared having regard to:
the safety of the rotorcraft, and of the people on board the rotorcraft, during the flight; and
the rotorcraft’s performance; and
the expected rotorcraft operating limitations and conditions for the flight; and
meteorological conditions for the flight;
the flight plan must contain the information prescribed by the Part 133 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.
The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight each contravene this subregulation if:
the Part 133 Manual of Standards prescribes information about the flight for the purposes of this subregulation; and
that information is not recorded in the operational flight plan for the flight:
before the flight ends; or
if it is not practicable to record the information before the flight ends—as soon as practicable after the flight ends.

Subregulation (1) or (3) does not apply to the operator or the pilot in command in relation to information required to be included in the operational flight plan under that subregulation if, by the time it is required to be recorded, the information is:
recorded in another document kept by the operator; or
readily available to the operator from another source.
Note: An example for paragraph (a) is a journey log kept by the operator for the flight.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (4): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.
The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if a requirement mentioned in subregulation (2) is not met for the flight.
The requirements are the following:
the pilot in command of the rotorcraft must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) before and during the flight;
each person in the operator’s organisation who is responsible for flight planning for the flight must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) before the flight;
each person in the operator’s organisation who is responsible for flight replanning for the flight must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) during the flight;
each person in the operator’s organisation who exercises operational control for the flight must have access to the information mentioned in subregulation (3) before and during the flight.
The information is the following:
authorised weather forecasts and authorised weather reports:
in relation to the flight; and
if a destination alternate aerodrome is required for the flight by the flight preparation (alternate aerodromes) requirements—in relation to the destination alternate aerodrome;
NOTAMs for the flight;
the suitability for a take-off or landing by the rotorcraft of:
the departure and planned destination aerodrome for the flight; and
if a destination alternate aerodrome is required for the flight by the flight preparation (alternate aerodromes) requirements—the destination alternate aerodrome.
(4) Subregulation (1) does not apply in relation to information mentioned in subparagraph (3)(c)(i) about the planned destination aerodrome, if:

when the flight begins, the rotorcraft is carrying sufficient fuel to allow the flight to be continued to another aerodrome that is suitable for the safe landing of the rotorcraft if the rotorcraft cannot land at the planned destination aerodrome; and

before starting an approach to land at the planned destination aerodrome, the pilot in command for the flight determines, in accordance with the procedures included in the operator’s exposition under regulation 133.170, that the planned destination aerodrome is suitable to land at.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subregulation (4): see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code.
If a rotorcraft conducts an IFR flight to or from an aerodrome, the rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include:
procedures for determining take-off minima that meet the requirements mentioned in subregulation (2); and
procedures for determining landing minima that meet the requirement mentioned in subregulation (3).
The requirements are the following:
the take-off minima must not be less than the take-off minima prescribed by the take-off minima requirements for the aerodrome;

the take-off minima must be sufficient to enable the pilot in command to control the rotorcraft, in an emergency, in a way that ensures there is no undue hazard to a person on the ground or water under the rotorcraft’s flight path;
for a multi-engine rotorcraft flown in performance class 1—the take-off minima must be sufficient to enable the pilot in command to reject or continue a take-off safely if one engine fails;
for a multi-engine rotorcraft flown in performance class 2—the take-off minima must be sufficient to enable the pilot in command to:
manoeuvre the rotorcraft safely to reach a suitable forced landing area; or
continue a take-off if one engine fails after the defined point after take-off;

for a multi-engine rotorcraft flown in performance class 2 with exposure—the take-off minima must be sufficient to enable the pilot in command to continue a take-off if one engine fails after the defined point after take-off.
The requirement is that the landing minima must not be less than the landing minima prescribed by the landing minima requirements for the aerodrome, including for an approach with visual circling.

If a rotorcraft conducts an IFR flight to or from an aerodrome with an approach involving visual circling, the rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include procedures for determining landing minima for the aerodrome.

The operator and the pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight mentioned in subregulation (1) or (4) each contravene this subregulation if the minima for the take-off or landing for the flight are less than the minima determined in accordance with a procedure mentioned in subregulation (1) or (4) (as the case requires).
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (5).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Flights to or from foreign countries that do not use ICAO procedures

content.p: This regulation applies if:
a rotorcraft conducts an IFR flight to or from an aerodrome:
in a foreign country; and
at which IMC exist; and
the country does not base the design of its instrument approach and departure procedures on ICAO Document 8168 (PANS-OPS).
The rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include the instrument approach and departure procedures for the aerodrome that are approved by the national aviation authority of the country.
The operator of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if a requirement mentioned in subregulation (4) is not met for the flight.
The requirements are the following:
each pilot assigned to the flight by the operator must have successfully completed training in the country’s instrument approach and departure procedures;
the flight must be conducted in accordance with the instrument approach and departure procedures for the aerodrome included in the operator’s exposition.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Authorised instrument approach procedures not in the AIP

content.p: The operator of a rotorcraft for an IFR flight contravenes this subregulation if:
during the flight, the rotorcraft conducts an instrument approach to an aerodrome for which an authorised instrument approach procedure is not published in the AIP; and
an authorised instrument approach procedure for the aerodrome is not included in the operator’s exposition.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A rotorcraft operator’s exposition must include the following:
each type of low-visibility operation conducted using the rotorcraft;
the aircraft systems required to be used for each type of those operations;
the aerodrome facilities required to conduct each type of those operations;
the training and qualifications required for the rotorcraft’s flight crew members for each type of those operations;
the requirements to be met by the rotorcraft’s flight crew members during each of those operations.

section.heading: IFR flights without destination alternate aerodromes

content.p: This regulation applies to a flight of a rotorcraft if:
the flight is an IFR flight; and
the operational flight plan for the flight does not include a destination alternate aerodrome.
The pilot in command of a rotorcraft for a flight contravenes this subregulation if:
during the flight, the pilot in command receives an authorised weather forecast for the planned destination aerodrome for the flight; and
because of the authorised weather forecast, a destination alternate aerodrome must be nominated in accordance with the flight preparation (alternate aerodromes) requirements; and

the rotorcraft is not carrying sufficient fuel to allow the flight to be continued to another aerodrome that is suitable for the safe landing of the rotorcraft if the rotorcraft cannot land at the planned destination aerodrome; and
the flight is continued to the planned destination aerodrome.
Subregulation (2) does not apply if:

within 30 minutes before the rotorcraft’s estimated arrival time at the planned destination aerodrome, the pilot in command receives an authorised weather forecast for the planned destination aerodrome; and
the authorised weather forecast indicates that the visibility or cloud ceiling height at the planned destination aerodrome is expected to be:
below the alternate minima for the planned destination aerodrome required by the flight preparation (alternate aerodromes) requirements; but
above the landing minima required by the landing minima requirements for the planned destination aerodrome.
