This is a compilation of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 that shows the text of the law as amended and in force on 30 June 2026 (the compilation date).
The notes at the end of this compilation (the endnotes) include information about amending laws and the amendment history of provisions of the compiled law.

The effect of uncommenced amendments is not shown in the text of the compiled law. The details of amendments made up to, but not commenced at, the compilation date are underlined in the endnotes. Any uncommenced amendments affecting the law are accessible on the Register (www.legislation.gov.au).

If the operation of a provision or amendment of the compiled law is affected by an application, saving or transitional provision that is not included in this compilation, details are included in the endnotes.
For more information about any editorial changes made in this compilation, see the endnotes.

The Legislation Act 2003 provides for First Parliamentary Counsel to make presentational changes to a compilation. Presentational changes are applied to give a more consistent look and feel to legislation published on the Register, and enable the user to more easily navigate those documents.

If the compiled law is modified by another law, the compiled law operates as modified but the modification does not amend the text of the law. Accordingly, this compilation does not show the text of the compiled law as modified. Any modifications affecting the law are accessible on the Register.
If a provision of the compiled law has been repealed in accordance with a provision of the law, details are included in the endnotes.

Subpart 137.A—Applicability and definitions
Subject to this regulation, this Part applies to aerial application operations using aeroplanes.
Operators
This Part applies to a person who is applying for an AOC, on or after the commencing day, to authorise the person to undertake application operations.
If:

a person has applied, on or after the application day but before the commencing day, for an AOC to authorise the holder to undertake agricultural operations or purposes substantially similar to agricultural operations; and
before the commencing day, the person has not been issued with the AOC;
this Part applies to the person and the application as if:
the application had been made on the commencing day; and
the application was for an authorisation to undertake application operations.
If, on the commencing day, a person holds an AOC that covers agricultural operations or purposes substantially similar to agricultural operations:
the person may, after the commencing day, prepare and submit to CASA an operations manual; and
this Part applies to the person and the manual as if the person was applying for an AOC on or after the commencing day to authorise the person to undertake application operations.

This Part applies on and after the day that falls 12 months after the commencing day to a person who has an AOC that authorises the person to undertake agricultural operations or purposes substantially similar to agricultural operations if:
that AOC is in effect on that day; and
this Part does not otherwise apply to the person.
Pilots
If:
a pilot is engaged in an application operation on or after the commencing day; and
the pilot is not employed by an operator for that operation;
this Part applies to the pilot for that operation.
If:
this Part applies to an operator on a particular day; and
a pilot employed by the operator undertakes an application operation for the operator on that day;
this Part applies to the pilot for that operation.
In this regulation:
application day means the day that falls 30 days before the day this Part commences.
commencing day means the day this Part commences.
In this Part:
aerial application operation (or application operation) means:
a flight that is carried out by an aeroplane to apply application material; and
a flight by an aeroplane that is for, or partly for, 1 or more of the following:
inspection of a work area;
pilot training or checking relating to a flight mentioned in paragraph (a);
training of a crew member other than the pilot;
travel from a landing area to a work area and back;
the carriage of a passenger specified in regulation 137.135 for a purpose set out in that regulation; and
preparation for any activities mentioned in paragraphs (a) and (b).
application material means fertiliser, trace elements, seeds, baits, water, pesticides or other material.
apply, in relation to application material, means to drop or spray the material onto the ground or water.
crew member includes a person who is on board an aeroplane to give, or receive, training in an aspect of application operations.
employ, in relation to a pilot, includes to engage as an independent contractor.
GPS marking system means a system that uses global positioning system equipment to show the flight path required for an aeroplane when applying application material.
head of aeroplane maintenance control, in relation to an operator, means the person who holds the position whose duties include those mentioned in regulation 137.070.
head of flight operations, in relation to an operator, means the person who holds the position whose duties include those mentioned in regulation 137.065.
key personnel position, in relation to an operator, means the positions of head of aeroplane maintenance control and head of flight operations for the operator.
landing area means a place, whether or not an aerodrome, where an aeroplane is able to take off and land.

MEL, or minimum equipment list, for an aeroplane, means an approved list that provides for the operation of the aeroplane with particular equipment inoperative, and sets out any special conditions for such operation.
operations manual, in relation to an operator or an application operation carried out by an operator, means:
the manual, and the schedule of differences (if any), approved under regulation 137.050; and
any amendments approved under regulation 137.080, 137.085 or 137.090, as appropriate.
Note: An operations manual may comprise a standard operations manual and a schedule of differences: see subregulation 137.035(2).
operator, in relation to an aeroplane, means a person who holds an AOC that authorises the use of the aeroplane in application operations.
populous area, in relation to a flight by an aeroplane, means an area where, if the aeroplane’s engine failed, the aeroplane would not be able to glide safely clear of any occupied building.
resting time, for a pilot, means any time during a tour of duty when the pilot:
has no duties to perform; and
has access to accommodation that is conducive to rest and includes a comfortable chair.
role equipment means equipment fitted to an aeroplane for an application operation, including booms, spreaders and mirrors.
schedule of differences, for an operator, means the schedule prepared by the operator under paragraph 137.045(3)(c) and approved by CASA under regulation 137.050.
sleeping time, for a pilot, means any time during a tour of duty when the pilot:
has no duties to perform; and
has access to a comfortable room that:
is subject to minimal noise levels; and
is well ventilated; and
is equipped with a method of controlling the entry of light; and
is equipped with a comfortable bed and chair.
standard operations manual means an operations manual approved under regulation 137.040.
work area, in relation to an application operation, means:
the area of ground or water where application material is to be applied; and
the area over which the aeroplane concerned flies as it approaches and departs from the area mentioned in paragraph (a).
Subpart 137.B—General
If a provision of this Part provides that anything (including a document, body or activity) must be approved, CASA may approve the thing, in writing, for the provision.
If a provision in these Regulations is inconsistent with a provision in this Part, the provision in this Part prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.
If an aeroplane does not conform to a type certificate or type acceptance certificate in the normal, restricted or utility category:
the operator of the aeroplane must not allow it to be used for an application operation; and
a pilot must not use it to carry out an application operation.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Note: CASA may grant an exemption from a provision of these Regulations: see Subpart 11.F.

The operator of an aeroplane must take all reasonable measures to ensure that, if the pilot in command of the aeroplane, acting in accordance with a provision of these Regulations, directs anybody to do something, or not do something, the person complies with the direction.
Subpart 137.C—Operator certification and supervision
A person applying for an AOC to cover application operations must prepare a manual that:
specifies procedures to be followed by crew members and other persons to ensure the safety of the operations that are to be covered by the AOC; and
includes the names of the persons who are to be the CEO and holders of the key personnel positions.
The person may comply with subregulation (1) by:
nominating a standard operations manual to apply to the person’s operations; and
preparing a schedule of differences to the standard operations manual.
The manual may:
consist of 1 or more volumes; and
include material prepared by someone other than the person making the application; and
incorporate another document or documents by reference.
Note: CASA approves the manual under regulation 137.050 when approving the application for the AOC.
CASA may approve, in writing, a manual prepared by a person other than an operator, as a standard operations manual.
The manual must specify procedures to be followed by crew members of aeroplanes and other persons engaged in application operations to ensure the safety of the operations.

section.heading: Application for an AOC or variation of an AOC

content.p: An application by a person for an AOC to cover application operations must be submitted to CASA at least 90 days before the date of intended operation.
The manual that, for subsection 27AB(2) of the Act, must be lodged with CASA by the person need not include landing area information.
If the person nominates a standard operations manual the application must include:
a statement identifying the standard operations manual; and
an undertaking to comply with the standard operations manual as in force from time to time; and
a schedule to the standard operations manual, prepared by the applicant, showing:
the ways (if any) in which the person’s application operations are proposed to differ from those described in the standard operations manual adopted by the person under paragraph (b); and
the names of the persons who are proposed to be the CEO and holders of the key personnel positions.
The manual or schedule (if any) that relates to the application must be submitted to CASA at least 60 days before the date of intended operation.
An application for a variation of an AOC must be submitted to CASA at least 30 days before the date of the proposed change to the operation.
Note: For matters about which CASA must be satisfied before issuing an AOC, see section 28 of the Act.
CASA may accept an application later than required under subregulation (1) or (5), or a late submission under subregulation (4).
CASA must, in writing, approve or refuse to approve:
an application for an AOC; and
an application for a variation of an AOC.
If CASA approves an application for an AOC under subregulation (1), it is taken to have approved:
the applicant’s manual; and
if applicable—the schedule mentioned in paragraph 137.045(3)(c).
CASA is taken to have refused an application for an AOC if it has not approved or refused the application within the period of 90 days starting on the later of the following:
the day the application is made;
the day the applicant has complied with any notice given by CASA under section 27AC of the Act.
CASA is taken to have refused an application for a variation of an AOC if it has not approved or refused the application within the period of 90 days starting when the application is made.
An operator must conduct application operations in accordance with:
the operations manual; and
if the operator has an exemption given by CASA under Part 11—the exemption.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The operator must ensure that the manual, and information relating to any exemption, is available to crew members and other persons engaged in application operations for the operator.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.
(1) An operator must nominate an individual to be chief executive officer (CEO) of the operator’s organisation.
The CEO must be responsible for ensuring that all application operations and aeroplane maintenance can be carried out to the standard required by these Regulations.
An operator must nominate individuals to hold the key personnel positions in the organisation.

If, having regard to the size of an operator’s organisation or the nature and scope of operations authorised by the operator’s AOC, it would not adversely affect the safety of the operations to do so, an operator may:
appoint a person to a key personnel position on a part-time basis; or
appoint a person to more than 1 key personnel position.
An operator must ensure that, at all times, a person is occupying, or acting in, each key personnel position.
Subject to subregulation (5), an operator must nominate an individual to be head of flight operations in the operator’s organisation.
The duties of the head of flight operations must include being responsible for the following:
monitoring the operator’s compliance with the Act, these Regulations and the conditions to which the operator’s AOC is subject, and reporting on compliance to the operator’s CEO;
monitoring the adequacy of the operator’s systems and procedures to ensure safe operations under the operator’s AOC, and reporting on the adequacy of the systems and procedures to the CEO;
arranging rosters for the pilots employed to carry out application operations for the operator;
maintaining an efficient system for recording flight and duty times for each pilot;
maintaining up-to-date records of all licences, ratings, medical certificates and endorsements held by each pilot;
maintaining a system that will ensure compliance with the relevant loading procedures for each type of aeroplane used in operations carried out under the operator’s AOC;
ensuring that the operator keeps any documents required by the Act, these Regulations and the conditions of the operator’s AOC;
setting and monitoring the standard of application operations, including activities on the ground, carried out under the operator’s AOC;
ensuring that the checking required by Subpart 137.N is carried out and, if a pilot fails a check, that the appropriate retraining and re-checking are carried out;
allocating an aeroplane for use in each operation carried out under the operator’s AOC.

If an operator uses only 1 aeroplane for application operations, the person occupying the position of head of flight operations must have at least 300 hours total flight time as pilot in command in application operations.

If an operator uses more than 1 aeroplane for application operations, the person occupying the position of head of flight operations must hold an agricultural pilot (aeroplane) grade 1 rating within the meaning given in Civil Aviation Order 40.6.
A person who, under Civil Aviation Order 82.0, is approved as Chief Pilot of an operator, is taken to be the head of flight operations for the operator.
An operator must nominate an individual to be head of aeroplane maintenance control in the operator’s organisation.
The duties of the head of aeroplane maintenance control must include ensuring that the operator complies with Subpart 137.M.

section.heading: Replacement of holder of key personnel position

content.p: If an operator proposes a replacement of the holder of a key personnel position, the operator must:
notify CASA as soon as is practicable before the proposed replacement; and
if the replacement does not take effect—notify CASA accordingly.

section.heading: Amendments to operations manual by operator

content.p: This regulation applies to an operator that:
is using an operations manual prepared by the operator; and
proposes a change to a procedure or another matter that, because of its nature, would require amendment of the manual.
The operator must:
prepare an amendment to the manual to reflect the proposed change; and
give the amendment to CASA as soon as practicable after preparing it and before implementing the change.
CASA must, in writing, approve or refuse to approve the proposed amendment.
This regulation applies to an operator that:
has adopted a standard operations manual; and
proposes a change to a procedure or another matter that, because of its nature, would require amendment of the schedule of differences.
The operator must:
prepare an amendment to the schedule to reflect the proposed change; and
give the amendment to CASA as soon as practicable after preparing it and before implementing the change.
CASA must, in writing, approve or refuse to approve the proposed amendment.
A person that has prepared a standard operations manual may prepare an amendment of the manual.
The person must submit the amendment to CASA.
CASA must, in writing, approve or refuse to approve the amendment.
Subpart 137.D—Operational procedures
The pilot in command of an aeroplane may only conduct an application operation in VMC.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Use of weather forecasts or observations

content.p: This regulation applies to the operator of the aeroplane and its pilot in command if the operator is planning an application operation that is to take place more than 50 nautical miles from the take-off aerodrome.
The operator and pilot must:
use a weather forecast or report prepared by the Bureau of Meteorology or another approved body; or
if the pilot is not reasonably able to obtain a weather forecast or report of a kind mentioned in paragraph (a)—satisfy subregulation (4).
Penalty: 5 penalty units.
The operator must provide any equipment necessary to obtain the forecast or report.
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
The operator and pilot satisfy this subregulation if the pilot:
uses his or her observations, or weather information from a source other than those mentioned in paragraph (2)(a); and
the pilot reasonably believed it was safe to use the observations or information.
A contravention of subregulation (2) or (3) is an offence of strict liability.
Despite any other provision of these Regulations, the pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation may use any landing area that can be used safely for take-offs and landings.

section.heading: Safety of persons other than crew at landing areas

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane must, for the safety of persons during application operations at a landing area:
use appropriate procedures, including those necessary for the safe loading and unloading of aeroplanes; and
provide appropriate equipment, including any necessary lighting.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The procedures must be set out in the operations manual.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
An operator must use appropriate safety procedures for the refuelling of each of the operator’s aeroplanes that is used in an application operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The operations manual must set out the procedures.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Documents to be carried on a flight

content.p: The pilot in command of an aeroplane being used for an application operation must have a copy of the aeroplane’s flight manual, or an approved alternative document, on board the aeroplane on every flight.
Penalty: 10 penalty units.

The pilot must also have the documents or copies mentioned in subregulations (4) and (5) on board the aeroplane on a flight if the aeroplane will be more than 1 hour’s flying time (at cruise speed in still air) from the operator’s principal operating base.
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
However, if:
(a) the aeroplane is to be based for more than 7 days at a place that is not the operator’s principal operating base (a substitute base); and
the aeroplane is less than 1 hour’s flying time (at cruise speed in still air) from the substitute base;
the documents or copies mentioned in subregulations (4) and (5) may be kept at the substitute base.
For subregulations (2) and (3), the documents are:
the aeroplane’s flight and maintenance records; and
each of the following documents, or copies of the documents:
the aeroplane’s certificate of registration;
the aeroplane’s certificate of airworthiness (or, if applicable, special flight permit);
the current medical certificate for, and licence of, the pilot.
However, if the operations manual states that only a specified part of a document mentioned in subregulation (1) or paragraph (4)(a) must be carried during a flight, only that part need be carried.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.
While an aeroplane is engaged in an application operation its flight controls may be manipulated by a person only if the person is:
the pilot in command of the aeroplane; or
a pilot who is being trained in application operations; or
a person authorised to do so by CASA.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
If an aeroplane engaged in an application operation is on the ground with the engine running, the pilot in command must be at the controls unless:
the pilot is refuelling the aeroplane in accordance with the operations manual; or
the following apply:
the pilot remains near the aeroplane;
the wheel brakes are locked and, if practicable, the wheels are chocked;
the aeroplane’s power controls are friction locked and, if possible, the propeller is feathered;
the engine is retarded to idle and, if possible, ground idle.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
Subregulation (4) applies if a person who is not, under these Regulations, entitled to manipulate the aeroplane’s flight controls:
occupies a control seat fitted with fully or partially functioning controls; or
is seated in a position where he or she could interfere with the controls.
The pilot in command of the aeroplane must:
instruct the person not to interfere with the controls; and
be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the person has understood the instruction.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.
Strict liability applies to the physical element mentioned in paragraph (4)(a).

section.heading: Use of seats, seatbelts and harnesses

content.p: A person in an aeroplane engaged in an application operation must occupy a seat and wear a seatbelt or harness whenever the aeroplane is moving under its own power.
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
However, subregulation (1) does not apply to a person in the aeroplane if, during the operation:
he or she is acting in accordance with an instruction by the pilot in command; or
he or she is wearing an approved restraint device and either:
has satisfactorily completed a course of training in the operation and is directly involved in the operation; or
is being trained in the operation.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.

If an aeroplane is engaged in an application operation, neither the operator nor the pilot in command may allow a passenger to be carried unless subregulation (2), (3) or (4) applies to the operation and the passenger.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
This subregulation applies if the passenger is an officer, or delegate of CASA, who is on board the aeroplane to carry out his or her duties.
This subregulation applies if:
the passenger is on board the aeroplane to identify the area where the application material is to be applied; and
no application material is applied during the operation.
This subregulation applies if:
the passenger is on board the aeroplane to carry out duties necessary for his or her employment; and
both the operator and the pilot agree to the carriage of the passenger.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Minimum height and lateral separation for operation

content.p: Subject to subregulations (2), (3) and (4) the pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation may fly at any height while:
over the work area; or
travelling from the landing area used for loading the aeroplane to the work area.
In a populous area, the aeroplane must not fly closer than 100 metres, measured horizontally, from an occupied building.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
In an area other than a populous area the aeroplane must not fly less than 350 feet AGL while closer than 100 metres, measured horizontally, from an occupied building.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The aeroplane may fly closer to a building and to the ground than provided for in subregulation (2) or (3) if:
more than 48 hours before the proposed operation, the occupier of the building was notified in writing about the operation and did not object to the operator about it; or
if it was not reasonably practicable to give written notice—the occupier was notified verbally before the operation and did not object to the operator about it.
A contravention of subregulation (2) or (3) is an offence of strict liability.
A person may conduct an application operation over a populous area only if:
the person is an operator; and
the procedures for the operation are set out in the operations manual; and
the operation was requested by a person that, under a law of a State or Territory, may authorise the operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
An operator must, before conducting the operation, make a plan for the operation that:
includes consultation with the person that requested the operation; and
identifies any obstructions to flight and sets out how these will be avoided; and
identifies the most suitable emergency landing area for the operation; and
sets out any coordination with ATC that is necessary for the operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation must plan a flight for the operation so that, at all times, the aeroplane has enough fuel to complete the flight safely.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
If an operations manual applies to the pilot, it must set out:
the procedures that the pilot must follow to ensure that the aeroplane carries enough fuel; and
a procedure to ensure that in-flight fuel checks and fuel management are carried out.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.

The pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation that involves a take-off from, or landing at, an aerodrome need not conform with the circuit traffic protocol specified in the AIP for the aerodrome if:
the aeroplane is fitted with a radio; and
the pilot:
maintains a continuous listening watch on the aerodrome frequency; and
broadcasts his or her intentions in accordance with the AIP; and
gives priority to other traffic.
However, subregulation (1) does not apply if the flight is subject to ATC instructions.
(3) In this regulation, AIP includes a document that is equivalent to the AIP.

(1) For this regulation, 2 or more aeroplanes are engaged in a close proximity operation if they are flying so close to each other during an application operation as to create a collision hazard if special measures are not taken.
A person must not operate an aeroplane in a close proximity operation if the person is not an operator.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane must not engage in a close proximity operation unless the operation is coordinated by:
if the operation is to be conducted by 1 operator—the operator’s head of flight operations, or another person nominated by the operator; or
otherwise—a suitably qualified pilot agreed to by all pilots involved in the operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The coordinator must give, to all pilots involved in the operation, instructions about the following:
transit between the landing area and the work area;
radio communications, including loss-of-communication procedures;
refuelling arrangements;
the conduct of the operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
During the operation each pilot must:
maintain safe lateral separation from the other aeroplanes by visual and radio contact; and
comply with the instructions of the person coordinating the operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (2), (3), (4) or (5) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to an application operation conducted at night.
The pilot in command of the aeroplane to be used in the operation must, by inspection during daylight, be familiar with:
the work area; and
the route between the work area and the landing area.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The operator of the aeroplane must plan the operation so the distance from a work area to a landing area is less than 30 minutes flying time at normal cruise power in still air, unless:
the aeroplane is equipped, and certificated under Part 21, for night VFR flight; and
the pilot holds, in addition to any rating required for night application operations, the rating required for a VFR flight at night.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.

The operator must not allow the operation to commence unless the aeroplane is equipped with a two-way radio that enables the pilot to communicate with each person on the ground who has a role in the operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The pilot must not commence or continue the operation if horizontal visibility from the aeroplane is less than 5 km.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The operator must ensure that lights are placed at the work area to help the pilot with orientation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (2), (3), (4), (5) or (6) is an offence of strict liability.
A person must not operate an aeroplane for an application operation that involves firefighting unless the emergency control authority responsible for the firefighting:
has not, when the operation commences, taken control of the fighting of the fire; or
has taken control of the firefighting and asks the person to carry out the operation.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A pilot is authorised to conduct an application operation that:
involves firefighting; and
is requested by the relevant emergency control authority;
only if he or she has more than 500 hours experience as pilot in command in application operations when the operation commences.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.E—All-weather operations
Subpart 137.H—Aeroplane performance
Note: Reserved for future use.

The pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation must, before take-off, take reasonable steps to satisfy himself or herself that the take-off can be safely carried out by considering the aeroplane’s take-off weight and each other relevant factor.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
Before landing, the pilot must satisfy himself or herself that the landing can be safely carried out by considering the aeroplane’s landing weight and each other relevant factor.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.

The pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation may commence a take off over a populous area only if the aeroplane’s performance will allow it to be 200 feet or more AGL when it crosses the aerodrome boundary and climbing at 200 feet or more per minute.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.J—Weight and balance
The pilot in command of an aeroplane engaged in an application operation must not commence a take-off if the aeroplane’s gross weight exceeds:
the maximum gross weight shown in the aeroplane’s flight manual; or
any maximum gross weight that:
has been established for that type of aeroplane by a flight test supervised by CASA; and
is shown on a placard, approved by CASA and displayed in the aeroplane’s cockpit; or

the maximum gross weight shown on the type certificate, or type certificate data sheet, that is issued for the aeroplane by the national aviation authority of the State of Design (within the meaning given in Annex 8 to the Chicago Convention) of the aeroplane.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The pilot must calculate the take-off weight by a method that includes calculating the weight of:
the crew and any equipment carried; and
the aeroplane’s fuel and load.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of the aeroplane must not specify a minimum load to be carried by the aeroplane that is greater than the load that the pilot reasonably considers to be safe.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1), (2) or (3) is an offence of strict liability.
The pilot in command of an aeroplane to be used in an application operation must:
supervise the loading of the aeroplane; and
not commence the operation unless the load is placed in a way that is consistent with the data used for the calculation of the aeroplane’s weight and balance.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.K—Instruments and equipment

Subject to subregulation (3), the operator of an aeroplane that is to be used in an application operation must ensure that instruments and items of equipment, other than role equipment, used in the aeroplane are:
other than items mentioned in subregulation (3)—approved; and
properly installed so they are fit for their purpose, and do not interfere with the operation of any other equipment; and
except as provided in the applicable MEL—serviceable.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
For paragraph (1)(b), an instrument or item of equipment is properly installed if:
there is a Part 21 approval that covers the installation; and
the instrument or item is installed in accordance with its approved design; and
the instrument or item is compatible with the configuration of the aircraft; and
the instrument or item is installed by a person who:
has been trained to carry out the installation; and
is authorised, under these Regulations, to carry out the installation.
The following items are not required to be approved:
electric torch;
timepiece;
a GPS marking system;
chart holder;
first-aid kit;
survival and pyrotechnic signalling equipment.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
In this regulation:
approved design: see subregulation 42.015(1).
Part 21 approval: see subregulation 42.015(1).
The operator of an aeroplane must not allow the aeroplane to be used in an application operation unless:
equipment on the aeroplane that is operated during flight by only 1 crew member is installed so that it can readily be operated from the member’s station; and
an instrument that need only be read by 1 crew member is installed:
so the crew member can easily read the instrument from his or her station; and
as close as practicable to the crew member’s line of vision in the direction of the flight path.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The operator of an aeroplane must not allow the aeroplane to engage in an application operation unless it is fitted with the equipment mentioned in each item of Table 137.215-1.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

tr.th: Table 137.215-1 Equipment for all application operations
Table 137.215-1 Equipment for all application operations

tr.td: A timepiece showing the time in hours, minutes and seconds (unless the pilot in command carries such a timepiece)
A sensitive pressure altimeter that: (a) reads in feet; and (b) has a sub-scale setting, calibrated in hectopascals, that can be set to any barometric pressure that may occur during flight
An airspeed indicator calibrated in knots
An outside air temperature indicator calibrated in degrees Celsius
If the aeroplane is equipped with radio—a headset, whether or not built into a helmet, with a boom microphone or an equivalent microphone
Any other instruments and equipment required to be fitted for type certification.

content.p: The operator must not allow the aeroplane to engage in an application operation at night unless it is fitted with the equipment mentioned in each item of Table 137.215-2.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

tr.th: Table 137.215-2 Equipment for night application operations
Table 137.215-2 Equipment for night application operations

tr.td: At least 2 serviceable work lights that are suitable for the operation, installed so as to minimise glare in the cockpit
A system of cockpit lighting that is appropriate to the operation
Either: (a) a turn indicator; or (b) an attitude indicator that provides pitch and roll information at all attitudes

content.p: A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.
The operator of an aeroplane that requires a crew of more than 1 person must not allow it to engage in an application operation unless it is equipped with an intercom system that:
can be used by all members of the crew; and
includes headsets, whether or not built into a helmet, and microphones that are not of a handheld type.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to the operation if:
the use of any item of intercom equipment may adversely affect the safety of the operation; and
another appropriate method of communication between the crew is arranged before the operation commences.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
This regulation applies to an aeroplane, other than an aeroplane that has been certified in the normal category.
The operator of the aeroplane must not allow it to engage in an application operation unless:
the pilot’s seat is equipped with a four-point restraint harness with a single point release; and
a harness or seatbelt for any other crew member is equipped with a single point release.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.M—Aeroplane maintenance

section.heading: Fitting and removal of role equipment

content.p: A person must not fit role equipment to, or remove role equipment from, an aeroplane that is used in an application operation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
Subregulation (1) does not apply to a person who:
has been trained by an operator, or an approved person, in the fitting and removal of a kind of role equipment; and
fits or removes equipment of that kind.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.N—Pilots

section.heading: Pilot in command must be authorised under Part 61

content.p: The operator of an aeroplane commits an offence if:
the aeroplane is used to conduct an application operation; and
the pilot in command of the aeroplane is not authorised under Part 61 to pilot the aeroplane in the operation.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An offence against this regulation is an offence of strict liability.
(1) For this regulation, a pilot holds a valid operator proficiency check if:
he or she has satisfactorily completed a check that satisfies the criteria in subregulations (3), (4), (5) and (9); and
under subregulations (7) and (8), the check is valid.
The operator of an aeroplane commits an offence if:
the aeroplane is used to conduct an application operation; and
the pilot in command of the aeroplane does not hold a valid operator proficiency check.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
An operator proficiency check for a pilot who is employed by an operator must be conducted by:
the operator’s head of flight operations; or
a flight examiner or instructor authorised under Part 61 to conduct application operations.
An operator proficiency check for the operator’s head of flight operations must be conducted by an examiner or instructor mentioned in paragraph (3)(b).

Despite subregulations (3) and (4), an operator proficiency check for a pilot who, in the 12 months immediately before the check, has completed less than 50 hours flight time in application operations must be conducted by an examiner or instructor mentioned in paragraph (3)(b).
A synthetic flight trainer may be used for a check, or part of a check, if CASA approves its use for the purpose.
A check is valid for 12 months from the day on which the check is completed.

(8) However, if the check is completed less than 3 months before the day on which the check would otherwise expire (the expiry day), the check is valid for 12 months commencing at the end of the expiry day.

To complete an operator proficiency check the pilot must demonstrate that he or she is familiar with the systems, the normal and emergency flight manoeuvres, performance, fuel consumption rates, and weight and balance requirements for an aeroplane that he or she flies.
Note: A check of a pilot of a single seat aeroplane may be conducted by observation from the ground and may include review of GPS data logs, job planning and post flight records.
A contravention of subregulation (2) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.P—Manuals, logs and records
An operator must maintain a current aircraft flight manual, or another approved document, for each aeroplane used by the operator for application operations.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
An operator must:
make a record of the checking that is:
required, under Subpart 137.N, for each pilot employed by the operator; and
completed by each pilot; and
allow each pilot to examine and copy the records that relate to him or her.
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Note: Records made for this regulation must be retained: see regulation 137.255.

The operator of an aeroplane that is used for application operations must keep an aircraft maintenance record relating to the aeroplane (including a record of the time in service of each component for which that information is kept):
for at least 90 days after the aeroplane concerned is in a condition that prevents it being flown in the future; and
in a form that is suitable for, and allows access to, the information.
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane must keep each record mentioned in column 2 of an item in Table 137.255:
for at least the period mentioned in column 3 of the item; and
in a form that is suitable for, and allows access to, the information.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.

tr.td: Until the pilot ceases to be employed as a pilot by the operator
The 2 most recent records of any training undertaken by a pilot employed by the operator if: (a) the training is required under the operations manual; and (b) the record is not retained for item 2
Until the pilot ceases to be employed as a pilot by the operator
A report about an event relating to the safety of an application operation made by a pilot employed by the operator
90 days from the day on which it is made
Pilot flight, duty and rest times
15 months from the day of the most recent entry in the document
36 months from the day of the most recent entry in the document
Pilot recurrent training and annual proficiency check for Subpart 137.N
36 months from the day of the most recent entry in the document

section.heading: Maintenance record to be given to new operator

content.p: A person that ceases to be the operator of an aeroplane that is used for application operations must, if another person becomes the operator, give the aeroplane’s aircraft maintenance record, or a copy of the record, to the other person.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Subpart 137.Q—Flight duty time limitations and rest requirements
This Subpart sets out requirements about duty and rest times for a pilot who conducts application operations.

section.heading: Subpart not to affect subsection 1 of CAO 48.1

content.p: This Subpart does not affect the operation of subsection 1 of Civil Aviation Order 48.1.
The pilot must not fly more than:
1 200 hours in 365 consecutive days; or
170 hours in 28 consecutive days.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Off-duty period before and after tour of duty

content.p: Subject to subregulations (2) and (3), the pilot must not undertake duties relating to his or her employment by an operator, including being on call or planning less than:
8 hours before commencing a tour of duty; or
8 hours after completing a tour of duty of 10 hours or less; or
10 hours after completing a tour of duty of more than 10 hours.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.

No less than 8 hours after completing a tour of duty of more than 10 hours, the pilot may choose to recommence duty up to 1 hour earlier than the time required under paragraph (1)(c) if the pilot believes he or she is mentally and physically able to do so.
The pilot must not recommence duty under subregulation (2) if, in doing so, he or she would be in breach of regulation 137.275, 137.285, 137.290, 137.295 or 137.300.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
The pilot must not undertake, and a person must not require the pilot to undertake, a tour of duty that exceeds 14 hours.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
However, the pilot may extend a tour of duty in accordance with subregulation (3), (4) or (5) if:
the pilot reasonably believes he or she is mentally and physically able to do so; and
in doing so, the pilot would not be in breach of regulation 137.275, 137.280, 137.290, 137.295 or 137.300.
After the pilot has completed 14 hours of a tour of duty, he or she may extend the tour of duty by no more than 1 hour.
If, during a tour of duty, the pilot has had 3 or more consecutive hours of resting time, the pilot may extend the tour of duty by no more than the lesser of the following:
50% of the duration of the resting time;
2 hours.
If, during a tour of duty, the pilot has had 2 or more consecutive hours of sleeping time, the pilot may extend the tour of duty by no more than the lesser of the following:
the duration of the sleeping time;
3 hours.
A contravention of subregulation (1) is an offence of strict liability.
In any 14 consecutive days the pilot must have a continuous period of at least 36 hours during which he or she carries out no duties for an operator.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A person must not require the pilot to contravene subregulation (1).
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Limit on time spent on tours of duty

content.p: The pilot must not spend more than:
44 hours on tours of duty in any 3 consecutive days; or
98 hours on tours of duty in any 7 consecutive days.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
However, if:
the pilot has 1 or more periods of resting time during any of the days mentioned in subregulation (1); and
each period is 6 or more continuous hours;
the maximum amount of time for the subregulation is increased by 50% of the duration of the resting time (or the total of those resting times).
Despite subregulation (2), the maximum time for subregulation (1) is not increased if, in doing so, the pilot would be in breach of regulation 137.275, 137.280, 137.285, 137.290 or 137.300.
A person must not require the pilot to contravene subregulation (1).
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (4) is an offence of strict liability.

section.heading: Pilot to be fit for duty

content.p: The pilot must not commence an application operation if he or she is not fit for duty.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The operator of an aeroplane to be used in an application operation must not allow the pilot to commence the operation if the operator has reason to believe that the pilot is not fit for duty.
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
(3) For subregulations (1) and (2), a pilot is not fit for duty if, for example:
he or she has not had adequate rest, food or drink; or
he or she is adversely affected by a medical condition or a psychoactive substance.
Note: The expression psychoactive substances refers to alcohol, drugs and volatile solvents, but not coffee and tobacco: see clause 60 of Part 2 of the Dictionary.
In paragraph (3)(b):
medical includes psychological and psychiatric.
A contravention of subregulation (1) or (2) is an offence of strict liability.

Subpart 138.A—Preliminary
(1) This Part applies in relation to the operation of an aircraft for an aerial work operation if:
the aircraft is an aeroplane or rotorcraft; and
Part 101 does not apply to the operation of the aircraft.
Despite subregulation (1), a provision of this Part does not apply in relation to the operation of an aircraft if:
the aircraft is engaged in any of the following:
a police, national security or customs operation;
a search and rescue operation conducted by, or at the request of, a search and rescue body; and
in the circumstances, it is reasonable that the provision not apply to the operation.

Despite subregulation (1), a provision of this Part or the Part 138 Manual of Standards applies in relation to an operator of an aircraft for an aerial work operation only if the operator holds an aerial work certificate authorising that operation.

Despite subregulation (3), a provision of this Part or the Part 138 Manual of Standards applies to the operator of an aircraft for an aerial work operation whether or not the operator holds an aerial work certificate authorising that operation if the provision is expressed to so apply.
Note: See Part 137 for matters relating to aerial application operations.

section.heading: Definition of aerial work operation etc.

content.p: (1) An aerial work operation means one or more of the following (and each of the following is a kind of aerial work operation):
an external load operation;
a dispensing operation;
a task specialist operation;
an operation of a kind prescribed by the Part 138 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.
(2) An external load operation means carrying or towing a load outside an aircraft in flight and includes training for such an operation.
(3) A dispensing operation means dropping or releasing any substance or object from an aircraft in flight and includes training for such an operation.
(4) A task specialist operation means carrying out a specialised activity using an aircraft in flight and includes training for such an activity.
(5) Despite subregulation (1), an aerial work operation does not include the following:
a medical transport operation;
an external load operation involving winching a person, if the operation is conducted as part of an air transport operation;
glider towing;
a person undertaking a parachute descent;

an aerial application operation (including any external load operation undertaken as part of that operation) to apply fire retardants (including water), or oil or chemical dispersants, if the operation is conducted by a person holding a civil aviation authorisation under Part 137 to undertake the operation;
(f) any other aerial application operation;
(g) any other operation of a kind prescribed by the Part 138 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.
a change in relation to any of the following:
the location and operation of the operator’s main operating bases, including the opening or closing of main operating bases;
the operator’s key personnel;
a person authorised to carry out the responsibilities of any of the key personnel if the position holder is absent from the position or cannot carry out the responsibilities of the position;
the formal reporting lines for a managerial or operational position with safety functions and responsibilities that reports directly to any of the key personnel;
the operator’s process for making changes that relate to the safe conduct and management of the operator’s aerial work operations;
the kinds of aerial work operations the operator is authorised to conduct under the operator’s aerial work certificate;

the kind of operations involving a Class D external load conducted by the operator, including beginning to operate that kind of operation (but not including ceasing to conduct that kind of operation);

for an aerial work operator that is not required to have either a training and checking system under regulation 138.125 or a safety management system under regulation 138.140—the flight rules under which the operator conducts the operator’s aerial work operations (but not including starting operations under the visual flight rules if operations were already conducted under the instrument flight rules); or
any of the following changes in relation to the aircraft used in the operator’s aerial work operations:

the operator first starts to use an aircraft for which a pilot of the aircraft would need a type rating for the aircraft and no other aircraft is already used by the operator that requires the same type rating;
the operator first starts to use an aircraft that is in a different category of aircraft (within the meaning of Part 61) compared to the category of aircraft already used by the operator;
the operator first starts to use an aircraft that is a multi-engine aeroplane or a multi-engine rotorcraft; or
a change in relation to any of the following that does not maintain or improve, or is not likely to maintain or improve, aviation safety:
the plans, processes, procedures, programs and systems for the safe conduct and management of the operator’s aerial work operations;
the qualifications, experience and responsibilities required by the operator for any of the operator’s key personnel;
any other aeronautical or aviation safety related services provided to the operator by third parties;
any leasing or other arrangements for the supply of an aeroplane or rotorcraft used in the operator’s aerial work operations; or

a change required to be approved by CASA under these Regulations, other than a change that results in the reissue or replacement of an instrument previously issued by CASA in which the conditions or other substantive content of the instrument are unchanged.
(1) A task specialist, for an aerial work operation, means a crew member for a flight:
who carries out a function for the flight relating to the aerial work operation; and
who is not a flight crew member or an air crew member for the flight.
(2) Despite subregulation (1), a task specialist:
includes a crew member of a kind prescribed by the Part 138 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph; and
does not include a crew member of a kind prescribed by the Part 138 Manual of Standards for the purposes of this paragraph.

section.heading: Issue of Manual of Standards for Part 138

content.p: For subsection 98(5A) of the Act, CASA may issue a Manual of Standards for this Part prescribing matters:
required or permitted by these Regulations to be prescribed by the Part 138 Manual of Standards; or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Part.
Note: A Manual of Standards is a legislative instrument: see subsection 98(5AA) of the Act.
If a provision of this Part, or of the Part 138 Manual of Standards, refers to a person holding an approval under this regulation, the person may apply to CASA, in writing, for the approval.
Subject to regulation 11.055, CASA must grant the approval.
Subregulation 11.055(1B) applies to the granting of an approval under this regulation for either of the following provisions:
paragraph 138.090(2)(a);
paragraph 138.100(3)(a).
Subpart 138.B—Certification

division.heading: Requirement for certification for certain operations

section.heading: Requirement to hold aerial work certificate

content.p: A person contravenes this subregulation if:
the person conducts an aerial work operation (other than an aerial work operation covered by subregulation (2)); and
the person does not hold an aerial work certificate that authorises the person to conduct the operation.
An aerial work operation in an aircraft is covered by this subregulation if either or both of the following apply:
the operation is spotting or photography and no remuneration is received by any of the following for the operation:
the pilot;
the person mentioned in subregulation (3);
a person or organisation on whose behalf the operation is conducted;
the operation:
is conducted over land owned or occupied by the person mentioned in subregulation (3); and
is not conducted over a populous area or public gathering; and
is not an external load operation involving the carriage of a person as an external load.
The person is:
if the aircraft is required to be registered—the registered operator of the aircraft; or
otherwise—the owner of the aircraft.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
A person may apply to CASA, in writing, for an aerial work certificate.
The application must include the following:
the applicant’s name (including any operating or trading name), contact details and ABN (if any);
if the address of the applicant’s operational headquarters is different from its mailing address—the address of its operational headquarters;
if the applicant is a corporation registered in Australia that has an ACN—its ACN and the address of its registered office;
if the applicant is a corporation not registered in Australia—the place it was incorporated or formed;
the aerial work operations that the applicant proposes to conduct;

(f) a written undertaking that, if CASA issues the certificate, the organisation established by the applicant to conduct the applicant’s proposed aerial work operations (the applicant’s organisation) will:
be capable of operating in accordance with the applicant’s proposed operations manual and the civil aviation legislation; and
operate in accordance with the applicant’s proposed operations manual and the civil aviation legislation.
The application must be accompanied by:
a copy of the applicant’s proposed operations manual; and
if the applicant proposes to conduct operations mentioned in regulation 138.125—a copy of the applicant’s proposed training and checking manual; and
if the applicant proposes to conduct operations mentioned in regulation 138.140—a copy of the applicant’s proposed safety management system manual.
The application must be signed by the person appointed, or proposed to be appointed, as the chief executive officer of the applicant’s organisation.
Subject to regulation 11.055, CASA must issue the certificate if satisfied of each of the following:
the applicant’s proposed operations manual complies with regulation 138.155;
the applicant can conduct the proposed aerial work operations safely and in accordance with its operations manual and the civil aviation legislation;

(c) the organisation established, or proposed to be established, by the applicant to conduct the applicant’s proposed aerial work operations (the applicant’s organisation) is suitable to ensure that the operations can be conducted safely, having regard to the nature of the operations;
the chain of command of the applicant’s organisation is appropriate to ensure that the operations can be conducted safely;
the applicant’s organisation has a sufficient number of suitably qualified and competent personnel to conduct the operations safely;
the facilities of the applicant’s organisation are sufficient to enable the operations to be conducted safely;
the applicant’s organisation has suitable procedures and practices to control the organisation and ensure the operations can be conducted safely;
each of the key personnel appointed, or proposed to be appointed, to a position in the applicant’s organisation:
is a fit and proper person to be appointed to the position; and
has the qualifications and experience required by Division 138.B.4 for the position; and
has the qualifications and experience for the position (if any) required by the applicant’s operations manual; and
has the additional qualifications and experience (if any) required by CASA under regulation 138.120 for the position.
For paragraph (1)(b), without limiting the matters that CASA may consider, CASA must consider the following:
the applicant’s proposed:
operations manual; and
training and checking manual (if any); and
safety management system manual (if any);
whether the applicant can comply with the proposed operations manual, training and checking manual and safety management system manual;
the content of the undertaking mentioned in paragraph 138.035(2)(f);
details of, and reasons for, any suspension or cancellation of:
a civil aviation authorisation issued to the applicant; or
an equivalent authorisation issued to the applicant under the law of a foreign country; or
an equivalent authorisation issued to the applicant by a multinational aviation authority;
the suitability of the applicant’s corporate and organisational structures for the proposed operations;
any other information:
accompanying the application; or
in any other document given to CASA by the applicant for the application, including any document requested by CASA in relation to the application.
For subparagraph (1)(h)(i), the matters CASA may consider in deciding whether a person is a fit and proper person include the matters mentioned in subregulation 11.055(4).

If CASA decides to issue the certificate, CASA must determine the aerial work operations the applicant is authorised to conduct, including any limitations or conditions in relation to the aerial work operations.
The certificate must include:
the matters mentioned in subregulation (4); and
a certificate reference number determined by CASA.
If CASA issues the certificate to the applicant, CASA is taken to have also approved the applicant’s proposed:
operations manual; and
training and checking manual (if any); and
safety management system manual (if any).
Each of the following is a condition of an aerial work certificate issued to an aerial work operator:
the operator must comply with:
each provision of this Part that applies to the operator; and
each direction given to the operator, or obligation imposed on the operator, by CASA under a provision of these Regulations; and
each other provision of the civil aviation legislation that applies to the operator’s aerial work operations mentioned in the certificate;
each of the operator’s key personnel must comply with:
each provision of this Part that applies to the person; and
each direction given to the person, or obligation imposed on the person, by CASA under a provision of these Regulations; and
each other provision of the civil aviation legislation that applies to the operator’s aerial work operations mentioned in the certificate;
each vacancy in the operator’s key personnel must be:
notified to CASA within the period specified in the operator’s operations manual; and
filled within the period specified in the operator’s operations manual;
each of the operator’s personnel must comply with each provision of the civil aviation legislation that applies to the operator’s aerial work operations mentioned in the certificate;
if the operator is an individual—the individual must be the chief executive officer of the operator’s organisation;
if the operator is required by regulation 138.125 to have a training and checking system:

the positions of chief executive officer and head of training and checking may be occupied by the same person only if the operator holds an approval under regulation 138.025 for this subparagraph; and
the positions of head of operations and head of training and checking may be occupied by the same person only if the operator holds an approval under regulation 138.025 for this subparagraph;
if the operator is required by regulation 138.140 to have a safety management system:
the positions of chief executive officer and safety manager may be occupied by the same person only in an unforeseen circumstance, and only for the period mentioned in subregulation (2); and
the positions of head of operations and safety manager may be occupied by the same person only in an unforeseen circumstance, and only for the period mentioned in subregulation (2).
For subparagraphs (1)(g)(i) and (ii), the period is:
no more than 7 consecutive days for each unforeseen circumstance; or
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 138.025 for this paragraph in relation to an unforeseen circumstance—the period mentioned in the approval for the unforeseen circumstance.

section.heading: Compliance with conditions of aerial work certificates

content.p: An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if the operator contravenes a condition of its aerial work certificate.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

division.heading: Changes relating to aerial work operators

content.p: An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if the operator:
makes a change mentioned in subregulation (2); and
does not, before making the change:
amend the operator’s operations manual to reflect the change; and
give CASA written notice of the change and a copy of the amended part of the operations manual clearly identifying the change.
For the purposes of paragraph (1)(a), the changes are the following:
a change to the operator’s name (including any operating or trading name) or contact details;
if the address of the operator’s operational headquarters is different from the operator’s mailing address—a change to the address of the operator’s operational headquarters.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Application for approval of significant changes

content.p: An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator makes a significant change other than a significant change mentioned in subregulation (2) or (3); and
CASA has not approved the significant change.
An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if:

the operator makes a significant change that is the permanent appointment, or the acting appointment (for a period of greater than 35 days), as any of the operator’s key personnel of a person previously authorised to carry out the responsibilities of the position in a circumstance mentioned in subparagraph 138.155(1)(e)(iv); and
the operator does not apply to CASA for approval of the change, in accordance with subregulation (4), within 7 days after the change is made.
An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if:

the operator makes a significant change that is the permanent appointment as any of the operator’s key personnel of a person not previously authorised to carry out the responsibilities of the position in a circumstance mentioned in subparagraph 138.155(1)(e)(iv); and
the operator does not apply to CASA for approval of the change, in accordance with subregulation (4), within 3 days after the change is made.
An application for approval of a significant change must:
be in writing; and
set out the change; and
be accompanied by a copy of the part of the operator’s operations manual affected by the change, clearly identifying the change.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1), (2) or (3).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.
CASA must approve a significant change for an aerial work operator if satisfied that the requirements mentioned in subregulation 138.040(1) will continue to be met.
If CASA approves the significant change, CASA is taken to have also approved the changes to the operator’s operations manual covered by the application.

section.heading: Changes must be made in accordance with process in operations manual

content.p: An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator makes a change; and
the change is not made in accordance with the process included in the operator’s operations manual in accordance with paragraph 138.155(1)(m).
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: CASA directions relating to operations manual or key personnel

content.p: If CASA is satisfied that it is necessary in the interests of aviation safety, CASA may direct an aerial work operator to change its operations manual:
to remove particular information, procedures or instructions from the operations manual; or
to include particular information, procedures or instructions in the operations manual; or
to revise or vary the information, procedures or instructions in the operations manual.
CASA may direct an aerial work operator to remove any of the operator’s key personnel from the person’s position if satisfied that the person is not:
carrying out the responsibilities of the position; or
if the person is the chief executive officer—properly managing matters for which the person is accountable.
A direction under this regulation must:
be in writing; and
state the time within which the direction must be complied with.
An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if:
CASA gives the operator a direction under this regulation; and
the operator does not comply with the direction within the time stated in the direction.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (4).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

An aerial work operator must maintain an organisational structure that effectively manages the operator’s aerial work operations, taking into account the size, nature and complexity of the operations.

An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if any of the operator’s key personnel carries out a responsibility of the person’s position in a way that contravenes the operator’s operations manual or this Subpart.
A person commits an offence of strict liability if the person contravenes subregulation (2).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

section.heading: Key personnel cannot carry out responsibilities

content.p: An aerial work operator contravenes this subregulation if:
the operator becomes aware that any of its key personnel cannot carry out, or is likely to be unable to carry out, the person’s responsibilities for a period of longer than 30 days; and
the operator does not tell CASA of the matter mentioned in paragraph (a) within the time mentioned in subregulation (2).
For paragraph (1)(b), the time is:
if there is not another person authorised to carry out the responsibilities for all or part of the period—24 hours after the operator becomes aware of the matter; or
if there is another person authorised to carry out the responsibilities for all or part of the period—3 days after the operator becomes aware of the matter.
A person commits an offence if the person contravenes subregulation (1).
Penalty: 50 penalty units.

An aerial work operator must ensure that, before a person appointed as any of the operator’s key personnel begins to carry out the responsibilities of the position, the person has completed any training that is necessary to familiarise the person with the responsibilities.

section.heading: Responsibilities and accountabilities of chief executive officer

content.p: The chief executive officer of an aerial work operator’s organisation is responsible for the following:

ensuring that, for the safe conduct of the operator’s aerial work operations in accordance with the operator’s aerial work certificate and operations manual, and the civil aviation legislation, the operator:
has sufficient suitably experienced, qualified and competent personnel; and
has a suitable management structure; and
is adequately financed and resourced;
ensuring that the operator:
sets and maintains standards for the operations in accordance with the operator’s operations manual; and
complies with the civil aviation legislation; and
for each foreign registered aircraft (if any) used in the operations—maintains the aircraft in accordance with the law of the country in which the aircraft is registered; and
has procedures that ensure that all of the operator’s personnel understand the operator’s safety policy; and
has processes for identifying and addressing deficiencies in the operator’s aerial work operations;
if the operator is required to have a safety management system—ensuring that the operator:
implements and manages the operator’s safety management system; and
has an organisational structure that ensures that the safety manager is independent and not subject to undue influence;
establishing and regularly reviewing the operator’s safety performance indicators and targets;
ensuring that the operator’s operations manual is monitored and managed for continuous improvement;
ensuring that key personnel satisfactorily carry out the responsibilities of their positions in accordance with:
the operator’s operations manual; and
the civil aviation legislation.

The chief executive officer of an aerial work operator’s organisation is accountable to the operator and CASA for ensuring the responsibilities mentioned in subregulation (1) are carried out effectively.

section.heading: Qualifications and experience of head of operations

content.p: The head of operations of an aerial work operator must:
be qualified to pilot an aircraft in each kind of aerial work operation that the operator conducts; and

hold the pilot type rating or class rating (within the meaning of Part 61) for the type or class of aircraft that is used to conduct the greatest proportion of the operator’s aerial work operations; and
have the experience required under subregulation (2); and
have a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations; and

have sufficient safety and regulatory knowledge to enable the operator to conduct the operator’s aerial work operations safely and in accordance with its operations manual and the civil aviation legislation.
For paragraph (1)(c), the experience required is:
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 138.025 for this paragraph—the experience mentioned in paragraph (3)(a) or (b); or
if paragraph (a) does not apply—the experience mentioned in paragraphs (3)(a) and (b).
For subregulation (2), the experience is the following:
at least 300 hours flight time on an aircraft of the category used to conduct the greatest proportion of the operator’s aerial work operations;
at least 6 months experience in the conduct or management of air operations.
CASA may, by written notice given to a head of operations, or a proposed head of operations, of an aerial work operator, direct the person to undertake an assessment mentioned in subregulation (5).
For subregulation (4), the assessment:
is an assessment conducted by CASA or a person nominated by CASA to demonstrate a person’s suitability as head of operations for the operator; and
may include assessment in an aircraft or flight simulation training device.
In this regulation:
category has the meaning given by regulation 61.015.
The head of operations of an aerial work operator must safely manage the operator’s aerial work operations.
Without limiting subregulation (1), the responsibilities of the head of operations include the following:

monitoring and maintaining, and reporting to the chief executive officer on, the operator’s compliance with the provisions of the civil aviation legislation and the operator’s operations manual that apply to the operations;
setting and maintaining the operator’s standards for the operations in accordance with the operator’s operations manual;
developing, managing and maintaining the operator’s dangerous goods manual (if any);
ensuring the proper allocation and deployment of aircraft and personnel for use in the operations;
ensuring that the operator’s personnel are provided with the information and documentation necessary to properly carry out their responsibilities;
managing the maintenance and continuous improvement of the operator’s fatigue risk management system (if any);
ensuring the operator’s personnel understand the operator’s safety policy;

if the operator is required to have a training and checking system—ensuring that training and checking of the operator’s operational safety critical personnel (other than flight crew) conducted by or for the operator is conducted in accordance with the operator’s operations manual.

section.heading: Qualifications and experience of head of training and checking

content.p: This regulation applies to an aerial work operator that is required by regulation 138.125 to have a training and checking system.
The head of training and checking must:
be qualified to fly each kind of aerial work operation that the operator conducts; and
hold the pilot type or class rating (within the meaning of Part 61) for the type or class of aircraft used to conduct the greatest proportion of the operator’s aerial work operations; and
have the experience required under subregulation (3); and
have a satisfactory record in the conduct or management of air operations; and

have sufficient safety and regulatory knowledge to enable the operator to conduct the operator’s aerial work operations safely and in accordance with its operations manual and the civil aviation legislation.
For paragraph (2)(c), the experience required is:
if the operator holds an approval under regulation 138.025 for this paragraph—the experience mentioned in paragraph (4)(a) or (b); or
if paragraph (a) does not apply—the experience mentioned in paragraphs (4)(a) and (b).
For subregulation (3), the experience is the following:
at least 300 hours flight time conducting training in an aircraft of the category used to conduct the greatest proportion of the operator’s aerial work operations;
at least 6 months experience in the conduct or management of air operations.

CASA may, by written notice given to a head of training and checking, or proposed head of training and checking, of an aerial work operator, direct the person to undertake an assessment mentioned in subregulation (6).
For subregulation (5), the assessment:
is an assessment conducted by CASA or a person nominated by CASA to demonstrate suitability as head of training and checking for the operator; and
may include assessment in an aircraft or flight simulation training device.
In this regulation:
category has the meaning given by regulation 61.015.

section.heading: Responsibilities of head of training and checking

content.p: This regulation applies to an aerial work operator that is required by regulation 138.125 to have a training and checking system.
The head of training and checking must safely manage the training and checking activities of the operator for the operator’s flight crew.
Without limiting subregulation (2), the responsibilities of the head of training and checking include the following:
ensuring that the operator complies with each provision of the civil aviation legislation that relates to the qualifications, training or checking of the operator’s flight crew;
reporting to the head of operations on the operator’s compliance with the provisions mentioned in paragraph (a);
